questions.explanation: Backlog ordering reflects overall priority, which balances business value with risk, urgency, dependencies, and effort rather than value in isolation. An item that unblocks several high-value items and carries high risk therefore rises in the order even when its own value is only moderate.  Takeaway: Backlog order weighs value plus risk, dependencies, urgency, and effort.
choices: Place it near the bottom of the order because its own business value is only moderate
Place it high because ordering weighs value together with risk and dependencies, not value alone
Remove it from the backlog entirely because it is not the highest-value item by itself
Ignore its risk entirely because only raw business value should determine backlog order

questions.question: On a predictive project, internal inspection has confirmed a deliverable meets its specifications. What must still happen for the deliverable to be formally accepted, and in which process group?
questions.explanation: Confirming a deliverable meets specifications is Control Quality, which checks correctness but does not obtain sign-off. Formal acceptance by the customer or sponsor happens in Validate Scope, a Monitoring and Controlling process that follows quality inspection. Close Project or Phase finalizes the project after acceptance has already occurred, and Direct and Manage Project Work produces deliverables rather than accepting them.  Takeaway: Control Quality checks correctness; formal acceptance occurs in Validate Scope, a Monitoring and Controlling process.
choices: Nothing more is needed, since passing inspection is the same as formal acceptance
It is accepted later during Close Project or Phase in the Closing process group
The customer formally accepts it in Validate Scope, a Monitoring and Controlling process
It is accepted automatically within Direct and Manage Project Work during Executing

questions.question: A contractor finishes a stone footbridge engineered to last a century. A trainee argues it could not have been a project, because a project must be "temporary" and this bridge will stand for generations. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Temporary describes the endeavor that creates the result, not the durability of the deliverable, so building a long-lasting bridge is still a project. A long service life does not turn the one-time build into operations, and a single structure is not a program.  Takeaway: Temporary refers to the effort, not to how long the result lasts.
choices: The trainee is correct; a deliverable built to last for decades cannot be the result of a project.
It was actually a program, because a long-lasting structure must be run as related components.
"Temporary" refers to the effort of building the bridge, not to how long the finished bridge lasts, so it was a project.
It was operations, because the finished bridge will be in continuous public use by the community for many years after it opens.

questions.question: A specialty coffee roaster ships its signature house blend to the same 60 cafes on a fixed weekly cycle. Separately, it forms a small team to design and launch a brand-new canned cold-brew line for a one-time regional trade show. How are these two efforts best classified?
questions.explanation: Operations are ongoing, repetitive work that sustains the business, so the recurring weekly blend shipments are operations, while a temporary endeavor that creates a unique result is a project, which fits the one-time cold-brew launch. Treating recurring shipments as a project misreads temporary, and calling both operations ignores the unique, one-time nature of the launch.  Takeaway: Ongoing repetitive work is operations; a temporary effort with a unique result is a project.
choices: Both are projects, because each is carefully planned and delivers value the roaster's loyal customers will notice.
The weekly shipments are operations because they are ongoing and repetitive, while the cold-brew launch is a temporary, unique project.
The weekly shipments are a project because they follow a strict cycle, while operating the finished cold-brew line later is the true operations work.
Both are operations, because the roaster carries out each of them as part of running its normal everyday business.

questions.question: Emotional intelligence is often described as having four domains. Which of the following is one of them?
questions.explanation: The four domains of emotional intelligence are self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and relationship management, so relationship management is one of them. Positional authority, contract administration, and resource leveling are project or management concepts unrelated to the emotional intelligence domains.  Takeaway: The EQ domains are self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and relationship management.
choices: Positional authority
Contract administration
Resource leveling
Relationship management

questions.question: A team transitioning from predictive to adaptive work asks how the detailed scope items they used to place in a WBS now appear in Scrum. What is the best answer?
questions.explanation: In adaptive work the detailed scope is expressed as product backlog items that are ordered and refined over time, playing a role similar to decomposed scope in a WBS. The definition of done is a shared quality standard rather than the list of scope items, and the sprint goal is a single objective rather than the full scope.  Takeaway: Detailed adaptive scope lives as ordered product backlog items.
choices: They become the definition of done that applies to every single item
They become ordered items that make up the product backlog
They become the sprint goal chosen for the very first sprint
They become enterprise environmental factors for the whole project

questions.question: A Kanban team wants to understand how long items take from the moment work starts until they are done, and to spot where items pile up between states. Which pairing of metric and chart best serves these needs?
questions.explanation: Cycle time measures how long an item takes from when work begins until it is finished, and a cumulative flow diagram reveals bottlenecks by showing work accumulating between states. Velocity and burndown are iteration-based Scrum measures, so they do not target flow timing or state-by-state pile-ups the way Kanban metrics do.  Takeaway: Kanban uses cycle time and cumulative flow diagrams to study flow.
choices: Velocity for the timing and a burndown chart for the pile-ups
Cycle time for the timing and a cumulative flow diagram for the pile-ups
Capacity for the timing and a velocity chart for the pile-ups
Story points for the timing and the sprint goal for the pile-ups

questions.question: A project used two external vendor contracts alongside its internal staff, and it is now closing. What should happen regarding procurement closure?
questions.explanation: Procurement closure applies wherever procurements exist, so the two vendor contracts must be formally closed as part of closing the project. Skipping closure because internal staff did most of the work, or assuming contracts close themselves, leaves the agreements formally open.  Takeaway: Close procurements formally wherever contracts actually exist.
choices: Skip procurement closure, because most of the work was done by internal staff
Close only the internal work, since contracts close themselves when the work ends
Defer closing the contracts until a future project can reuse them
Formally close the two vendor contracts as part of closing the project

questions.question: A quality manager separates the project's quality spending into money spent to prevent and check for defects versus money spent because defects occurred. These two groups are best described as:
questions.explanation: Cost of quality divides into cost of conformance (prevention and appraisal - money spent to avoid and detect defects) and cost of nonconformance (internal and external failure - money spent because defects occurred). The other pairs are general accounting cost categories, not the cost-of-quality split.  Takeaway: Cost of quality = conformance (prevention + appraisal) versus nonconformance (internal + external failure).
choices: Cost of conformance and cost of nonconformance
Direct cost and indirect cost
Fixed cost and variable cost
Sunk cost and opportunity cost

questions.question: On a new initiative, one person secures the funding and provides executive backing, while another plans and delivers the day-to-day work. Which pairing names these roles correctly?
questions.explanation: The sponsor funds and champions the initiative, while the project manager plans and delivers it. The other pairings hand funding to people who do not provide it, such as the project manager, business analyst, or product owner, and misassign who delivers the work.  Takeaway: The sponsor funds and champions; the project manager delivers.
choices: The project manager secures the funding and backing, while the sponsor plans and delivers the day-to-day work.
The business analyst secures the funding, while the sponsor plans and delivers the day-to-day project work.
The product owner secures the funding, while the project manager provides the executive backing for the work.
The sponsor secures the funding and provides backing, while the project manager plans and delivers the work.

questions.question: Midway through development, a downstream operations team that was never consulted announces that the planned solution will break their daily workflow, forcing costly rework. Which principle does this best illustrate?
questions.explanation: A missed stakeholder means a missed requirement, and stakeholder identification is ongoing, so the operations team should have been found and engaged earlier. Freezing requirements would not have surfaced a team no one had identified, and downstream teams affected by the solution clearly are stakeholders.  Takeaway: A missed stakeholder is a missed requirement - keep identifying stakeholders throughout.
choices: Requirements should have been frozen at kickoff so that no additional needs could arise later in the project.
A stakeholder who is missed is a missed requirement, so stakeholder identification must continue throughout the project.
Downstream operations teams are not really stakeholders and can be addressed at some point after release.
The project manager should have approved the operations team's workflow personally, without any further review.

questions.question: A project runs under a fixed-price contract in a heavily regulated sector. The sponsor argues that regulation alone forces a fully predictive approach. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Contract type and regulatory setting influence the controls, documentation, and governance a project needs, but they do not by themselves dictate the development approach; suitability turns on how stable and well understood the requirements are and how much change is expected. Adaptive or hybrid delivery can operate in fixed-price or regulated contexts with appropriate governance. Claims that fixed-price always requires predictive, or that regulation always forbids or always requires adaptive, each overstate one factor.  Takeaway: Fixed-price and regulated settings do not auto-require predictive; suitability depends on requirement stability and expected change.
choices: Disagree; suitability depends on requirement stability and expected change, not the contract or regulation alone
Agree, because regulated work legally forbids any iterative or adaptive delivery method whatsoever
Agree, because a fixed-price contract removes all scope uncertainty and therefore mandates a predictive approach
Disagree, but only because regulated projects must always be delivered adaptively to satisfy the auditors

questions.question: A power-plant upgrade must be completed before a legally mandated emissions deadline that cannot be moved. The team separately notes that lawmakers might tighten the emission limits partway through the project. How are the fixed deadline and the possible rule change best classified, in that order?
questions.explanation: A known, immovable deadline is a limiting factor and therefore a constraint, while a possible future tightening of the limits is an uncertain future event and therefore a risk. Labeling both the same, or reversing which is which, misapplies the definitions of constraint and risk.  Takeaway: A fixed, known limit is a constraint; a possible future event is a risk.
choices: Both are risks, because each one depends on external decisions the team cannot control.
The fixed deadline is a constraint that limits the project, while the possible rule change is an uncertain future risk.
Both are constraints, because each one involves government regulation affecting the project.
The fixed deadline is an uncertain risk, while the possible future rule change is a constraint that firmly limits the work.

questions.question: At the end of each phase, a pharmaceutical project holds a formal review where leadership decides whether to continue to the next phase, adjust the plan, or stop the project. What is this review point called?
questions.explanation: A phase gate is a formal end-of-phase review where leadership decides whether to proceed, adjust, or stop, which matches the described checkpoint. A stand-up is a short recurring sync, a retrospective reflects on completed work, and a workaround responds to an unplanned problem, so none of those fits.  Takeaway: A phase gate is an end-of-phase go or no-go decision point.
choices: A phase gate, also known as a phase review or stage gate.
A daily stand-up held to synchronize the team each morning.
A retrospective conducted only after the project has closed.
A change control workaround applied to an unplanned problem.

questions.question: A team lead states that once the requirements document is written and signed, business analysis work is finished for the rest of the project. Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Business analysis is a set of activities - eliciting, analyzing, documenting, managing, and helping validate requirements - carried out across the whole life cycle. Documenting requirements is one activity, not the finish line, because managing changes and helping validate the solution continue afterward, so the work does not stop at sign-off or wait until deployment.  Takeaway: Business analysis runs across the whole life cycle, not just up to requirements sign-off.
choices: Accurate, because business analysis is finished the moment the requirements are documented and signed off.
Business analysis stops entirely once documentation is complete, and then it restarts only in the event that the project fails its final acceptance test.
Business analysis does not apply until after the solution has already been deployed to end users.
Not accurate, since business analysis continues across the life cycle, including managing changes and helping validate the solution.

questions.question: A build plan states, "We assume the vendor's safety certification will still be valid at installation," and also, "Only union-certified electricians may perform the wiring." How are these two statements best classified?
questions.explanation: An assumption is something taken to be true without proof, matching the belief that the certification will remain valid, while a constraint is a limiting factor, matching the union-labor requirement. Reversing the two, or forcing both into one category, misapplies the definitions.  Takeaway: Taken as true without proof is an assumption; a limiting factor is a constraint.
choices: Both are constraints, because either statement could restrict how the work is carried out.
Both are assumptions, because each is merely a statement that was written down in the plan.
The certification statement is an assumption taken as true without proof, while the union-labor rule is a limiting constraint.
The certification statement is actually a firm constraint on the work, while the union-labor rule is really just an assumption.

questions.question: On a project schedule, which of the following entries would correctly be shown with a duration of zero?
questions.explanation: A milestone is a significant point with zero duration, and receiving regulatory approval is such a point rather than work that consumes time. Installing the cluster, running acceptance testing, and developing materials are activities that each consume work periods.  Takeaway: Milestones mark significant points and carry zero duration.
choices: Install and configure the database cluster
Conduct the two-week user acceptance testing
Regulatory approval received from the authority
Develop the full set of training materials

questions.question: Which document provides detailed information about each WBS component, such as a description of the work, the responsible party, and acceptance criteria?
questions.explanation: The WBS dictionary is the companion document that gives detailed information for each WBS component, including a statement of work, the responsible organization or person, and acceptance criteria. The project charter authorizes the project, the risk register records identified risks and responses, and the stakeholder register captures stakeholder information, none of which detail the WBS elements.  Takeaway: The WBS dictionary details each WBS component's work description, owner, and acceptance criteria.
choices: The WBS dictionary
The project charter
The risk register
The stakeholder register

questions.question: In the 'three C's' of a user story, which element captures the discussion where the team and stakeholders work out the details behind the card?
questions.explanation: In the three C's, the Conversation is the ongoing discussion that works out the details behind the brief card. The Card is only the short reminder and Confirmation is the acceptance criteria; Contract is not one of the three C's at all.  Takeaway: The three C's are Card (reminder), Conversation (details), and Confirmation (acceptance criteria).
choices: Card, the brief written reminder of the story on an index card or tool
Conversation, the ongoing discussion that fleshes out the story's details
Confirmation, the acceptance criteria used to verify the story is complete
Contract, the signed agreement that locks the story's scope permanently

questions.question: Warehouse staff describe a tidy step-by-step picking procedure, but error rates suggest the real process differs from what they report. Which technique best reveals what actually happens on the floor?
questions.explanation: Observation or job shadowing shows reality versus what people say, so it exposes how picking is really done when reported and actual behavior differ. Asking again through a questionnaire just repeats the stated version, brainstorming imagines a future ideal, and an outdated manual describes neither current nor real practice.  Takeaway: Use observation or job shadowing to see real behavior versus what people say they do.
choices: A follow-up questionnaire asking the staff to restate their picking procedure.
A brainstorming session to design an ideal future picking procedure.
Observation or job shadowing of staff performing the actual picking work.
A review of the picking procedure manual written three years ago.

questions.question: A team plans to include every Must-have item in its 'MVP' so the first release will be as complete as possible. Why does this reflect a misunderstanding of MVP?
questions.explanation: An MVP is the smallest usable version that lets the team test key assumptions and gain validated learning, so equating it with all Must-have items misses the point. It is not restricted to Could-haves, it is a real usable release rather than a throwaway, and it is deliberately small rather than maximal.  Takeaway: An MVP is the smallest release that enables validated learning, not all the Must-haves bundled together.
choices: Because an MVP must contain only Could-have items and never any Must-have items
Because an MVP is the smallest version that enables validated learning, not the full set of Must-haves
Because an MVP is a throwaway prototype that is never shown to real users
Because an MVP is defined as the release with the largest possible scope

questions.question: A predictive team lead says a 'Definition of Done' cannot apply to their work because it is a Scrum-only idea. Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: The Definition of Done is a broad, shared standard for what 'complete' means. Scrum formalizes it as an artifact, but the underlying idea of a shared completion standard can be adopted in any approach, including predictive work. It is not the same as item-level acceptance criteria, and it is a quality standard rather than a schedule.  Takeaway: A shared completion standard can be used in any approach; Scrum formalizes it as the Definition of Done.
choices: Correct, a Definition of Done exists only in Scrum and never applies to predictive work
A Definition of Done is identical to acceptance criteria, so the team already has one per item
A Definition of Done is a general shared standard for completion and can be used in any approach
A Definition of Done is a fixed-date schedule, so it belongs to the plan rather than the work

questions.question: An analyst wants quick, comparable input on feature preferences from all 3,000 app users spread across many time zones. Which technique best fits?
questions.explanation: A survey gathers breadth - quick, comparable input from a very large, dispersed group - which is exactly what is needed here. Interviewing or shadowing thousands of users is impractical, and a single workshop is meant to build agreement among a manageable group, not to poll 3,000 people at once.  Takeaway: Use surveys for breadth across many respondents; interviews and observation give depth for a few.
choices: Individual one-on-one interviews conducted with all 3,000 users.
A single facilitated workshop convened for all 3,000 users at once.
A survey or questionnaire distributed across the entire user base.
Job shadowing of every user throughout a full workday.

questions.question: A stakeholder believes the sprint review exists so that leadership can formally sign off and approve the release. How should this belief be clarified?
questions.explanation: The sprint review is a working session to inspect the increment and adapt the product backlog collaboratively with stakeholders, not a formal approval or sign-off gate. Sprint planning is where the sprint goal is set, and the review is neither a private developer meeting nor a one-way status report.  Takeaway: The sprint review inspects and adapts; it is not an acceptance gate.
choices: The sprint review is a private, developer-only meeting held to plan out the next sprint's work in detail
The sprint review is a formal status meeting where the Scrum Master reports metrics to senior leadership
The sprint review is the event where the team commits to the sprint goal for the coming sprint
The sprint review is where the team and stakeholders inspect the increment and adapt the backlog, not sign off

questions.question: During refinement, the team cannot estimate a high-priority story because it depends on whether an unfamiliar third-party API can meet a strict latency target, and no one knows. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: A spike is a short, time-boxed investigation that reduces technical or functional uncertainty enough to estimate and plan. Padding the estimate hides the risk instead of resolving it, and splitting reduces size but not the underlying feasibility unknown, so the team would still be guessing. Blocking and removing the item overreacts to a knowable question.  Takeaway: When uncertainty blocks estimation, a time-boxed spike buys just enough knowledge to plan; padding or splitting does not resolve an unknown.
choices: Run a short, time-boxed spike to investigate the API before estimating the story.
Pad the story with extra points to absorb the unknown and pull it into the next sprint.
Split the story into smaller stories so each becomes small enough to estimate.
Mark the story blocked and remove it from the backlog until the vendor responds.

questions.question: Three months after a new self-service returns portal went live, the analyst is asked to determine whether it is delivering the expected benefit. Which activity best answers that question?
questions.explanation: Solution evaluation measures whether the delivered solution achieves the intended business outcomes, so the analyst compares actual performance against the target benefits. Re-running acceptance tests only confirms conformance to spec (verification), and counting delivered requirements measures output, not the value realized. Team satisfaction with the code says nothing about the benefit.  Takeaway: Solution evaluation asks whether the live solution delivers the expected benefit: outcomes, not passed tests or delivered scope.
choices: Compare the portal's actual results against the target benefits defined for it.
Re-run the acceptance tests to confirm the portal still meets its written specifications.
Survey the development team about their satisfaction with the code quality.
Count how many of the original backlog requirements were delivered.

questions.question: An auditor asks the team to show that every approved requirement has been designed, built, and tested. Which artifact is designed to demonstrate that coverage?
questions.explanation: A requirements traceability matrix records explicit trace links from each requirement through design, build, and test, which is exactly what demonstrates coverage. A product backlog orders adaptive work but does not by itself prove test coverage, and a roadmap shows direction rather than requirement-to-test links.  Takeaway: Use the RTM to prove each requirement is covered from origin through test; the backlog orders work.
choices: A requirements traceability matrix, which links each requirement through design, build, and test
A product backlog, which is the ordered list the team pulls work from each iteration
A product roadmap, which shows goals and themes with rough timing over time
A Definition of Done, which is the shared standard for calling any item complete

questions.question: Which of the following pieces of information is typically recorded in the risk register?
questions.explanation: The risk register records identified risks along with details such as their planned responses and owners. Critical-path sequencing belongs to the schedule, and an acceptance certificate is a closure record, so neither is part of the risk register.  Takeaway: The risk register holds each risk with its analysis, response, and owner.
choices: The planned response for each identified risk
The sequence of activities on the critical path
The signed customer acceptance certificate
The organization's quarterly earnings report

questions.question: A new team member asks whether the term business analysis names a single job title on the project. What is the most accurate answer?
questions.explanation: Business analysis is a set of activities rather than a fixed job title, and those activities can be performed by various people on a project. It is not the authority to fund or approve scope, which belongs to the sponsor and the business, and it is not a single early phase because the activities recur throughout the life cycle.  Takeaway: Business analysis is a set of activities, not one job title or a single early phase.
choices: It is always a single dedicated job title on the project, held full-time by exactly one designated person who reports directly to the project manager.
It is a set of activities - eliciting, analyzing, documenting, managing, and helping validate requirements - that different people may perform.
It is the authority to fund the project and to approve its overall scope and budget.
It is a one-time phase completed and closed out before the project charter is ever signed.

questions.question: An analyst finishes the business case for a proposed initiative and finds that the expected costs clearly exceed the benefits. What is the correct conclusion about the business case?
questions.explanation: A business case evaluates whether an initiative is worthwhile and can legitimately recommend not proceeding when costs outweigh benefits. It does not authorize work, which is the charter's role, and it does not remove the need for a charter.  Takeaway: A business case can legitimately recommend not proceeding.
choices: It may legitimately recommend that the organization not proceed
It must recommend proceeding, since it was formally commissioned
It automatically authorizes the project to begin regardless of the numbers
It removes the need to ever create a separate project charter

questions.question: On a Scrum Team, who is accountable for ordering the product backlog and deciding the relative value of the items in it?
questions.explanation: The product owner is accountable for the product backlog, including ordering it and deciding the value and priority of its items. The Scrum Master supports the process and the developers decide how much to pull into a sprint, but neither owns backlog value decisions.  Takeaway: The product owner orders the backlog and owns value priority.
choices: The product owner
The Scrum Master
The developers as a group
The project sponsor

questions.question: A completed customer-support platform is being handed to the IT operations team that will run and maintain it going forward. This handover is an example of...
questions.explanation: Handing the finished product to the group that will operate and maintain it is a transition, a normal part of closing. A workaround addresses an unplanned risk, a change request alters a baseline, and risk transfer shifts risk to a third party, none of which describes a planned handover.  Takeaway: Closure includes transitioning the product to operations or the customer.
choices: a workaround for an unplanned problem
a change request against the scope baseline
a transition of the product to operations
a risk response using the transfer strategy

questions.question: A municipal government replaces its paper permit process with an online system so residents can apply from home instead of visiting city hall. Viewing the project as a vehicle for change, what has it fundamentally done?
questions.explanation: A project acts as a vehicle for change by moving an organization from its current state to a desired future state through the outputs it delivers, which here is the online permit system enabling remote applications. It does not leave the current process untouched, guarantee strategic success, or eliminate the ongoing operations that sustain the new capability.  Takeaway: Projects move an organization from a current state to a desired future state.
choices: It kept the city's current permit process untouched while merely adding extra weekly status reports.
It offered the city a firm, certain guarantee that its broader digital strategy would definitely succeed.
It permanently removed any need for the city to run ongoing permit operations after go-live.
It moved the city from its current manual state to a desired future state through its output.

questions.question: A team delivers a login feature in one iteration, a search feature in the next, and a checkout feature after that, each fully usable when it is released. This pattern is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery builds the product as a series of usable additions, which matches shipping login, then search, then checkout as separate working slices. Iterative delivery would instead refine one deliverable repeatedly rather than adding distinct new features.  Takeaway: Incremental adds usable slices one after another.
choices: Iterative delivery, because a single feature is refined again and again
Big-bang delivery, because everything is released only at the very end
Predictive delivery, because the scope is fixed and never changes
Incremental delivery, because each cycle adds a new usable slice

questions.question: Without asking anyone, an interior designer adds imported marble trim and gold fixtures the client never requested, saying "it elevates the space." No change process was used. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation: Gold-plating occurs when the team adds features or polish the customer did not ask for, which describes the unrequested marble and fixtures. Scope creep comes from uncontrolled changes to requested scope, and this addition originates with the team rather than from an approved change or normal elaboration.  Takeaway: When the team adds unrequested extras, that is gold-plating.
choices: Scope creep that was introduced by the client's own repeated requests.
Gold-plating, because the team added extras the customer never requested.
An approved change that was properly made to the scope baseline.
Progressive elaboration of the project's requirements over time.

questions.question: A large organization needs many agile teams to align and plan together on a shared cadence across a longer horizon. Which of the following is a scaling framework that uses a Planning Interval for this alignment?
questions.explanation: SAFe is a framework for scaling agile across many teams, aligning them on a shared cadence using a Planning Interval. Kanban and Extreme Programming operate primarily at the single-team level, and the Daily Scrum is an event rather than a scaling framework.  Takeaway: SAFe scales multiple teams; PI stands for Planning Interval.
choices: SAFe, a scaling framework that plans across a Planning Interval
Kanban, a single-team flow method that relies on WIP limits
Extreme Programming, a single-team engineering-focused approach
The Daily Scrum, a short 15-minute event held by a team

questions.question: A CAPM candidate is asked to define a project life cycle. Which description is most accurate?
questions.explanation: A project life cycle is the series of phases a project moves through from initiation to completion. The charter authorization meeting, the post-handover operations period, and the stakeholder list are separate concepts and do not describe the life cycle.  Takeaway: A project life cycle is the set of phases from start to completion.
choices: The series of phases a project passes through from its start to its completion.
The single meeting in which the sponsor formally authorizes the project charter.
The ongoing operational period that begins after the product is handed over.
The complete list of every stakeholder who holds an interest in the project.

questions.question: A business analyst is choosing communication methods for different situations. Select the TWO situations where interactive communication is the most appropriate choice.
questions.explanation: Interactive communication suits negotiation and the real-time clarification of sensitive or easily misunderstood content, because both need immediate back and forth. Broadcasting a date to a large audience is push communication, a reference manual accessed on demand is pull communication, and a routine status report is a one-way push distribution.  Takeaway: Interactive fits negotiation and sensitive real-time clarification; push broadcasts, pull is on-demand.
choices: Negotiating a compromise between two stakeholders with directly conflicting needs.
Broadcasting a fixed go-live date to a large, geographically dispersed audience.
Clarifying a sensitive, easily misunderstood requirement in real time.
Making a large reference manual available for occasional, on-demand lookup.
Distributing a routine weekly status report to a group of executives.

questions.question: Before engaging stakeholders on a system upgrade, an analyst wants to understand the current business rules and the mistakes made on a similar past project. Which combination best fits this preparation?
questions.explanation: Document analysis of existing materials plus a lessons-learned review surfaces current business rules and known past pitfalls, which is the right groundwork before engaging people. Brainstorming with no preparation is premature, relying on executive memory is unreliable, and dismissing written records ignores a valuable source of existing rules.  Takeaway: Start with document analysis and lessons learned to understand existing rules and past pitfalls.
choices: Document analysis of existing materials together with a review of lessons learned.
A large brainstorming session held before doing any preparation at all.
A survey asking executives to recall every current business rule from memory.
Observation alone, on the belief that written records are never useful.

questions.question: A team builds a rough version of an entire dashboard, then repeatedly revisits and refines that same dashboard based on feedback until it is polished. Which term best describes this way of working?
questions.explanation: Iterative work improves the same deliverable through repeated cycles of refinement, which matches revisiting one dashboard until it is polished. Incremental work instead adds new usable slices of functionality, so it does not describe reworking a single artifact over and over.  Takeaway: Iterative refines the same thing; incremental adds new usable slices.
choices: Incremental, because each cycle delivers a brand-new, separate feature
Iterative, because the team refines the same deliverable over successive cycles
Predictive, because the design is frozen right after the first version ships
Flow-based, because there are no repeating cycles involved at all

questions.question: A project manager scoring competing vendor bids realizes one bid came from a longtime personal friend. Which action best reflects the value of fairness in the Code of Ethics?
questions.explanation: Fairness requires impartial, consistent evaluation and disclosing conflicts of interest, so scoring all bids against the same criteria and disclosing the relationship is correct. Favoring the friend, automatically rejecting the bid, or stalling the decision all fail to treat every bidder impartially.  Takeaway: Fairness means evaluating impartially against consistent criteria and disclosing conflicts.
choices: Give the friend's bid a modest edge as a reward for years of loyal friendship.
Automatically disqualify the friend's bid outright to prove there was no favoritism.
Delay the award decision indefinitely so the uncomfortable choice never has to be made.
Score every bid against the same criteria while disclosing the relationship.

questions.question: Which activity is performed during the Closing process group of a predictive project?
questions.explanation: Closing consists of the activities that finalize all work, archive project records and lessons learned, release resources, and formally close the project or phase. Decomposing scope and developing baselines are planning activities, and obtaining the customer's formal acceptance of deliverables is Validate Scope, a Monitoring and Controlling process that occurs before closure.  Takeaway: Closing finalizes activities, archives records, and formally closes the project or phase after acceptance has occurred.
choices: Decomposing the project scope into individual work packages and activities
Finalizing activities, archiving records, and formally closing the project or phase
Obtaining the customer's formal acceptance of the completed deliverables
Developing and approving the project's schedule and cost baselines

questions.question: A stakeholder asks the team to predict how much work a future sprint can hold. The Scrum Master explains the difference between velocity and capacity. Which statement is accurate?
questions.explanation: Velocity is a historical measure of how much work a team has actually completed in past sprints, while capacity reflects the effort available for the upcoming sprint given holidays, leave, and other commitments. The two are not interchangeable, and velocity is an optional forecasting aid rather than a Scrum-mandated metric.  Takeaway: Velocity is past completed work; capacity is available effort ahead.
choices: Velocity is the historical work the team has completed, while capacity is the effort available for the upcoming sprint
Velocity and capacity are simply two different names for exactly the same underlying measurement of work
Capacity is the historical work completed in the past, while velocity is the effort available for next sprint
Velocity is required by Scrum and must be formally reported to leadership after each and every sprint

questions.question: A project will redesign the employee onboarding process. The team asks who is accountable for how well the onboarding process performs overall versus who runs it each day. Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: The process owner is accountable for how well a process performs, while the process manager runs it day to day. The first pairing reverses those two roles, and the remaining options assign process accountability to people who do not hold it.  Takeaway: Process owner is accountable for the process; process manager runs it daily.
choices: The process manager is accountable for the onboarding process's overall performance, while the process owner runs it day to day.
The process owner is accountable for the onboarding process's overall performance, while the process manager runs it day to day.
The business analyst is accountable for the process, while the sponsor runs it day to day.
The project manager is accountable for the process, while the product owner runs it day to day.

questions.question: A support team uses no fixed timeboxes; instead it limits how many items can be in progress at once and pulls the next item only when capacity frees up. Which approach does this describe?
questions.explanation: Kanban is a flow-based method built on limiting work in progress and pulling new work as capacity allows, without fixed iterations. Scrum uses fixed timeboxes, Extreme Programming centers on engineering practices, and SAFe scales multiple teams, so none of those matches a pull-based flow with WIP limits.  Takeaway: Kanban is flow-based: WIP limits and pull, no fixed iterations.
choices: Scrum, because it organizes all work into fixed-length sprints
Extreme Programming, because it concentrates on engineering practices
Kanban, because it is flow-based with work-in-progress limits and a pull system
SAFe, because it coordinates many teams across a planning interval

questions.question: A hotel guest never praises a booking site for having a working checkout, but becomes very dissatisfied when checkout fails. In the Kano model, what kind of feature is a reliable checkout here?
questions.explanation: In the Kano model a must-be (basic) feature is an expected capability whose absence causes strong dissatisfaction while its presence is barely noticed, which fits a working checkout. A delighter surprises users positively, and a performance feature scales satisfaction with the amount delivered.  Takeaway: A Kano must-be feature is an expected basic; missing it dissatisfies, having it is barely noticed.
choices: A delighter, because its presence produces a surprising jump in satisfaction
A performance feature, because satisfaction rises in proportion to how much is provided
A must-be (basic) feature, because its absence causes strong dissatisfaction but its presence is expected
An indifferent feature, because guests do not care whether it is present or absent

questions.question: A developer finishing a task asks which item to work on next while the product owner is temporarily unavailable to advise. Which general heuristic best guides the choice?
questions.explanation: A common heuristic is to pull the highest-priority item that is ready, so the team keeps delivering the most valuable work that can actually be started. Choosing the easiest item, the lowest-priority item, or a random item ignores the backlog order that reflects priority.  Takeaway: Pull the highest-priority ready item next.
choices: Pick whichever item looks easiest, regardless of its position in the backlog
Pick the item sitting at the very bottom of the backlog to clear it out
Pick any item completely at random in order to avoid personal bias
Pick the highest-priority item that is ready to be worked on

questions.question: A project's critical path is 30 days. A non-critical activity that has 5 days of total float is delayed by 8 days. All else being equal, what happens to the project finish?
questions.explanation: The activity can absorb up to its 5 days of total float with no effect on the finish. The 8-day delay exceeds that float by 8 - 5 = 3 days, so the project finish slips by 3 days to 33 days. Assuming no change ignores that the delay is larger than the float, adding the full 8 days ignores the float entirely, and adding 5 days mistakes the amount of float for the amount of slip.  Takeaway: A non-critical activity delays the project only by the amount its delay exceeds its total float.
choices: No change; the project still finishes in 30 days
Delayed by 8 days; the project now finishes in 38 days
Delayed by 5 days; the project now finishes in 35 days
Delayed by 3 days; the project now finishes in 33 days

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship among the project management process groups?
questions.explanation: Process groups are logical groupings of project-management activities, not project phases. They overlap and recur throughout the life of a project or a single phase, so planning, executing, and monitoring and controlling take place repeatedly and concurrently. Treating them as one-time sequential phases, or claiming executing must fully end before monitoring can begin, misrepresents how the activities actually interact.  Takeaway: Process groups are overlapping, recurring activity categories, not sequential project phases.
choices: They are strictly sequential phases performed once in a fixed order
Monitoring and Controlling begins only after Executing has fully finished
They are categories of activities that overlap and recur across the project or a phase
Each process group runs exactly once and never repeats during the project

questions.question: While planning an adaptive project, the team relies on the company's reusable coding standards and its lessons-learned repository from past sprints. In project management terms, these company assets are classified as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Organizational process assets are the organization's internal plans, processes, templates, and knowledge bases such as coding standards and a lessons-learned repository, and the project can draw on and often tailor them. Enterprise environmental factors are conditions outside the team's direct control, such as market conditions or regulations.  Takeaway: OPAs are internal, usable assets; EEFs are external conditions.
choices: Enterprise environmental factors, because they originate outside the organization
Constraints, because they can never be tailored or adjusted by the team
Organizational process assets, because they are internal resources the project can use
Market conditions, because they mainly influence customer demand for the product

questions.question: After the schedule is approved, a stakeholder asks what the schedule baseline is used for during the rest of the project. What is its primary purpose?
questions.explanation: The schedule baseline is the approved version of the schedule used as the reference to measure and manage progress; variances are found by comparing actual dates against it, and it changes only through formal change control. It is not an informal draft, a milestone-only list, or the working-time calendar.  Takeaway: The schedule baseline is the approved schedule used to measure progress and detect variances.
choices: It is the approved schedule against which actual progress is measured to detect variances
It is an informal draft that the team updates freely whenever any date slips
It lists only the project's milestones and contains no activity-level detail
It is the same thing as the project calendar of working and non-working days

questions.question: During a retrospective, a new team member argues that being agile mainly means having no documentation and no plan at all. How should the Scrum Master best correct this view of the agile mindset?
questions.explanation: The agile mindset favors working product and responsiveness to change, but it does not eliminate planning or documentation; teams keep the planning and documentation that adds value and drop what does not. Claiming that agile bans documentation or forbids changing the plan both misstate the values.  Takeaway: Agile trims low-value planning and docs; it does not abolish them.
choices: Agile values working product and responding to change while still planning and documenting where it adds value
Agile forbids all documentation of any kind so that the team can move as fast as it possibly can on delivery
Agile requires a complete, detailed plan up front and strongly discourages ever changing it once it is set
Agile means the team works with no priorities and no order to its work

questions.question: During an adaptive project, a team assumes that showing the increment at the Sprint Review automatically constitutes formal acceptance of the deliverables. What is the correct understanding?
questions.explanation: Formal acceptance of deliverables rests with the customer, sponsor, or another authorized authority; the Sprint Review is a working session for inspecting the increment and gathering feedback, not a sign-off gate. The team demonstrating the work does not itself grant acceptance. Formal acceptance, when required by contract, governance, or organizational policy, is obtained from the authorized party rather than granted automatically by the demo.  Takeaway: A Sprint Review gathers feedback; when formal acceptance is required, it comes from an authorized authority.
choices: The Sprint Review is a formal sign-off gate that legally accepts the increment
Formal acceptance comes from the customer, sponsor, or authorized authority; the Sprint Review is for feedback
Acceptance is granted by the development team as soon as the demo finishes
No formal acceptance of deliverables is ever needed on adaptive projects

questions.question: A risk is assessed as having a high probability of occurring and a high impact if it does. What does combining these two dimensions produce?
questions.explanation: Probability and impact are combined into a rating that prioritizes the risk and drives how much attention and response it warrants. A reserve is a funding response, an owner is a person assigned to it, and a trigger is a warning sign, none of which is the product of combining probability and impact.  Takeaway: Probability plus impact yields a rating that prioritizes each risk.
choices: The risk's monetary reserve, set aside in the budget
The risk owner, who is chosen automatically from the ratings
The risk's priority rating, used to decide how much attention it needs
The risk's trigger, the event that signals it is about to occur

questions.question: A stakeholder assumes the business analyst and the project manager have the same job. Which statement best distinguishes the two?
questions.explanation: The business analyst concentrates on requirement activities such as eliciting, analyzing, and managing requirements, while the project manager focuses on delivering the project. The two are not the same role, delivery is not the analyst's job, and funding belongs to the sponsor rather than the analyst.  Takeaway: The analyst works the requirements; the project manager delivers the project.
choices: They are essentially the same role, and the two titles can be used interchangeably on every project.
The business analyst is the one who delivers the project on schedule and on budget, while the project manager writes and owns all of the project requirements.
The business analyst focuses on eliciting, analyzing, and managing requirements, while the project manager focuses on delivering the project.
The business analyst funds the project and its budget, while the project manager approves the overall project scope.

questions.question: Representatives from sales, finance, and support hold conflicting views on scope, and the analyst needs them to reach a shared, agreed set of requirements in one focused session. Which technique fits best?
questions.explanation: A facilitated workshop brings the groups together to build agreement and resolve conflict in one session, which is what a cross-department scope dispute needs. Separate surveys collect isolated opinions without reconciling them, document analysis studies existing materials, and observing one representative reveals behavior rather than resolving disagreement.  Takeaway: Use workshops to build agreement and resolve conflict among stakeholders.
choices: A facilitated requirements workshop with the three departments in the room together.
A separate anonymous survey sent individually to each of the three departments.
Silent document analysis of each department's old procedure manuals.
One-on-one observation of a single sales representative at work.

questions.question: At a growing company, one person currently handles both long-term product strategy and the day-to-day ordering of the Scrum backlog, and leadership wants to split the work into two roles. Which split is correct?
questions.explanation: A product manager typically sets overall product strategy and direction, while a product owner is a Scrum accountability focused on ordering the backlog; the precise split can vary by organization. The two are distinct rather than identical, and neither one funds the product, which is the sponsor's role.  Takeaway: Product manager equals product strategy; product owner equals a Scrum accountability that orders the backlog.
choices: The product manager sets overall product strategy and direction, while the product owner orders the backlog in Scrum.
The product owner sets the overall product strategy, while the product manager orders the sprint backlog.
Both titles carry identical duties, so splitting them changes nothing in practice.
The product manager funds the product, while the product owner is responsible for delivering it.

questions.question: A planner breaks a major deliverable into progressively smaller components until the work can be reliably estimated and assigned. What is this technique called?
questions.explanation: Decomposition is the technique of subdividing project scope and deliverables into smaller, more manageable components, and it is how the work breakdown structure and its work packages are built. Fast tracking and crashing are schedule compression techniques, and resource leveling adjusts start and finish dates to balance resource demand; none of those creates the WBS hierarchy.  Takeaway: Decomposition subdivides deliverables into smaller components to build the WBS and its work packages.
choices: Fast tracking
Crashing
Decomposition
Resource leveling

questions.question: Over a month, a client repeatedly asks a web team to "just add one more field" to a signup form, and the team keeps agreeing without updating the baseline or raising any change request. What is occurring?
questions.explanation: Scope creep is the uncontrolled expansion of scope without going through change control, which fits repeatedly accepting new fields and skipping the baseline update. Gold-plating differs because it comes from the team adding extras rather than from the customer's requests being accepted uncontrolled.  Takeaway: Uncontrolled scope growth without change control is scope creep.
choices: Gold-plating, because the team keeps piling on extra work of its own accord.
Proper progressive elaboration of the evolving form design.
Scope creep, because the scope keeps expanding without change control.
A schedule milestone that is quietly beginning to slip.

questions.question: A team wants to strengthen practices such as pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, and refactoring. Which agile approach is best known for these engineering practices?
questions.explanation: Extreme Programming is defined by disciplined engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, and refactoring. Kanban centers on flow management, Scrum on its events and accountabilities, and SAFe on scaling, so none of them is primarily an engineering-practice framework.  Takeaway: XP is the engineering-practice framework.
choices: Kanban
Scrum
SAFe
Extreme Programming

questions.question: A team ran all specification-based test cases successfully and, at a demo, users confirmed the feature genuinely solves their problem. Which statement best describes what the team accomplished?
questions.explanation: Passing the specification-based tests verifies the feature was built to spec, and users confirming it solves their problem validates it against the real need, so both were accomplished. Verification and validation are distinct but complementary activities, and both can succeed together.  Takeaway: Verify (built to spec) and validate (meets the real need) are distinct and can both succeed.
choices: Only validation, because passing spec-based tests has nothing to do with verification
Both verification and validation, since the feature was built to spec and confirmed against the real need
Only verification, because a user demo cannot contribute to validating a solution
Neither, because verification and validation can never both succeed on the same feature

questions.question: Why does identifying stakeholders matter so much to gathering complete requirements?
questions.explanation: Each stakeholder is a source of needs, so a stakeholder who is never identified leaves their requirements uncaptured. The count of stakeholders does not set the budget, later-emerging stakeholders may still raise valid needs, and identifying people does not replace the work of eliciting their requirements.  Takeaway: Identify stakeholders because each one is a source of needs; a missed one is a missed requirement.
choices: Because each identified stakeholder is a source of needs, and a missed stakeholder usually means a missed requirement.
Because the sheer number of stakeholders identified automatically sets the project's total approved budget.
Because only the stakeholders who were identified at kickoff are ever permitted to raise requirements.
Because thoroughly identifying stakeholders removes the need to elicit any requirements from them later.

questions.question: The only mobile crane your project can use is contractually reserved to another site until October 10 and cannot be released early. In planning, this is best treated as...
questions.explanation: A known, fixed limitation on the plan is a constraint, and the crane's confirmed reservation until October 10 is exactly that. It would be a risk only if the availability were uncertain, and nothing has yet gone wrong, so it is not an issue.  Takeaway: A known, fixed limitation is a constraint; uncertain availability is a risk.
choices: a risk, because the crane might still be released to you sooner
an assumption, to be confirmed only once execution actually begins
an issue, which must be escalated to the sponsor right away
a constraint, because the crane's unavailability is already known and fixed

questions.question: A budget printer meets every one of its documented specifications but offers only basic features compared with premium models. How is it best characterized?
questions.explanation: Quality is the degree to which a product fulfills its requirements and is fit for use, so a printer that meets all its specifications is high quality regardless of how many features it has. Grade is a category based on features or technical characteristics, so a deliberately basic feature set is low grade. Treating fewer features as automatically low quality, or reversing the two terms, confuses the concepts.  Takeaway: Quality means meeting requirements and fitness for use; grade is a feature category. A product can be high quality and low grade.
choices: Low quality and low grade
High quality and high grade
High quality but low grade
Low quality but high grade

questions.question: A biotech startup is building a lab-instrument interface whose requirements are expected to shift repeatedly as early users experiment, and stakeholders want to try working features every few weeks. Which approach fits best, and why?
questions.explanation: An adaptive approach is chosen when requirements are volatile and stakeholders want frequent, incremental value, both of which describe this interface. Predictive and waterfall approaches lock scope early and are ill-suited to requirements expected to change repeatedly.  Takeaway: Volatile requirements plus a need for frequent value point to an adaptive approach.
choices: Predictive, because a complete plan written up front will keep the requirements from shifting.
Waterfall, because moving through strict sequential phases will get the interface out sooner.
Adaptive, because it welcomes changing requirements and delivers usable value in short cycles.
Predictive, because delivering early working features would first require a fully frozen scope baseline.

questions.question: Project planning must balance several interdependent areas. Choose TWO items that are core planning components addressed within the project management plan. (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Core planning components such as schedule and communications are addressed in the project management plan, alongside cost, quality, risk, and resources, because these interdependent areas must be balanced together. A product advertising slogan, a customer's private financial data, and a competitor's confidential figures are not planning components of the project management plan.  Takeaway: Schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources, and communications are the core planning components.
choices: How the project schedule will be developed and controlled.
How project communications will be managed and distributed.
The final advertising slogan the finished product will use in its campaign.
The customer's personal credit score and private banking history details.
The competing vendor's confidential internal quarterly profit margins.

questions.question: A team must choose the next item and lists each item's expected value and estimated effort. They want the best return for the least work first. Which prioritization approach are they applying?
questions.explanation: Comparing each item's value against its effort to favor high value for low effort is value-versus-effort prioritization. MoSCoW sorts by obligation category and Kano classifies by satisfaction type, neither of which is a direct value-to-effort tradeoff.  Takeaway: Value-versus-effort prioritization favors high-value, low-effort items first.
choices: MoSCoW, sorting items into Must, Should, Could, and Won't categories
Kano analysis, classifying items as basic, performance, or delighter
First-in-first-out, taking whichever item was written earliest
Value-versus-effort, favoring high-value items that take relatively little effort

questions.question: An analyst draws a diagram with the new system as a single box in the center, surrounded by the external people and systems it exchanges data with, showing the inputs and outputs that cross the boundary. What is this diagram?
questions.explanation: A context diagram shows the system as a single boundary with the external entities it interacts with and the data crossing that boundary, scoping what is inside versus outside the solution. A work breakdown structure decomposes deliverables, a traceability matrix links requirements to design and tests, and a cause-and-effect diagram explores root causes.  Takeaway: A context diagram frames the system's boundary and its external interfaces, showing what is in and out of scope.
choices: A context diagram.
A work breakdown structure.
A requirements traceability matrix.
A cause-and-effect diagram.

questions.question: A team decomposes the project's deliverables into smaller and smaller components until the lowest level can be reliably estimated and assigned to an owner. What is this lowest level of the WBS called?
questions.explanation: The lowest level of the work breakdown structure is a work package, the point at which work can be reliably estimated and assigned. A milestone marks a point in time, the scope statement describes the scope narrative, and a change request proposes a baseline change, so none of those is the lowest WBS level.  Takeaway: The lowest level of the WBS is the work package.
choices: A work package.
A project milestone.
The project scope statement.
A submitted change request.

questions.question: What does the project charter formally accomplish once it is approved?
questions.explanation: An approved charter authorizes the project's existence and grants the project manager authority to apply organizational resources to the work. Detailed task durations, risk ratings, and final acceptance are captured in the schedule, the risk register, and closure records respectively, not in the charter's authorizing role.  Takeaway: The charter authorizes the project and empowers the project manager.
choices: It authorizes the project and gives the project manager authority to apply resources
It lists every detailed task along with its estimated duration
It records each identified risk with its probability and impact rating
It certifies the customer's final acceptance of the completed deliverables

questions.question: Match each quality tool to its primary use.
questions.explanation: A fishbone diagram groups candidate root causes by category, and a Pareto chart ranks defect types to expose the vital few driving most problems. A control chart tracks whether a process stays within control limits over time, a histogram displays a frequency distribution, and a scatter diagram tests correlation between two variables, so each tool answers a different question.  Takeaway: Each basic quality tool answers a distinct question: root cause, the vital few, process stability, distribution, or correlation.
pairs: Cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram
Organizing the possible root causes of a problem by category
Pareto chart
Ranking defect types to reveal the few causing most of the problems
Control chart
Judging whether a process stays within its expected variation over time
Histogram
Showing how often measured values fall into each range
Scatter diagram
Testing whether two variables are related

questions.question: During execution, a stakeholder verbally asks a team member to add a new feature to the product. Following the change management plan, what should happen first?
questions.explanation: Changes on a predictive project follow the change management plan: the request is captured formally, evaluated for impact, and approved or rejected by the defined authority, and baselines are updated only after approval. Implementing immediately bypasses that control. Baselines are approved and controlled rather than permanently frozen, so refusing all change is wrong, and updating the baseline before approval reverses the required order.  Takeaway: Log the change, assess it through integrated change control, get approval, then update baselines.
choices: The team member adds the feature immediately so the stakeholder stays satisfied with the project
The scope baseline is updated to include the feature, and approval is requested afterward
The request is refused outright because approved baselines can never be changed at all
A formal change request is logged and assessed through integrated change control before any baseline changes

questions.question: Between sprints, the product owner reorders several backlog items because a competitor released a new feature. A predictive-minded stakeholder asks which change control board approved this. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Reprioritizing and reordering the product backlog is expected, routine work owned by the product owner and does not require formal change control. Formal change requests and control boards are typical of predictive, plan-based governance; adaptive and hybrid projects can still apply formal governance where warranted, but ordinary backlog reprioritization does not go through a change control board.  Takeaway: Backlog reordering is routine PO work, not formal change control.
choices: A change control board must approve every backlog reordering before the next sprint
Reordering the backlog first requires a formal change request and an impact analysis
Only the Scrum Master may reorder the backlog, and only after obtaining sign-off
Reordering the backlog is a routine product owner activity, not formal change control

questions.question: A network has these activities (duration in days; predecessors in parentheses): A = 3 (none), B = 5 (A), C = 7 (A), D = 4 (B), E = 6 (C), F = 2 (D and E). Which is the critical path and its length?
questions.explanation: Two paths run through the network. A-B-D-F = 3 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 14 days, and A-C-E-F = 3 + 7 + 6 + 2 = 18 days. The critical path is the longest one, A-C-E-F at 18 days, which sets the shortest possible project duration. A total of 16 days for A-C-E-F is an addition slip, and attaching the correct 18-day length to A-B-D-F names the wrong chain of activities.  Takeaway: The critical path is the longest-duration path; sum each path and choose the maximum.
choices: A-B-D-F, 14 days
A-C-E-F, 16 days
A-C-E-F, 18 days
A-B-D-F, 18 days

questions.question: In a functional (hierarchical) organization, what is the project manager's typical level of authority?
questions.explanation: In a functional organization the department (functional) manager controls resources and budget, so the project manager has little or no formal authority and often only coordinates. Full PM authority is projectized, roughly equal authority is a balanced matrix, and no PM controls overall organizational strategy.  Takeaway: Functional = weakest PM authority; projectized = strongest.
choices: Little or no formal authority; the functional manager controls the resources and budget.
Full authority, with the team reporting only to the project manager.
Authority shared roughly equally with the functional manager.
Complete control over the organization's overall strategy.

questions.question: A company deploys a new CRM system. At go-live, the team asks when the project's benefits, such as higher customer retention and repeat revenue, will actually be realized. What is the most accurate answer?
questions.explanation: A project delivers an output at go-live, but benefits are the value realized as the organization actually uses that output, so many benefits accrue later during operations. Assuming all value appears instantly at go-live confuses the output with the benefit, and value delivery is the point of the project rather than an optional extra.  Takeaway: Outputs are delivered at handover, but benefits are realized as the output is used in operations.
choices: All of the benefits are fully realized the instant the system goes live at the end of the project.
The benefits are realized during the build phase, before the system is ever placed into use.
Benefits are optional extras, so a project is not really expected to deliver measurable value.
Many benefits are realized later, as the organization uses the system during ongoing operations.

questions.question: On a burnup chart, the team notices that the top scope line jumped upward midway through the release. Which event most likely caused this shift?
questions.explanation: On a burnup chart the scope line moves only when total scope changes, such as adding or removing work or re-estimating it, so an upward jump signals that scope was added. Completing items faster raises the completed-work line rather than the scope line, and merely reordering the backlog changes neither line's height.  Takeaway: The burnup scope line moves on scope change, not on progress or reordering.
choices: The team completed several backlog items faster than it had planned to
The team reordered the backlog to work on higher-priority items first
New items were added to the release scope during the release
The team began holding its Daily Scrum earlier in the day

questions.question: An event that the team never identified or planned for suddenly disrupts the project, and no response exists in the risk register. What is the appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: An unidentified, unplanned event that has occurred with no prepared response is handled with a workaround, an unplanned response created in the moment. There is no pre-approved contingency to execute because the risk was never identified, and doing nothing while the disruption continues is not acceptable.  Takeaway: Workarounds address unplanned risks; planned responses handle identified ones.
choices: Execute the pre-approved contingency response already listed for this risk
Develop a workaround, since the event was unplanned and has no prepared response
Take no action, because only identified risks may be responded to
Wait for the risk to appear in the next register update before acting

questions.question: A newly assigned project manager drafts much of the project charter and then asks whether they may sign it to authorize the project. What is correct?
questions.explanation: A project manager can help develop the charter and is responsible for integrating and delivering the work, but authorization comes from the sponsor, not from the PM signing their own charter. Drafting the document does not confer authorization, and the delivery team does not authorize the charter either.  Takeaway: The PM helps develop and delivers the charter; the sponsor authorizes it.
choices: Yes, drafting the charter gives the project manager the authority to authorize it
Yes, but only if the sponsor happens to be unavailable to sign
No, the PM may help develop the charter, but the sponsor authorizes it
No, only the delivery team is permitted to authorize the charter

questions.question: Before starting a backlog item, the developers want a clear, agreed statement of exactly what must be true for that particular item to be considered successful. What are they defining?
questions.explanation: Success criteria, often expressed as an item's acceptance criteria, state exactly what must be true for that item to be accepted as successful. Velocity is a forecasting measure, and enterprise environmental factors and organizational process assets are project inputs rather than item-level success statements.  Takeaway: Define per-item success criteria before starting the work.
choices: The team's velocity target for the current sprint
The enterprise environmental factors for the project
The item's success criteria, such as its acceptance criteria
The organizational process assets for the project

questions.question: A stakeholder confuses the product roadmap with the release plan. Which statement best distinguishes the two?
questions.explanation: A roadmap communicates direction, goals, and themes with rough timing, while a release plan specifies the scope targeted for a particular release. They are not identical, the roadmap is not a fixed-date commitment, and neither one is the backlog or a single story.  Takeaway: A roadmap shows direction over time; a release plan details the scope of a specific release.
choices: The roadmap shows direction, goals, and themes over time; the release plan details what ships in a specific release
The roadmap commits exact delivery dates; the release plan only shows vague long-term themes
They are identical documents, so either can replace the other on any project
The roadmap is the ordered backlog of stories; the release plan is a single user story

questions.question: Which document defines the process for how changes will be requested, evaluated, approved, and recorded on a predictive project?
questions.explanation: The change management plan is the component of the project management plan that describes how change requests will be submitted, evaluated, approved or rejected, and documented, including the authority that decides. The project charter authorizes the project, the lessons learned register captures knowledge gained, and the quality metrics document defines how quality is measured; none of these governs the change process.  Takeaway: The change management plan defines how change requests are submitted, evaluated, approved, and recorded.
choices: The project charter
The change management plan
The lessons learned register
The quality metrics document

questions.question: Your project depends on a specialized software license, and the vendor has not confirmed whether it will renew the license before your build phase starts. How is this best classified?
questions.explanation: Uncertainty about whether the license will be renewed in time is a risk, since it is an uncertain condition that could affect the project. A constraint would apply only if the outcome were already known and fixed rather than uncertain.  Takeaway: Uncertain availability is a risk; a known, fixed limit is a constraint.
choices: A constraint
An assumption
A risk
A milestone

questions.question: An aerospace team builds a satellite's physical bus on a fixed, plan-based schedule while developing its ground-control software in short, feedback-driven sprints. Which development approach is in use?
questions.explanation: A hybrid approach deliberately combines predictive and adaptive methods on the same project, which fits scheduling the hardware predictively while building the software in sprints. Labeling it purely predictive or purely adaptive ignores that both styles are in use at once.  Takeaway: Combining predictive and adaptive work on one project is a hybrid approach.
choices: Hybrid, because it combines predictive and adaptive methods within one project.
Purely predictive, because the overall project follows a defined schedule.
Purely adaptive, because the team is clearly running software sprints.
Iterative only, because the software is refined through repeated cycles.

questions.question: An adaptive team's release plans are constrained by a government data-privacy regulation and by the commercial database software the company has already licensed. These influences are best categorized as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Enterprise environmental factors are conditions inside or outside the organization that the team does not directly control, such as regulations and pre-existing licensed infrastructure. Organizational process assets differ because they are internal materials the project owns and can tailor, like templates and historical information.  Takeaway: Regulations and pre-existing infrastructure are EEFs, not OPAs.
choices: Enterprise environmental factors, because they are conditions the team does not directly control
Organizational process assets, because the team itself created and now fully owns them
Product backlog items, because they each describe a feature that the team must build
Definition of done, because they set the shared quality bar applied to every item

questions.question: Arrange the steps of change control in the correct order.
