questions.explanation: A change starts as a documented request so nothing is decided informally. It is logged and its impact analyzed, then routed to the change control board (or the authorized decision maker). Only approved changes update the baselines, and the decision is communicated so everyone works to the current plan. Changing baselines before approval invites scope creep.  Takeaway: Requests are documented, impact-assessed, decided by the change authority, then baselines are updated and the outcome communicated, never changed before approval.
sequence: Document the proposed change in a formal change request
Log the request and assess its impact on scope, schedule, and cost
Submit the analyzed request to the change control board for a decision
Update the affected baselines and project documents once approved
Communicate the outcome to the relevant stakeholders

questions.question: A start-up is building a mobile app in a market where customer preferences shift monthly, and the team wants to release small pieces early to learn from real users. Which project characteristic most strongly signals that an adaptive approach is a good fit?
questions.explanation: Adaptive approaches are chosen when uncertainty is high and requirements are expected to evolve, so short cycles and frequent feedback continuously refine the product. Locked, fully signed-off scope and a well-understood repeatable process instead point to a predictive approach because little change is anticipated.  Takeaway: High change and uncertainty favor adaptive; stability favors predictive.
choices: The full set of features is locked and signed off before any coding begins
A fixed-scope contract prohibits any change once the work has started
Requirements are expected to change as the team learns from real user feedback
The process is well understood and repeats the same way every cycle

questions.question: Two engineers disagree over a design choice. The project manager brings them together, has each explain the reasoning and constraints behind their position, and works with them toward a solution that satisfies both sets of concerns. Which conflict-resolution approach is this?
questions.explanation: Collaborating, or problem-solving, digs into the underlying reasoning so both parties' needs are met, producing a durable win-win. Compromising has each side concede something for a middle solution, which is not what happens here. Smoothing stresses points of agreement to keep the peace, and forcing imposes one position; neither addresses the real problem.  Takeaway: Collaborating resolves conflict by understanding both positions and meeting both sets of needs, unlike a compromise where each side concedes.
choices: Collaborating (problem-solving).
Compromising (reconciling).
Smoothing (accommodating).
Forcing (directing).

questions.question: On a predictive, plan-based project, against what does the team measure schedule and cost performance to detect variances?
questions.explanation: Predictive performance is measured against the approved, change-controlled baselines (scope, schedule, cost); a variance is the difference between actual results and the baseline. Backlog ordering, velocity, and stand-up notes are adaptive tools, not the predictive measurement reference.  Takeaway: Predictive performance is measured against approved, controlled baselines.
choices: The approved, controlled schedule and cost baselines.
The current ordering of the product backlog.
The team's most recent velocity figure.
The notes from the daily stand-up.

questions.question: Arrange the procurement management processes in order.
questions.explanation: Procurement begins with Plan Procurement Management (decide what and how to buy), then Conduct Procurements (obtain seller responses and award contracts), then Control Procurements (manage performance and the relationship during the work). Contract closeout is handled within Control Procurements and project/phase closure, not as a separate current process. Managing before awarding is the usual sequencing error.  Takeaway: Plan the buy, conduct to award, then control during the work; closeout happens within control/closure.
sequence: Plan Procurement Management
Conduct Procurements
Control Procurements

questions.question: On one project, a client keeps getting extra features slipped into scope with no change control, while, separately, a developer adds an unrequested animated theme "to impress users." What best names these two situations, in that order?
questions.explanation: Scope creep is uncontrolled scope growth without change control regardless of source, so the client-driven additions accepted without change control are scope creep. Gold-plating is the team adding extras the customer never asked for, which is exactly the developer's unrequested theme, so the two situations are not the same category.  Takeaway: Uncontrolled additions are scope creep; team-added unrequested extras are gold-plating.
choices: Both are gold-plating, because in each case extra features end up added to the product.
Both are scope creep, because in each case the scope grows beyond the approved baseline.
The client-driven additions are gold-plating, while the developer's extra theme is scope creep.
The client-driven additions are scope creep, while the developer's extra theme is gold-plating.

questions.question: An analyst needs to understand, in depth, the undocumented reasoning a single veteran claims adjuster uses to settle complex claims. Which elicitation technique fits best?
questions.explanation: An interview draws out depth and detail from one individual, which suits probing an expert's undocumented reasoning. A survey gathers breadth across many respondents rather than depth, brainstorming generates new ideas instead of capturing an existing process, and a vendor brochure does not reveal the adjuster's reasoning.  Takeaway: Use interviews for depth from an individual; use surveys for breadth across many.
choices: A broad survey emailed to the entire claims department for quick input.
A one-on-one interview with the veteran claims adjuster.
A brainstorming session to invent brand-new claim-handling ideas.
A review of the software vendor's product brochure.

questions.question: How does a directive PMO differ from a supportive PMO?
questions.explanation: A directive PMO takes control by managing projects directly (highest control); a supportive PMO offers templates, best practices, and training with low control; a controlling PMO sits between them by requiring compliance. Reversing these roles or calling them identical is wrong.  Takeaway: Supportive (low control) -> Controlling (compliance) -> Directive (runs the projects).
choices: A directive PMO manages the projects directly with high control; a supportive PMO provides templates, training, and guidance with low control.
A directive PMO only stores documents, while a supportive PMO runs the projects.
They have identical authority; the two names are interchangeable.
A supportive PMO enforces mandatory standards, while a directive PMO is purely advisory.

questions.question: A new analyst asks how business analysis differs between predictive and adaptive projects and whether the analyst controls the order of the backlog on adaptive work. Which statement is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Business analysis serves the same purpose in both approaches, understanding needs and defining requirements, but predictive baselines a specification while adaptive continuously refines a backlog, and the analyst informs priority without owning the order. It is performed in both approaches, and the mechanisms differ, so they are not identical.  Takeaway: BA has the same purpose in both approaches; only the mechanism differs, and the BA never owns backlog order.
choices: The purpose differs entirely, and the analyst personally sets the backlog order on adaptive work
Business analysis is only performed on predictive projects, so the question does not apply to adaptive work
The purpose is the same in both; predictive baselines a spec while adaptive refines a backlog, and the analyst does not own the order
Predictive and adaptive business analysis are identical in every mechanism, including formal change control on both

questions.question: Activity P has an Early Finish (EF) of day 12. Its only successor, activity Q, has an Early Start (ES) of day 18 (day-numbering where free float = min(ES of successors) - EF - 1). What is the free float of activity P?
questions.explanation: Free float = min(ES of successors) - EF - 1 = 18 - 12 - 1 = 5 days. This is how far P can slip without delaying the early start of its successor Q. Getting 6 days drops the -1 day adjustment this numbering uses, and 0 days would assume there is no gap between P finishing and Q starting, which the dates contradict.  Takeaway: Free float = earliest successor ES minus this activity's EF minus 1; it protects the successor's early start.
choices: 5 days
6 days
0 days
4 days

questions.question: A team labels 'Customer Self-Service' as a very large body of work that will be broken down into many smaller items, and labels 'Reset password' as one specific capability within it. Which labeling is correct?
questions.explanation: An epic is a large body of work that is decomposed into smaller items, while a feature is a specific capability the product offers, so the large item is the epic and the specific capability is the feature. A user story is a small slice smaller than a feature, and not every decomposable item is an epic.  Takeaway: An epic is large and gets decomposed; a feature is a single capability within it.
choices: 'Customer Self-Service' is a user story and 'Reset password' is an epic that contains it
Both are epics, since any item that can be decomposed is by definition an epic
Both are features, since any capability the product offers is called a feature
'Customer Self-Service' is an epic and 'Reset password' is a feature within it

questions.question: During refinement, a story cannot be accepted because no one can describe how it would be checked or demonstrated once built. Which INVEST characteristic is most clearly missing?
questions.explanation: INVEST calls for stories to be testable, meaning there is a clear way to confirm the story is satisfied; with no way to check or demonstrate it, that characteristic is missing. Independence concerns ordering dependencies and negotiability concerns leaving room to discuss details, neither of which is the issue described.  Takeaway: If you cannot define how to confirm a story is met, it fails the 'Testable' of INVEST.
choices: Independent, because the story relies on another story being built first
Negotiable, because the story's details were fixed too early to discuss
Valuable, because the story delivers no benefit to any user or customer
Testable, because there is no way to confirm when the story is satisfied

questions.question: A logistics team notes that IF it commits to the fuel order before month-end, the supplier MIGHT grant a bulk discount that would lower project costs. How is this best classified?
questions.explanation: A risk is a future uncertain event, and a risk with a positive effect is an opportunity, which matches a possible cost-reducing discount. It is not an issue because it has not occurred, and calling it an assumption would mean treating the discount as certain rather than uncertain.  Takeaway: An uncertain future event that could help the project is an opportunity, or positive risk.
choices: A risk, specifically an opportunity, because it is uncertain, future, and could benefit the project.
An issue, because anything that affects the project's fuel costs is a current problem to solve.
A constraint, because any matter that touches the project budget acts as a limiting factor.
An assumption, because the team is effectively counting on the discount being granted.

questions.question: A candidate asks which of the Code's four values automatically overrides the others whenever two of them appear to conflict. Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: The Code's four values are unranked, so no single value automatically overrides another and the practitioner applies judgment to the situation. (The Code states both aspirational and mandatory standards under each value.) Claiming a fixed ranking such as responsibility or honesty always winning, or deferring to whichever value the sponsor names, misstates how the values work together.  Takeaway: The four ethics values are unranked; conflicts are resolved by judgment, not a fixed hierarchy.
choices: Responsibility always outranks the other three values in any conflict.
Honesty always wins out, because telling the truth is the single highest duty.
The four values are unranked, so the practitioner applies judgment to the specific situation.
Whichever value the sponsor names first is the one that automatically takes priority.

questions.question: Resources on a project include both team resources and physical resources. Choose TWO items that are physical resources.
questions.explanation: Physical resources are the equipment, materials, facilities, and infrastructure a project uses or consumes, which describes the delivery trucks and the construction materials. The test engineer, business analyst, and sponsor are people, making them team resources rather than physical ones.  Takeaway: Physical resources are equipment and materials; people are team resources.
choices: The fleet of delivery trucks used on site
The senior test engineer assigned to the project
The steel and concrete materials for the construction
The business analyst gathering requirements
The project sponsor who approves funding

questions.question: A story, 'As a shopper, I want to pay for my order,' is too large for one iteration. The team wants to split it so the first slice still delivers usable, demonstrable value. Which split best does that?
questions.explanation: A good split is a vertical slice: each piece delivers working, demonstrable value on its own, so supporting one payment method first lets shoppers actually pay. Splitting by interface versus logic, by database versus service versus screen, or by tests versus code are horizontal or task splits whose first slice runs nothing a user can use until every layer is done.  Takeaway: Split stories into vertical slices that each deliver usable value, not horizontal layers that only work once every layer is finished.
choices: Deliver payment by saved credit card first, then add PayPal and gift cards in later slices.
Build the payment user interface in the first slice and the payment processing logic in a later slice.
Complete the database schema first, then the service layer, then the payment screen.
Write all the automated tests in the first slice and implement the feature afterward.

questions.question: A schedule's forward pass gives the critical path an early finish of day 40, but the customer has imposed a mandatory finish of day 36. Using total float = LF - EF on that path, what does this tell the project manager?
questions.explanation: Setting the late finish to the imposed date of day 36 gives total float = LF - EF = 36 - 40 = -4 days. Negative float signals that the current plan cannot meet the imposed date and that compression such as crashing or fast tracking is needed. Positive or zero float would mean the plan already meets the date, and float can indeed be negative whenever an imposed constraint is earlier than the calculated finish.  Takeaway: Negative total float means the plan cannot meet an imposed date without schedule compression.
choices: Total float is positive, so there is spare slack remaining before the imposed finish date
Total float is zero, so the current plan exactly meets the imposed finish date
Total float is negative (about -4 days), so the plan cannot meet the imposed date as scheduled
Total float can never be negative, so the imposed finish date poses no scheduling problem

questions.question: A steering committee pressures the business analyst to personally decide which of three competing features will deliver the most business value and to commit the organization to that choice. What is the analyst's most appropriate response?
questions.explanation: The analyst elicits, analyzes, and documents information to inform the decision, but business value and priority belong to the business or product decision-maker, not to the analyst. Refusing to analyze withholds the very help the analyst should give, and the project manager delivers the project rather than owning business value.  Takeaway: The analyst informs value decisions; the business or product decision-maker owns them.
choices: Accept the decision and personally own it, on the reasoning that analyzing the requirements is what makes the analyst the true owner of business value.
Refuse to provide any analysis at all, so that the committee is forced to decide entirely on its own.
Provide analysis of value, risk, and dependencies to inform the choice, while the business or product decision-maker owns the value decision.
Escalate the choice to the project manager, who holds the final authority over business value decisions.

questions.question: A team is learning Scrum terminology. Which statement correctly describes the three accountabilities on a Scrum Team?
questions.explanation: A Scrum Team consists of three accountabilities: the product owner, the Scrum Master, and the developers. A project sponsor, a business analyst, or a generic stakeholder is not one of the Scrum accountabilities, so options naming those are incorrect.  Takeaway: Scrum's three accountabilities are product owner, Scrum Master, developers.
choices: Project manager, business analyst, and quality assurance lead
Product owner, Scrum Master, and the project sponsor
Product owner, Scrum Master, and the developers
Scrum Master, the stakeholders, and the developers

questions.question: A stakeholder asks the project manager to start sending progress updates by text message. The communications management plan already specifies a weekly emailed status report for this stakeholder. What should the project manager do first?
questions.explanation: When a communications plan already defines the agreed approach, the project manager follows it and routes any needed adjustment through the normal change process. Switching methods on the spot bypasses the plan, refusing outright treats the plan as unchangeable, and escalating a routine request to the sponsor is premature.  Takeaway: When a communications plan exists, follow it and change it through change control.
choices: Immediately switch this stakeholder to text messages without taking any further steps
Ignore the request entirely, because the communications plan can never be altered
Escalate the request straight to the sponsor for a decision before doing anything
Follow the communications management plan, and use change control if a change is warranted

questions.question: A product owner proposes this acceptance criterion for a search feature: 'The search should be fast and return good results.' Why is this criterion inadequate?
questions.explanation: Good acceptance criteria are specific, unambiguous, and testable so anyone can objectively confirm the item is done, yet 'fast' and 'good results' are subjective and unmeasurable. Writing from the user's viewpoint is acceptable, the modal verb is not what weakens it, and acceptance criteria are meant to be item-specific rather than product-wide.  Takeaway: Acceptance criteria must be specific, unambiguous, and testable; 'fast' and 'good' cannot be objectively verified.
choices: It is not specific or measurable, so the team cannot objectively verify when it is met.
It is written from the user's perspective rather than the developer's perspective.
It uses the word 'should' instead of 'must,' which invalidates the criterion.
It describes a single feature rather than the entire product scope.

questions.question: In a use case for 'Withdraw Cash,' the analyst documents what happens when the account has insufficient funds so the normal path cannot continue. Which part of the use case is being written?
questions.explanation: A use case documents alternate and exception flows to describe what happens when the normal path cannot proceed, such as insufficient funds. The main success flow is the normal path, a precondition is a starting state, and the actor list names participants rather than describing a deviation.  Takeaway: Deviations from a use case's normal path are captured in its alternate and exception flows.
choices: An alternate or exception flow, which handles deviations from the main success path
The main success flow, which is the normal step-by-step path to the goal
A precondition, which is a state that must be true before the use case begins
The actor list, which names who or what interacts with the system

questions.question: A product owner writes for a single story: 'Given a valid coupon code, when the customer applies it at checkout, then the order total is reduced by the coupon amount.' What is this an example of?
questions.explanation: Specific, testable conditions written for a single backlog item, such as a Given-When-Then statement, are acceptance criteria. The Definition of Done is a broader standard applied across all items, and a business requirement states a higher-level goal rather than an item-level test.  Takeaway: Acceptance criteria are specific, testable, per-item conditions for accepting one story.
choices: Acceptance criteria, because they state specific, testable conditions for accepting one item
A Definition of Done, because they set the shared standard for every backlog item
A business requirement, because they express the outcome the organization wants
A product roadmap entry, because they show the direction of the work over time

questions.question: Ten minutes into a retailer's online flash sale, the checkout service crashes and customers cannot place orders right now. How is this best classified?
questions.explanation: An issue is a condition or event that has already happened and requires action now, which fits the checkout service that is currently down. A risk is a future, uncertain event, so it does not describe something that has already occurred.  Takeaway: Already happened is an issue; future and uncertain is a risk.
choices: A risk, because the crash could eventually reduce the sale's total revenue.
An issue, because it is a condition that has already occurred and needs resolving now.
An assumption, because the team had taken for granted that checkout would stay online.
A constraint, because the outage now limits what the project team is able to do.

questions.question: A team is contrasting iteration-based agile with flow-based Kanban. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Iteration-based agile organizes work into fixed-length timeboxes, while Kanban manages a continuous flow constrained by work-in-progress limits rather than iterations. Kanban does not impose fixed iterations and in fact measures timing through lead and cycle time, so the statements claiming otherwise are incorrect.  Takeaway: Iterations use fixed timeboxes; Kanban uses continuous flow with WIP limits.
choices: Iteration-based agile uses no timeboxes and simply pulls work continuously
Iteration-based agile organizes work into fixed-length timeboxes
Kanban requires a fixed two-week iteration for every single item
Kanban manages work as a continuous flow governed by work-in-progress limits
Kanban forbids measuring how long items take to be completed

questions.question: A tester measures finished units against defined tolerances and records which units pass or fail. This activity is an example of what?
questions.explanation: Quality control is output-focused: it inspects and measures completed deliverables against requirements to determine whether they conform, which is exactly what measuring units against tolerances does. Quality assurance instead audits the processes and standards used to create the work. Validate Scope concerns customer acceptance, and a management quality audit reviews standards rather than inspecting individual units.  Takeaway: Quality control inspects the output; quality assurance audits the process.
choices: Quality assurance, because it audits the process used to build the units
Quality control, because it inspects the output against its requirements
Validate Scope, because the customer is formally accepting the product
A management quality audit of the organization's overall standards

questions.question: During sprint planning, a manager tells the developers exactly which and how many backlog items they must complete this sprint. Why does this conflict with Scrum?
questions.explanation: In Scrum the developers decide how much work they can take on and own the resulting sprint backlog, so having a manager dictate the amount undermines their accountability. The Scrum Master facilitates rather than selects the work, and the product owner sets priority and value but does not assign individual tasks.  Takeaway: Developers choose the sprint's workload and own the sprint backlog.
choices: Because the Scrum Master is the only person who is allowed to select the sprint's items
Because the developers select how many items to pull into the sprint and own the sprint backlog
Because the product owner must personally assign each individual task to a developer
Because the sprint scope must never be discussed at all by anyone during sprint planning

questions.question: A team member is frustrated by a scheduling decision. The project manager listens closely and genuinely understands the person's viewpoint, yet keeps the decision in place. This demonstrates that empathy...
questions.explanation: Empathy is understanding another person's perspective and feelings, which does not require agreeing with them or reversing a decision. It differs from pity, and applying it is a strength rather than something to set aside for objectivity.  Takeaway: Empathy is understanding another's perspective, not agreeing with it.
choices: obliges the manager to change the decision once the feelings are understood
means understanding another's perspective without necessarily agreeing with it
is essentially the same thing as feeling pity for the team member
should be set aside so the manager can remain objective

questions.question: A predictive team assumes it must use use cases and an adaptive team assumes it must use user stories, purely because of their delivery approach. Which statement best corrects both assumptions?
questions.explanation: Both user stories and use cases can be used in predictive or adaptive work, and the right choice depends on the level of detail needed rather than the delivery approach label. They are different artifacts, a small slice versus a full interaction, and there is no rule requiring both for every requirement.  Takeaway: Pick user story or use case by the detail required, not by the predictive or adaptive label.
choices: Use cases belong only to predictive projects and user stories only to adaptive projects
User stories and use cases are the same artifact with two different names
Either can be used in either approach; the choice depends on how much detail is needed
A team must always write both a user story and a use case for every requirement

questions.question: Who is generally responsible for performing the technical activities that create the project's deliverables?
questions.explanation: The project team members carry out the hands-on activities that produce the deliverables. The PMO director, the sponsor, and the steering committee provide governance, funding, or oversight rather than performing the technical work.  Takeaway: The team performs the work that produces the deliverables.
choices: The project management office director
The project sponsor
The executive steering committee
The project team members

questions.question: In Scrum, which of the following best describes the increment?
questions.explanation: The increment is the concrete, usable output of a sprint, made up of completed work that meets the definition of done and adds to prior increments. The ordered list of everything needed is the product backlog, and the single sprint objective is the sprint goal.  Takeaway: The increment is usable, done work meeting the definition of done.
choices: The ordered list of everything the product might ever need, arranged by value
The single objective that the developers commit to for the current sprint
The 15-minute daily event in which the developers plan the coming day
The sum of usable, done work that meets the definition of done

questions.question: A team member argues that 'closing' should appear as the last phase in every project's phase list. Which correction is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Closing is a set of activities (a process group) performed to formally finish a project or phase. Whether it is named as a distinct life-cycle phase varies by organization and approach; it occurs across development approaches and is distinct from executing, where the work is carried out.  Takeaway: Closing is a process group / set of finalizing activities, not necessarily a distinct life-cycle phase.
choices: Closing is a process group / set of finalizing activities, not necessarily a distinct life-cycle phase
Closing is accurately described as the mandatory final phase of any project
Closing happens only on predictive projects and never on adaptive ones
Closing is just another label for the executing work performed near the end

questions.question: A newly hired coordinator insists, "Everything in our portfolio must share one common benefit, and every program we run is just a smaller portfolio." Which correction is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Portfolio components are selected to advance strategy and need not be related or share a single benefit, while a program is a group of related components managed for a shared benefit rather than a miniature portfolio. Claiming the two are the same, or that a portfolio's components must share one benefit, misstates both definitions.  Takeaway: A portfolio advances strategy with possibly unrelated components; a program coordinates related components for a shared benefit.
choices: The coordinator is correct on both counts, since a portfolio and a program are essentially the same structure viewed at two different sizes.
A portfolio's components must indeed all share one benefit, but a program is simply a larger portfolio rather than a smaller one.
Both statements are right about the shared benefit, although a program is more accurately described as a form of the organization's ongoing operations.
Portfolio components are chosen to advance strategy and need not share a benefit, while a program is a set of related components, not a small portfolio.

questions.question: An analyst wants quick, comparable input on feature preferences from all 8,000 members of an association, who are spread across many regions. Which technique fits best?
questions.explanation: A survey gathers breadth - quick, comparable input from a very large, dispersed group - which is exactly what polling 8,000 members needs. Interviewing or shadowing thousands of members is impractical, and a single workshop is meant to build agreement among a manageable group, not to poll a whole membership.  Takeaway: Use surveys for breadth across many respondents; interviews and observation give depth for a few.
choices: Job shadowing of every member through a full day of their activity.
Individual one-on-one interviews conducted with each of the 8,000 members.
A single facilitated workshop convened for all 8,000 members at one time.
A survey or questionnaire distributed to the entire association membership.

questions.question: A team argues about whether done should include automated tests and updated documentation, and wants one shared standard that every item must meet before it counts as complete. What are they defining?
questions.explanation: The definition of done is the shared quality standard that all items must satisfy before they count as complete, so it is where testing and documentation expectations belong. The sprint goal is a single objective and the product backlog is an ordered list, neither of which sets completion quality.  Takeaway: The definition of done is the shared completion standard for every item.
choices: The sprint goal, which is the single overarching objective set for the current sprint
The product backlog, the ordered list of all of the work items
The definition of done, the shared quality standard every item must meet
The velocity, the historical work the team completes each sprint

questions.question: Arrange the steps of planning poker relative estimation in the correct order.
questions.explanation: In planning poker the Product Owner presents and clarifies the item, each developer privately picks an estimate card, all reveal simultaneously, the highest and lowest estimators explain their reasoning, then the team discusses and re-votes until estimates converge. Private, simultaneous reveals reduce anchoring, and the discussion surfaces hidden assumptions behind the spread.  Takeaway: Planning poker reveals estimates simultaneously, then discusses the outliers and re-votes until the team converges.
sequence: The Product Owner presents and clarifies the backlog item to be estimated
Each developer privately selects an estimate card
All developers reveal their cards at the same time
The highest and lowest estimators explain their reasoning
The team discusses, then re-votes until the estimates converge

questions.question: As a new software-migration project moves into execution, the project manager gathers the team, sponsor, and key stakeholders for a kickoff meeting. What is the primary purpose of this meeting?
questions.explanation: A kickoff meeting brings the team and stakeholders together to align on goals, roles, scope, and how they will collaborate as work begins. Authorization and funding happen earlier through the charter, formal acceptance occurs at closing, and detailed risk analysis is a separate planning activity, so none is the kickoff's purpose.  Takeaway: A kickoff meeting aligns the team and stakeholders on goals, roles, and ways of working as execution starts.
choices: To obtain formal customer acceptance of the completed deliverables
To decide whether the project should be authorized and funded
To align the team, sponsor, and stakeholders on the project's goals, roles, and ways of working
To perform a detailed quantitative risk analysis for every identified work package before any work begins

questions.question: A bridge-refurbishment team completes design fully, then procurement fully, then construction, then inspection, moving to each stage only after the previous one is entirely finished, with scope fixed at the start. Which statement best describes this approach?
questions.explanation: Waterfall is a predictive pattern in which phases are executed sequentially, each starting only after the prior one finishes, with scope set early, which matches this refurbishment. It is not adaptive, since scope is fixed rather than open to late change, and running phases in sequence is not by itself a hybrid or iterative approach.  Takeaway: Waterfall is a predictive approach with strictly sequential phases and early-fixed scope.
choices: It is an adaptive approach, because the fixed sequence lets the team welcome late changes easily.
It is iterative, because each stage refines the very same deliverable over repeated cycles.
It is waterfall, a predictive pattern in which phases run strictly one after another.
It is a hybrid approach, because sequencing the phases blends predictive and adaptive methods.

questions.question: A project manager wants to compare each stakeholder's current level of engagement with the level the project actually needs from them. Which tool is designed to show that comparison?
questions.explanation: A stakeholder engagement assessment matrix plots each stakeholder's current engagement (unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading) against the level the project needs, so gaps become visible and can be planned for. The risk register, WBS dictionary, and cost baseline serve unrelated purposes.  Takeaway: Engagement assessment matrix = current vs desired engagement per stakeholder.
choices: The cost baseline, which sets the approved spending plan.
The risk register, which lists identified risks and their responses.
The WBS dictionary, which details each work package.
A stakeholder engagement assessment matrix, which maps current versus desired engagement.

questions.question: A reporting feature passes every test written against its specification, but when shown to analysts they say it does not answer the business question they actually have. In verification-and-validation terms, what happened?
questions.explanation: Verification confirms the solution was built to the specification, which the passing tests show, while validation confirms it meets the real need, which the analysts' feedback shows it does not. The two are distinct activities, so passing one while failing the other is possible.  Takeaway: Verify means built to spec; validate means it meets the real need, and they can disagree.
choices: The feature failed verification against the spec but passed validation with users
Both verification and validation clearly succeeded, so the feedback must be mistaken
Verification and validation mean the same thing, so the result is self-contradictory
The feature was verified against the spec but was not validated against the real need

questions.question: A product owner writes that a specific export-to-PDF feature must produce a file in under two seconds, while the team separately maintains a rule that all items must pass a security scan. How are these two things best classified?
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are conditions tied to one specific item, such as the export feature's two-second target, while the definition of done is a broader standard applied to every item, such as passing a security scan. Treating both as the same artifact blurs this item-specific versus increment-wide distinction.  Takeaway: Acceptance criteria are per item; the definition of done applies to all items.
choices: Both are the definition of done, since both describe quality expectations
Both are acceptance criteria, since both are testable conditions to check
The two-second target is the definition of done, while the security scan is instead the item's acceptance criteria
The two-second target is acceptance criteria; the security scan is part of the definition of done

questions.question: A scaling software firm currently has one person doing both long-range product vision and the day-to-day ordering of the Scrum backlog, and wants to describe the two distinct roles to new hires. Which description is correct?
questions.explanation: A product manager owns overall product strategy and direction, while a product owner is a Scrum accountability focused on ordering the backlog. The two roles are distinct rather than interchangeable, and neither one funds the product, which is the sponsor's role.  Takeaway: Product manager equals product strategy; product owner equals a Scrum accountability that orders the backlog.
choices: The product owner sets the multi-year product vision, while the product manager orders the Scrum backlog each sprint.
The product manager owns overall product strategy and direction, while the product owner orders the backlog in Scrum.
Both roles fund the product, differing only in their seniority and their reporting lines within the firm.
The two titles are interchangeable, so there is no real distinction between them to explain to new hires.

questions.question: A regulator on a medical-device project asks the team to prove that every approved requirement traces forward to a design element, to code, and to a passed test. Which artifact is built for this?
questions.explanation: A requirements traceability matrix records explicit forward links from each requirement to design, code, and test, which is exactly what proves coverage to a regulator. A product backlog orders work but does not by itself prove trace coverage, and a roadmap shows direction rather than requirement-to-test links.  Takeaway: Use the RTM to prove each requirement traces forward to design, build, and test.
choices: A product backlog, the ordered list of work the team pulls from during each iteration
A requirements traceability matrix linking each requirement to design, code, and test
A product roadmap, which shows goals and themes with only rough long-term timing
A Definition of Done, the shared completion standard for calling any single item done

questions.question: A predictive project team is setting up the reserves in its budget. Select the TWO statements that correctly describe contingency reserves and management reserves.
questions.explanation: Contingency reserves address identified, known-unknown risks and sit inside the cost baseline; management reserves cover unforeseen, unknown-unknown in-scope work and sit outside the baseline, needing management approval to release. The wrong options swap these definitions or merge the two funds, misstating how each reserve is planned and controlled.  Takeaway: Contingency reserves cover known risks inside the baseline; management reserves cover unknown-unknowns outside it.
choices: Contingency reserves are held to absorb the impact of risks that were not foreseen during planning.
Contingency reserves cover identified risks that remain in the plan, often called known unknowns.
Management reserves are included in the cost baseline and spent at the team's own discretion.
Management reserves are set aside for unforeseen work within scope, often called unknown unknowns.
Contingency and management reserves are simply two names for the same pool of money.

questions.question: A government agency is replacing its payroll system to comply with a newly enacted tax statute. The statutory requirements are fully documented and fixed, the technology is mature, and no change is expected once the plan is approved. Which development approach best fits, and why?
questions.explanation: A predictive, plan-based approach fits work whose scope is defined and stable up front, whose solution is well understood, and where little change is expected, so the project can be planned in detail and executed against baselines. Fixed statutory requirements and mature technology are exactly those conditions. Calling the work inherently uncertain contradicts the stated stability, and wanting frequent demonstrations is a signal for an adaptive cadence, not a valid reason to choose predictive.  Takeaway: Predictive fits stable, well-defined scope with a known solution and low expected change.
choices: Adaptive, because public-sector work must always be re-planned continuously to satisfy external oversight bodies
Predictive, because the requirements are stable, the solution is well understood, and change is unlikely
Adaptive, because any software replacement is inherently uncertain and needs frequent iterations
Predictive, because the agency director wants a working software demonstration delivered every two weeks

questions.question: On a data-warehouse project, a developer states that business analysis only happens during an early requirements phase and stops the moment coding begins. Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Business analysis is a set of activities carried out across the whole life cycle in both predictive and adaptive approaches, so it does not stop when coding starts. It is not confined to an early requirements phase, does not wait until after deployment, and is not exclusive to adaptive projects.  Takeaway: Business analysis runs across the whole life cycle in both predictive and adaptive approaches.
choices: Correct, because business analysis ends the instant coding begins on any project.
Business analysis activities continue across the whole life cycle in both predictive and adaptive approaches.
Business analysis applies only after the solution has been coded and then deployed to users.
Business analysis is performed only on adaptive projects that maintain a product backlog.

questions.question: A team asks why so much effort goes into identifying stakeholders early and repeatedly, when the requirements will be gathered later anyway. Which explanation is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Each stakeholder is a source of needs, so a stakeholder who is never identified leaves their requirements uncaptured, which is why identification is done early and repeatedly. The count of stakeholders does not set the budget, later-emerging stakeholders may still raise valid needs, and identifying people does not replace eliciting their requirements.  Takeaway: Identify stakeholders because each one is a source of needs; a missed one is a missed requirement.
choices: Thoroughly identifying stakeholders removes the need to elicit any requirements from them later on.
The number of stakeholders identified sets the project's approved budget automatically once counted.
Only the stakeholders identified at kickoff are ever permitted to submit requirements to the team.
Each stakeholder is a source of needs, so an unidentified stakeholder usually means an uncaptured requirement.

questions.question: A marine-freight team notes that IF it books cargo space before the carrier's quarter closes, the carrier MIGHT grant a loyalty rebate that would lower shipping costs. How is this best classified?
questions.explanation: A risk is a future uncertain event, and a risk with a positive effect is an opportunity, which matches a possible cost-reducing rebate. It is not an issue because it has not occurred, and calling it an assumption would treat the rebate as certain rather than uncertain.  Takeaway: An uncertain future event that could help the project is an opportunity, a positive risk.
choices: An issue, because anything at all affecting the project's shipping costs is a current problem to resolve now.
A risk, specifically an opportunity, because it is uncertain, in the future, and could benefit the project.
A constraint, because any matter that happens to touch the project budget acts as a limiting factor.
An assumption, because the team is effectively counting on the loyalty rebate being granted to them.

questions.question: A team must implement a well-defined tax-reporting rule set that is fully specified by law, unlikely to change during the project, and must be delivered as one certified release. Which approach does this situation most favor?
questions.explanation: Predictive approaches fit when requirements are stable, well understood, and unlikely to change, as with a fixed legal rule set delivered once. Signals of high volatility or unpredictable continuous arrival would instead point away from a fully predictive plan.  Takeaway: Stable, well-understood, unchanging requirements favor a predictive approach.
choices: Adaptive, because frequent scope changes are expected throughout the work
Adaptive, because the requirements are highly uncertain and volatile here
Predictive, because the requirements are stable and well understood
Kanban, because the work arrives as an unpredictable continuous flow

questions.question: A software team wants to strengthen technical discipline through pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, and frequent small releases. Which agile approach is built around these engineering practices?
questions.explanation: Extreme Programming is defined by engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, and small releases. Kanban centers on flow, Scrum on its events and accountabilities, and SAFe on scaling, so none is primarily an engineering-practice method.  Takeaway: Extreme Programming is the engineering-practice approach.
choices: Kanban
Scrum
SAFe
Extreme Programming

questions.question: A veterinary clinic sees walk-in and scheduled patients the same way every business day, year after year. The same clinic also assembles a temporary team to design and open a brand-new mobile surgery van for a single summer outreach campaign. How are these two efforts best classified?
questions.explanation: Operations are ongoing, repetitive work that sustains the business, so the recurring daily patient visits are operations, while a temporary endeavor that creates a unique result is a project, which fits the one-time outreach van. Treating routine visits as a project misreads what temporary means, and calling both operations ignores the unique, one-time nature of the van.  Takeaway: Ongoing repetitive work is operations; a temporary effort with a unique result is a project.
choices: Both are operations, because the clinic carries out each of them as an ordinary part of running its everyday business.
Both are projects, because each one is planned in careful detail and clearly matters to the animals in the clinic's care.
The daily patient visits are operations because they are ongoing and repetitive, while the outreach van is a temporary, unique project.
The daily patient visits are a project because they follow a strict daily routine, while later operating the van is the real operations work.

questions.question: A startup wants to learn whether commuters will pay for a carpool-matching app and is deciding what its first release should contain. Which choice best reflects an MVP?
questions.explanation: An MVP is the smallest usable version that lets real users test a key assumption and produce validated learning, here whether commuters will pay. It is not the full feature set, not a hidden internal prototype, and not defined by MoSCoW categories.  Takeaway: An MVP is the smallest usable release that produces validated learning.
choices: Build every planned feature first so the launch looks complete and avoids costly later rework
Release the smallest usable version that lets commuters try matching, to see if they will pay
Build a polished prototype that the team keeps internal and never shows to any real commuters
Include only the Could-have items and defer everything that has been labeled a Must-have item

questions.question: A regulator-certified avionics module has fully known, stable requirements that must not change, while a companion mobile app for it has fast-shifting requirements. A planner asks which development approach suits each. What is the best guidance?
questions.explanation: A predictive approach suits work with well-understood, stable requirements, such as the certified avionics module, while an adaptive approach suits volatile requirements, such as the shifting companion app. Forcing one approach onto both, or reversing which fits which, ignores how requirement stability drives the choice.  Takeaway: Stable, well-known requirements suit predictive; volatile requirements suit adaptive.
choices: Use adaptive for both, because iterating in short cycles always delivers faster than planning up front.
Use predictive for both, because a single consistent approach must cover the entire project.
Use predictive for the stable avionics module and adaptive for the shifting companion app.
Use adaptive for the stable module and predictive for the shifting app, to control the changes.

questions.question: An analyst is deciding whether an effort should be classified as operations rather than as a project. Choose TWO characteristics that would indicate the effort is operations. (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Operations are ongoing, repetitive work performing standard processes that sustain the business and produce consistent output, so those two traits indicate operations. A temporary endeavor, producing a unique result, and disbanding the team after a one-time deliverable are characteristics of a project rather than operations.  Takeaway: Operations are ongoing and repetitive with standard output; projects are temporary and unique.
choices: It is ongoing work that repeats to sustain the business over time.
It is a temporary endeavor with a clearly defined start and finish.
It produces a distinct, unique product, service, or result each time it runs.
It performs a standard, repeatable process that produces the same output.
It disbands its team permanently once a one-time result has been delivered.

questions.question: A junior scheduler insists that 'Closing' must be listed as the final phase in the project's phase list. Which correction is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Closing is a set of activities performed to formally complete a project or a phase, rather than a phase in its own right. It occurs across development approaches and is distinct from executing, where the deliverables are actually produced.  Takeaway: Closing is a set of finalizing activities, not a project phase.
choices: Closing is correctly described as the mandatory final phase of every single project plan
Closing is a set of activities that formally finish a project or phase, not a phase
Closing occurs only on predictive projects and is skipped on adaptive ones
Closing is simply another word for the executing work done near the end

questions.question: A survey shows customers grow steadily happier the faster a report generates and steadily unhappier the slower it is. In the Kano model, what kind of feature is report speed here?
questions.explanation: A performance feature is one where satisfaction rises or falls in proportion to how much is delivered, which matches satisfaction scaling with report speed. A must-be feature is barely noticed when present, and a delighter is an unexpected extra rather than a scaling attribute.  Takeaway: A Kano performance feature scales satisfaction up or down with the amount delivered.
choices: A must-be (basic) feature, expected and noticed mainly when it is missing
A delighter, an unexpected feature that thrills users when present
A performance feature, where satisfaction scales with how much is provided
An indifferent feature, one customers do not care about either way

questions.question: To hit a budget cap, a finance director tells the business analyst to unilaterally drop two features from the product and commit the organization to that reduced scope. What is the analyst's most appropriate response?
questions.explanation: The analyst elicits and analyzes information to inform the decision, but scope, value, and priority belong to the business or product decision-maker, with funding owned by the sponsor. Owning the cut personally oversteps the role, refusing to analyze withholds the help the analyst should give, and the project manager delivers the project rather than owning business value.  Takeaway: The analyst informs scope and value decisions; the business or product decision-maker owns them.
choices: Drop the two features at once, because analyzing the requirements makes the analyst the true owner of the scope decision.
Decline to give any analysis at all, forcing the finance director to make the cut with no supporting information.
Hand the decision to the project manager, who holds final authority over which features deliver the most business value.
Analyze the value, cost, and impact to inform the cut, but leave the scope decision to the business or product decision-maker.

questions.question: A product owner keeps a plan describing the product's features, releases, and life in the market, while the project manager keeps a separate plan describing how the scope, schedule, and cost baselines will be managed. Which document does the project manager's plan represent?
questions.explanation: The project management plan integrates the baselines and subsidiary plans and defines how the project is executed, monitored, and controlled, which is the project manager's plan here. Managing the product's features and market life belongs to the product management plan, while the business case and benefits plan justify and track value rather than govern the project's work.  Takeaway: The project management plan governs how the project runs; the product plan concerns the product itself.
choices: The product management plan, because managing the baselines is a product-level concern.
The business case, because it is what justifies the product's overall value in the market.
The benefits management plan, because it tracks the value the product ultimately delivers.
The project management plan, because it defines how the project's work is executed and controlled.

questions.question: Match each contract type to how its cost is handled.
questions.explanation: Under firm fixed price the seller carries the overrun risk; time and materials bills actual hours and materials to the buyer; cost-plus-fixed-fee reimburses costs plus a set fee; cost-plus-incentive-fee shares variances by a formula. Cost risk shifts from seller toward buyer as contracts move from fixed-price to cost-reimbursable.  Takeaway: Cost risk moves from seller to buyer as contracts shift from fixed-price to cost-reimbursable.
pairs: Firm fixed price (FFP)
The seller absorbs any cost overrun beyond the agreed price
Time and materials (T&M)
The buyer pays for the actual labor hours and materials used
Cost plus fixed fee (CPFF)
The buyer reimburses allowable costs plus a predetermined fee
Cost plus incentive fee (CPIF)
The buyer and seller share cost savings or overruns by a set formula

questions.question: A manager asks a new team member to summarize what business analysis actually consists of on a project. Which summary is best?
questions.explanation: Business analysis is a set of activities - eliciting, analyzing, documenting, managing, and helping validate requirements - performed across the life cycle. It is not the authority to fund or approve scope, which belongs to the sponsor and the business, and it is not a single one-time deliverable or a value-decision power.  Takeaway: Business analysis is a set of requirement activities, not a funding authority or a one-time document.
choices: The authority to approve the project's funding and to sign off on its final overall scope.
A set of activities that elicit, analyze, document, manage, and help validate requirements across the life cycle.
A single deliverable, namely the signed requirements document, produced once and then formally closed out.
The power to decide which of the proposed features will deliver the most business value to the organization.

questions.question: A stakeholder uses the words velocity and capacity as if they mean the same thing. How should the practitioner correctly distinguish them?
questions.explanation: Velocity measures the work a team has actually completed in past iterations, while capacity is the effort available for the upcoming iteration given leave and other commitments. The two are related but not interchangeable, and neither is merely a head count.  Takeaway: Velocity is past completed work; capacity is available effort ahead.
choices: Velocity is historical completed work per iteration; capacity is effort available next iteration
Velocity and capacity are simply two names for the identical measurement
Capacity is the historical completed work each iteration, while velocity is instead the effort available for the next iteration
Both terms simply refer to the number of people currently on the team

questions.question: A developer finishes a task and the product owner is briefly unavailable to advise on what to pick up next. Which general heuristic best guides the choice?
questions.explanation: A common heuristic is to pull the highest-priority item that is ready, so the team keeps delivering the most valuable work that can actually be started. Choosing the easiest item, the lowest item, or a random item ignores the backlog order that reflects priority.  Takeaway: Pull the highest-priority ready item next.
choices: Pick whichever item looks easiest, regardless of its position in the backlog
Pick the highest-priority item that is ready to be worked on
Pick the item at the very bottom of the backlog to clear it out
Pick an item completely at random in order to avoid any personal bias

questions.question: A high-end camera offers many advanced features but ships with numerous defects that violate its own published specifications. How is it best characterized?
questions.explanation: Quality is the degree to which a product fulfills its requirements and is fit for use, so a camera that violates its own specifications is low quality regardless of its feature count. Grade is a category based on features or technical characteristics, so a rich feature set is high grade. The product is therefore low quality but high grade; calling many features high quality confuses grade with quality.  Takeaway: Meeting requirements is quality; feature category is grade. A product can be high grade yet low quality.
choices: High quality and high grade
High quality but low grade
Low quality and low grade
Low quality but high grade

questions.question: A newly appointed project manager helped write most of the charter and now asks whether they may authorize the project by signing it themselves. What is correct?
questions.explanation: A project manager can help develop the charter and is responsible for integrating and delivering the work, but authorization comes from the sponsor rather than from the PM signing their own charter. Drafting the document does not confer authorization, and the delivery team does not authorize the charter either.  Takeaway: The PM helps develop and delivers the charter; the sponsor authorizes it.
choices: Yes, because whoever drafts the charter is entitled to authorize it
No, the PM may help develop the charter, but the sponsor authorizes it
Yes, provided the sponsor happens to be unavailable to sign it in time
No, only the delivery team is permitted to authorize the charter

questions.question: A rural bank replaces its in-person-only loan process with a mobile loan app so customers can apply from their phones instead of traveling to a branch. Viewed as a vehicle for change, what has this project fundamentally done?
questions.explanation: A project acts as a vehicle for change by moving an organization from its current state to a desired future state through the outputs it delivers, which here is the mobile loan app enabling remote applications. It does not leave the current process untouched, guarantee strategic success, or eliminate the ongoing operations that sustain the new capability.  Takeaway: Projects move an organization from a current state to a desired future state.
choices: It left the bank's existing loan process untouched while merely adding a few extra status reports.
It gave the bank a firm, certain guarantee that its wider digital strategy would surely succeed.
It permanently removed any need for the bank to run ongoing loan operations after the launch.
It moved the bank from its current manual state to a desired future state through its output.

questions.question: A business analyst is starting a large predictive insurance-claims project and wants one component that defines how requirements will be prioritized, traced, versioned, and how changes to approved requirements will be governed throughout delivery. Which component captures these decisions?
questions.explanation: The requirements management plan documents the process for how requirements will be prioritized, traced, versioned, and changed across the project. A traceability matrix records the links themselves but not the governing process, the business case justifies the investment, and the stakeholder register catalogs stakeholders; none defines how requirements are managed.  Takeaway: The requirements management plan defines the process for handling requirements, while the traceability matrix is only the record of their links.
choices: Requirements traceability matrix
Requirements management plan
Business case
Stakeholder register

questions.question: Stakeholders for a new analytics dashboard cannot describe clearly what they want, yet they give sharp, specific feedback the moment they see something concrete on screen. The analyst repeatedly builds quick, throwaway mock-ups to draw out and sharpen their requirements. Which elicitation technique is this?
questions.explanation: Prototyping draws out requirements by giving stakeholders something concrete to react to, refining throwaway mock-ups from their feedback - ideal when people cannot articulate needs abstractly. A facilitated workshop reconciles conflicting views among groups; document analysis mines existing materials; a survey collects broad, comparable input. The concrete, iterative mock-up signals prototyping.  Takeaway: Prototyping elicits hard-to-articulate requirements by having stakeholders react to concrete, throwaway mock-ups.
choices: Facilitated workshop
Prototyping
Document analysis
Structured survey

questions.question: After a well-received demo, a team member says the increment is automatically approved for release because the stakeholders liked it. Why is this conclusion questionable?
questions.explanation: Delivery readiness means the required release-scope items are Done against their acceptance criteria and completion standards, with formal acceptance where governance requires it; a demo is not itself an automatic sign-off gate. A demo is not limited to rejecting work, and roadmap dates do not by themselves determine readiness.  Takeaway: A demo is feedback, not automatic acceptance; readiness is required items Done plus any required formal sign-off.
choices: Because a demo is not automatic sign-off; readiness means required items Done against their criteria plus any needed acceptance
Because a demo session is designed only to reject an increment and can never move any of the work toward a release
Because only the delivery team, and never any of the reviewing stakeholders, is ever permitted to approve the increment
Because release readiness depends solely on whether the product roadmap's originally planned delivery dates were met

questions.question: A formal scope-change approval must be preserved as a precise, auditable record that can be referenced months later during an audit. Which communication choice best meets this need?
questions.explanation: Written communication is best when precise detail and a durable, auditable record matter, because it preserves exact wording that can be referenced later. A remembered conversation, a purged instant-message thread, and an unrecorded phone call all fail to leave a reliable, detailed record.  Takeaway: Use written communication when detail and a durable record matter.
choices: A hallway conversation with the change sponsor, summarized only from memory afterward.
A quick instant-message thread that the messaging tool automatically purges after thirty days.
Written communication that documents the approved change in detail for the record.
A phone call in which the approval is given verbally and is written down by no one.

questions.question: A business analyst moves from a predictive project to an adaptive one and asks how the requirements work changes and whether the purpose of business analysis is different. Which statement is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Business analysis serves the same purpose in both approaches, understanding needs and defining requirements, but predictive baselines a specification while adaptive continuously refines a backlog, and the analyst informs priority without owning the order. It is performed in both approaches, and the mechanisms differ, so they are not identical.  Takeaway: BA has the same purpose in both approaches; only the mechanism differs, and the BA never owns backlog order.
choices: The purpose is entirely different, and on adaptive work the business analyst personally sets the final backlog order
Business analysis is performed only on predictive projects, so it does not apply to adaptive agile work at all
The purpose is the same; predictive baselines a spec, adaptive refines a backlog, and the analyst never owns the order
The two are identical in every mechanism, including the use of the same formal change-control process on both

questions.question: An analyst completes the business case for a proposed program and finds that the projected costs far outweigh the benefits. What is the correct conclusion about the business case?
questions.explanation: A business case evaluates whether an initiative is worthwhile and can legitimately recommend not proceeding when costs outweigh benefits. It does not authorize the work, which is the charter's role, and it does not remove the need for a charter once a decision to proceed is made.  Takeaway: A business case can legitimately recommend not proceeding; the charter later authorizes the work.
choices: The business case must recommend proceeding because it was commissioned
The business case by itself authorizes the project to begin regardless
The business case removes any need to later develop a project charter
The business case may legitimately recommend not proceeding with the work

questions.question: During refinement a story reads 'As a developer, I want to refactor the logging module,' and stakeholders cannot identify any benefit it delivers to a user or customer. Which INVEST characteristic is most clearly missing?
questions.explanation: INVEST asks each story to be valuable by delivering a visible benefit to a user or customer, so an internal task with no such benefit fails that characteristic. Being unsizable or too large are different characteristics, and no ordering dependency is described here.  Takeaway: A story with no visible benefit to a user or customer fails the 'Valuable' of INVEST.
choices: Valuable, because the story delivers no visible benefit to a user or customer
Estimable, because the team is completely unable to size the refactoring work involved
Independent, because the story depends on another separate story being built first
Small, because the story is far too large to be finished within a single iteration

questions.question: Which of the following is most appropriately recorded in the risk register?
questions.explanation: The risk register records identified risks with details such as each risk's owner and planned response. The critical path belongs to the schedule, the acceptance certificate is a closure record, and the operating budget is an organizational financial document, so none of those belongs in the risk register.  Takeaway: The risk register holds each risk with its analysis, owner, and planned response.
choices: The critical path running through the project's network diagram
The customer's signed acceptance certificate for the deliverable
The organization's approved annual operating budget figures
The assigned owner and planned response for each identified risk

questions.question: Halfway through a two-week iteration, a stakeholder brings an important new request. The team uses fixed-length iterations. What is the most appropriate way to handle the timebox?
questions.explanation: In iteration-based agile the timebox length stays fixed to protect the cadence, so new work is ordered into a future iteration rather than jammed in. Lengthening or shortening the timebox, or quietly injecting work, breaks the fixed cadence the team relies on.  Takeaway: Keep the iteration length fixed; defer new work to a later iteration.
choices: Extend the current iteration until the new request is completely finished
Shorten the current iteration to force the team to wrap up early
Silently add the new request to the current iteration's committed scope
Keep the iteration length fixed and order the request into a later iteration

questions.question: Two months into a project, a company acquisition brings in a new department that will use the solution. What should the team do about stakeholder identification?
questions.explanation: Stakeholder identification is continuous, so a department that arrives through an acquisition should be added to the register when it emerges. The register is not frozen at initiation, waiting for a complaint leaves needs undiscovered, and stakeholders identified after kickoff can hold entirely valid requirements.  Takeaway: Stakeholder identification is ongoing; add new stakeholders whenever they emerge.
choices: Do nothing, because the stakeholder register is finalized during initiation and must never be changed afterward.
Wait until the new department formally complains that it was left out before adding anyone to the register.
Add the new department's representatives, because stakeholder identification is ongoing and new stakeholders can emerge at any time.
Ignore the new department, because any stakeholder identified after kickoff cannot hold a valid requirement.

questions.question: Over several weeks, an event client keeps asking the planning team to "just add one more session" to a conference agenda, and the team keeps agreeing without updating the baseline or raising any change request. What is occurring?
questions.explanation: Scope creep is the uncontrolled expansion of scope without going through change control, which fits repeatedly accepting new sessions and skipping the baseline update. Gold-plating differs because it comes from the team adding extras rather than from the customer's requests being accepted without control.  Takeaway: Uncontrolled scope growth without change control is scope creep.
choices: Gold-plating, because the team keeps piling on extra work of its own initiative.
Proper progressive elaboration of the still-evolving conference agenda.
A schedule milestone that is quietly starting to slip week by week.
Scope creep, because the scope keeps expanding without any change control.

questions.question: During a heated planning debate, a project manager makes sure every team member is heard, avoids demeaning language, and takes cultural differences among the team into account. Which value of the Code of Ethics is chiefly being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Respect involves treating people, their contributions, and their differences with consideration, which fits hearing every member and honoring cultural differences. Honesty concerns truthfulness, responsibility concerns ownership of decisions, and fairness concerns impartial, unbiased conduct, so none of those is the value shown here.  Takeaway: Treating people and their differences with consideration reflects the value of respect.
choices: Honesty, because the manager is being truthful about the project's real status.
Responsibility, because the manager is taking ownership of the project's outcomes.
Respect, because the manager treats people and their differences with consideration.
Fairness, because the manager is distributing the project's resources impartially.

questions.question: A game studio is prototyping a novel augmented-reality feature. Neither the underlying technology nor how players will react is well understood, and the team wants to test small builds with players and adjust. Which characteristic most strongly signals that an adaptive approach fits?
questions.explanation: Adaptive approaches suit high uncertainty, where the team learns by experimenting and adjusting frequently. Fixed, change-forbidding contracts and stable, repeatable processes signal that little change is expected, which points toward a predictive approach instead.  Takeaway: High uncertainty resolved by frequent experimentation favors an adaptive approach.
choices: High uncertainty in the technology and in user reactions, resolved by frequent experimentation
A binding fixed-scope contract that locks every single feature and forbids any change once the work has started
A stable, well-understood process that repeats identically for each release
A single mandated delivery at the end with no intermediate feedback allowed

questions.question: At the end of a sprint, a developer claims that demonstrating the increment at the Sprint Review by itself constitutes the customer's formal acceptance of the deliverables. What is the correct understanding?
questions.explanation: Formal acceptance of deliverables rests with the customer, sponsor, or another authorized authority, while the Sprint Review is a working session for inspecting the increment and gathering feedback rather than a sign-off gate. The development team demonstrating the work does not itself grant acceptance, and formal acceptance, when required by contract, governance, or organizational policy, comes from the authorized authority.  Takeaway: A Sprint Review gathers feedback; when formal acceptance is required, it comes from an authorized authority.
choices: The Sprint Review is a binding sign-off gate that legally accepts the increment
The development team itself accepts the increment the moment the demo concludes
Formal acceptance of deliverables is never actually required on adaptive projects
Formal acceptance rests with an authorized authority; the review is for feedback

questions.question: Which artifact combines the approved scope, schedule, and cost baselines into a single time-phased plan against which earned value performance is measured?
questions.explanation: The performance measurement baseline integrates the approved scope, schedule, and cost baselines into one time-phased plan, providing the reference against which earned value is measured. The project charter authorizes the project, the stakeholder register records stakeholder information, and the milestone list identifies significant events, none of which serves as the integrated measurement reference for earned value.  Takeaway: The performance measurement baseline integrates scope, schedule, and cost baselines for earned value measurement.
choices: The signed project charter document
The performance measurement baseline
The stakeholder engagement register
The project milestone list summary

questions.question: During qualitative analysis, a team scores a risk's probability and its impact and combines the two. What does combining these two dimensions produce?
questions.explanation: Probability and impact are combined into a rating that prioritizes the risk and drives how much attention it warrants. A reserve is a funding response, a trigger is a warning sign, and an owner is a person assigned to the risk, none of which is the direct product of combining probability and impact.  Takeaway: Probability combined with impact yields a rating that prioritizes each risk.
choices: The contingency reserve to hold in the cost baseline for it
A priority rating used to rank the risk against the others
The trigger condition that will signal the risk is emerging
The name of the risk owner responsible for its response

questions.question: For a single story about filtering search results by price, an analyst writes: 'Given products exist priced from 10 to 50 dollars, when the user sets the range to 20-40 dollars, then only products priced 20-40 dollars are shown.' What is this an example of?
questions.explanation: Specific, testable conditions written for a single item, such as this Given-When-Then statement, are acceptance criteria. The Definition of Done is a broader standard applied across all items, and a roadmap theme shows direction rather than an item-level test.  Takeaway: Acceptance criteria are specific, testable, per-item conditions for accepting one story.
choices: A Definition of Done, because it is the shared standard applied to every item in the backlog
Acceptance criteria, because they give specific, testable conditions to accept one item
