A non-functional requirement, because they set the response speed the filter must achieve
A product roadmap theme, because they show the planned direction of the work over time

questions.question: An adaptive team is told it may only write user stories because it is agile, yet one complex regulatory workflow needs every alternate and exception path documented in detail. What is the best guidance?
questions.explanation: Both user stories and use cases can be used in adaptive or predictive work, and the choice depends on the level of detail needed rather than the delivery-approach label. Use cases are not forbidden on adaptive projects, and there is no rule requiring both artifacts for every requirement.  Takeaway: Choose user story or use case by the detail required, not by the agile or predictive label.
choices: Convert the entire backlog into use cases because this one regulatory workflow is complex
Keep only user stories, since use cases are never allowed on an adaptive agile project
Use a use case for the detailed workflow and user stories elsewhere, choosing by detail needed
Write both a user story and a full use case for every requirement across the project

questions.question: A team lead lists 'Phase 2 approval obtained' on the schedule and assigns it a duration of zero. Is this appropriate?
questions.explanation: A significant point that consumes no work periods is a milestone, and obtaining a phase approval is exactly such a point, so a zero duration is correct. Not every entry needs a positive duration, an approval point is not an activity, and milestones are not limited to approvals alone.  Takeaway: A significant point consuming no work periods is correctly modeled as a zero-duration milestone.
choices: No, every schedule entry on the plan must be given some positive duration to be valid
No, an approval point should be recorded instead as a multi-day activity
Yes, but only because approvals are the one item allowed to be milestones
Yes, it marks a significant point with zero work periods, so it is a milestone

questions.question: When building a schedule network, a planner links most activities so that a successor cannot start until its predecessor finishes. Which precedence relationship is this, and why is it the common default?
questions.explanation: Finish-to-Start (FS) - the successor starts after the predecessor finishes - is by far the most common relationship because most real work is sequential. Start-to-Finish is rare, while Finish-to-Finish and Start-to-Start describe less common timing links that do not fit ordinary sequential work.  Takeaway: Finish-to-Start is the default precedence relationship: the successor begins after the predecessor finishes.
choices: Finish-to-Start, because most work naturally cannot begin until the prior work is complete
Start-to-Finish, because it is the most frequently used relationship in practice
Finish-to-Finish, because it forces both activities to end at the same moment
Start-to-Start, because it requires both activities to begin simultaneously

questions.question: During a forward pass, an activity has Early Start (ES) = day 7 and a duration of 6 work periods, using the convention EF = ES + duration - 1. What is its Early Finish (EF)?
questions.explanation: Early Finish = ES + duration - 1 = 7 + 6 - 1 = day 12. The -1 adjustment counts the first day as a full work period, so a 6-day activity that starts on day 7 finishes on day 12. Getting day 13 comes from omitting the -1 adjustment (7 + 6), which double-counts the start day.  Takeaway: EF = ES + duration - 1; the -1 accounts for counting the start day as a full period.
choices: Day 6
Day 8
Day 12
Day 13

questions.question: A stakeholder assumes the business analyst is just another name for the project manager. Which statement best distinguishes the two roles?
questions.explanation: The business analyst concentrates on requirement activities such as eliciting, analyzing, and managing requirements, while the project manager focuses on delivering the project. The two are not the same role, delivery is not the analyst's job, and funding belongs to the sponsor rather than the analyst.  Takeaway: The analyst works the requirements; the project manager delivers the project.
choices: They are essentially the same role, so the two titles can be used interchangeably on any project at all.
The business analyst delivers the project on time and budget, while the project manager writes and owns all requirements.
The business analyst secures the project's funding, while the project manager approves the overall scope and objectives.
The business analyst elicits, analyzes, and manages requirements, while the project manager focuses on delivering the project.

questions.question: A finished patient-scheduling application is being handed over to the hospital's IT operations group, who will run and support it going forward. This handover is best described as...
questions.explanation: Handing the finished product to the group that will operate and maintain it is a transition, a normal part of closing. A workaround addresses an unplanned risk, a change request alters a baseline, and risk transfer shifts risk to a third party, none of which describes a planned operational handover.  Takeaway: Closure includes transitioning the product to operations or the customer.
choices: a workaround created for an unplanned problem
a change request raised against the scope baseline
a transition of the product into ongoing operations
a risk response that transfers risk to a third party

questions.question: A component of the WBS is small enough that its cost and duration can be reliably estimated and it can be assigned to a single owner. Where does this component sit in the WBS?
questions.explanation: A work package is the work at the lowest level of the WBS, small enough that cost and duration can be reliably estimated and progress managed, which describes the component in the scenario. The top level represents the whole project or major deliverable, the WBS dictionary is a separate document that details components rather than being a WBS level, and a mid-level summary element is a parent, not the estimable lowest-level package.  Takeaway: A work package is the lowest-level WBS component where cost and duration are estimated.
choices: At the top level, representing the whole project
At the lowest level of the WBS
In the WBS dictionary rather than in the WBS itself
Between two control accounts as a mid-level summary

questions.question: A management control point where scope, schedule, and cost are integrated and compared against earned value for performance measurement is called what?
questions.explanation: A control account is the management control point at which scope, budget, and schedule are integrated and compared to earned value to measure performance; it typically groups several work packages. A work package is the estimable lowest-level element of work, a milestone is a zero-duration event, and a planning package is work within a control account that is identified but not yet decomposed into detailed work packages.  Takeaway: A control account integrates scope, schedule, and cost for earned value performance measurement.
choices: A work package
A milestone
A control account
A planning package

questions.question: While defining requirements for a new warehouse robotics system, an analyst systematically lists every point where the system must exchange data or signals with other systems, machines, and staff: the scanners it reads, the inventory database it updates, and the operators who supervise it. Which analysis technique is the analyst applying?
questions.explanation: Interface analysis identifies and details the inputs and outputs exchanged between the solution and the other systems, devices, and people it connects to. A context diagram would picture the boundary at a high level, but here the analyst is cataloging each individual interface. Gap and root cause analysis address entirely different problems.  Takeaway: Interface analysis pinpoints the specific inputs and outputs a solution exchanges with the systems, devices, and people around it.
choices: Context diagramming
Gap analysis
Interface analysis
Root cause analysis

questions.question: An industrial-design team builds a rough prototype of a single ergonomic chair, then reshapes and refines that same prototype over successive cycles as test feedback arrives, gradually improving one evolving design. Which approach is this?
questions.explanation: Iterative delivery repeatedly refines the same deliverable across successive cycles as understanding grows, which fits reshaping one evolving prototype. Incremental delivery instead ships separate usable pieces, and locking the design up front or blending two styles does not describe refining a single prototype over cycles.  Takeaway: Iterative delivery refines one evolving deliverable across repeated cycles.
choices: Incremental, because each cycle delivers a separate finished chair ready for sale.
Iterative, because the same deliverable is refined repeatedly until it is right.
Predictive, because the final chair design is locked before any prototyping begins.
Hybrid, because refining one prototype blends predictive planning with adaptive delivery.

questions.question: Call-center agents describe following a clean, standard script, but quality scores suggest the real handling differs from what the agents report. Which technique best reveals what actually happens on calls?
questions.explanation: Observation or side-by-side monitoring shows reality versus what people say, so it exposes how calls are really handled when reported and actual behavior differ. Asking again through a questionnaire just repeats the stated version, brainstorming imagines a future ideal, and an outdated manual describes neither current nor real practice.  Takeaway: Use observation or job shadowing to see real behavior versus what people say they do.
choices: Observation or side-by-side monitoring of agents handling actual live calls.
A follow-up questionnaire asking the agents to restate the script they follow.
A brainstorming session to design an ideal future call-handling script.
A review of the call-handling manual that was written several years ago.

questions.question: When an approved change forces the team to revise the schedule during Executing, which statement about the project management process groups does this best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Process groups are categories of activities, not one-time sequential phases, so they overlap and recur throughout the life of a project; revising the schedule after an approved change is Planning work performed again during Executing. Treating Planning as a single event, or requiring Monitoring and Controlling to end first, misstates how the activity groups interact, and one change does not restart the whole life cycle.  Takeaway: Process groups overlap and recur; Planning can happen again during Executing.
choices: Planning happens only once, so any later revision is not really a Planning activity
Process groups overlap and recur, so Planning activities can take place again during Executing
Monitoring and Controlling must fully finish before Planning may resume at any point
The project has restarted its entire life cycle from the beginning because a change occurred

questions.question: A water-treatment upgrade must finish before a fixed, non-negotiable court-ordered compliance date. The team separately notes that regulators might raise the required purity standard partway through the work. How are the fixed date and the possible standard change best classified, in that order?
questions.explanation: A known, immovable deadline is a limiting factor and therefore a constraint, while a possible future tightening of the purity standard is an uncertain future event and therefore a risk. Labeling both the same, or reversing which is which, misapplies the definitions of constraint and risk.  Takeaway: A fixed, known limit is a constraint; a possible future event is a risk.
choices: Both are risks, because each one depends on outside decisions the team cannot control.
Both are constraints, because each one involves a government requirement affecting the work.
The fixed date is a constraint that limits the project, while the possible standard change is an uncertain future risk.
The fixed date is an uncertain risk, while the possible future standard change is a constraint that firmly limits the work.

questions.question: An activity is estimated at 40 labor hours of effort. Two developers are assigned, they work on it in parallel, and each spends 5 hours per day on it. What is the activity's duration?
questions.explanation: Duration is the number of work periods needed: two developers sharing 40 hours do 20 hours each, and at 5 hours per day that spans 4 work days. Effort of 40 hours measures the labor consumed, which is a separate quantity from duration, so it does not answer how many work periods elapse.  Takeaway: Duration counts the work periods needed; effort measures the labor hours consumed.
choices: 40 work days, matching the total labor hours recorded
8 work days, found by dividing the 40 hours by 5
4 work days, the number of work periods the pair needs
2 work days, because effort is always halved for a pair

questions.question: Leadership asks for a one-page view of the product's goals and themes over the next three quarters, with only rough timing and no committed dates. Which artifact fits?
questions.explanation: A roadmap communicates direction, goals, and themes over time with approximate timing rather than firm dates, which is what leadership asked for. A baselined specification and a sprint backlog are different artifacts, and a fixed-date schedule commits the exact dates a roadmap deliberately avoids.  Takeaway: A roadmap shows direction, goals, and themes over time, not committed delivery dates.
choices: A product roadmap, showing direction, goals, and themes over time with rough timing
A baselined requirements specification that is kept under formal change control
A detailed sprint backlog that lists every task planned for the next iteration
A fixed-date release schedule that commits each planned feature to an exact delivery day

questions.question: A team sorts backlog items into Must, Should, Could, and Won't-have-this-time for a fixed release date. A stakeholder insists every Should-have item must ship or the release fails. What is the accurate response?
questions.explanation: In MoSCoW, Should-have items are important but not mandatory, so a release can be accepted without them when necessary. They are not equal to Must-haves, and they are eligible for the current release rather than automatically deferred.  Takeaway: In MoSCoW, Must-haves are mandatory; Should-haves are important but not required for acceptance.
choices: Correct, Should-have items are mandatory and no release can be accepted without shipping them
Should-have items are identical to Must-have items and carry exactly the same obligation
Should-have items are automatically deferred and can never ship in the current release
Should-have items are important but not mandatory, so a release can be accepted without them

questions.question: A regional hospital network is coordinating a new electronic health-records rollout, a nurse-training initiative, and a redesign of patient intake, all under one director, because integrating them delivers a smoother patient journey none of them could achieve alone. What is this grouping best called?
questions.explanation: A program is a group of related components managed in a coordinated way to gain benefits not available from managing them individually, which fits these interdependent hospital initiatives. A portfolio groups components chosen to advance strategy and they need not be related, and a single project would not contain several distinct initiatives.  Takeaway: Related components managed together for a shared benefit form a program.
choices: A portfolio, because several funded initiatives are being managed together across the entire hospital network.
A program, because related components are managed together to gain benefits not available from running them separately.
A single project, because the combined effort produces one unified patient-journey result for the whole network.
An operation, because the coordinated work supports the network's ongoing day-to-day patient services.

questions.question: A newly assigned team member insists that being agile means the team should never plan and should just start coding immediately. How should the agile practitioner best reframe this?
questions.explanation: The agile mindset keeps planning but performs it continuously and just in time rather than exhaustively up front, so plans adapt as the team learns. Claiming agile forbids planning or fixes a single unchangeable plan both misstate the mindset.  Takeaway: Agile plans continuously and just in time, not never and not only once.
choices: Agile requires one complete, detailed plan up front that is never revised afterward
Agile still plans, but planning is continuous and done just in time as learning grows
Agile bans planning entirely so the team can maximize its raw coding speed
Agile plans only once the product is fully built and already shipped to users

questions.question: A project was delivered entirely by internal staff, with no external contracts of any kind, and it is now closing. What is correct regarding procurement closure?
questions.explanation: Procurement closure applies only where procurements exist, and this project used no external contracts, so there is nothing to close under it. Performing it anyway, or manufacturing a placeholder contract just to trigger it, adds work with no procurement to justify it.  Takeaway: Procurement closure applies only where procurements actually exist.
choices: Perform full procurement closure anyway, as it is mandatory on every project
There are no procurements to close, so procurement closure does not apply
Open a placeholder contract solely so procurement closure can be performed
Defer procurement closure to a later project that may add vendor contracts

questions.question: A product owner is deciding the order of the backlog and asks which factors legitimately raise an item's priority. Which TWO factors appropriately increase an item's priority? (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Backlog priority rises with drivers such as high risk worth tackling early and dependencies that unblock other high-value work. Alphabetical order, personal preference, and description length are not legitimate drivers of business priority.  Takeaway: Risk and unblocking dependencies legitimately raise backlog priority; trivia does not.
choices: The item carries high risk that is better addressed early
The item's title happens to come first alphabetically
The item unblocks several other high-value items
The developer assigned to it simply prefers to do it first
The item has the longest, most detailed description of any item

questions.question: What is the key difference between pull communication and push communication?
questions.explanation: Pull communication places information in a repository (wiki, portal, knowledge base) that recipients retrieve on demand, suited to large audiences and reference material; push sends information out to specific recipients (email, report, dashboard) for broad awareness. Push does not confirm understanding, and neither is tied to a single medium.  Takeaway: Pull = recipients retrieve on demand; push = sender distributes to recipients.
choices: In pull communication, recipients access the information on their own when they need it; in push, the sender distributes it directly to specific recipients.
Pull and push are interchangeable terms for the same distribution method.
Pull communication is always face-to-face, while push communication is always written.
Push communication guarantees that each recipient has read and understood the message.

questions.question: A candidate asks whether the current PMI Code of Ethics ranks its four values so that one always wins whenever two of them seem to conflict. Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: The current Code's four values are unranked, so no single value automatically overrides another; the practitioner applies judgment to the specific situation. Under each value the Code states both aspirational standards and mandatory standards. Claiming honesty or responsibility always wins imposes a hierarchy that does not exist, and the Code lists four values, not two.  Takeaway: The four ethics values are unranked; conflicts are resolved by judgment, not a fixed hierarchy.
choices: Yes, honesty is the top-ranked value and automatically overrides the other three in any conflict.
No, the four values are unranked, so the practitioner applies judgment to the specific situation.
Yes, responsibility sits above the others and by itself settles any conflict between the values.
No ranking is needed because the current Code actually lists only two values rather than four.

questions.question: A digital library launches its catalog as a series of complete, usable subject collections, releasing history first, then science, then art, so patrons can fully search each collection the moment it goes live. Which delivery approach does this describe?
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery builds the product in usable pieces, each adding functionality patrons can begin using, which matches releasing complete, searchable collections one after another. Iterative delivery instead refines the same work over repeated cycles, and delivering everything at once is characteristic of predictive or waterfall work.  Takeaway: Incremental delivery ships usable pieces of the product over time.
choices: Predictive, because the entire catalog is delivered in a single final release.
Iterative, because the same collection is reworked over and over until it is perfect.
Waterfall, because the collections are produced in one strict, unbroken sequence.
Incremental, because each release adds a usable, functioning piece of the finished product.

questions.question: An analyst must capture 'Place Online Order' end to end: the actor who starts it, the condition that must be true before it begins, the normal sequence of steps, and what happens if payment is declined. Which artifact best fits?
questions.explanation: A use case captures a complete interaction, naming the actor, preconditions, and the main, alternate, and exception flows such as a declined payment. A user story is a small slice for a later conversation, and a traceability row records links rather than interaction steps.  Takeaway: A full interaction with actor, preconditions, and flows is a use case; a small slice is a user story.
choices: A single user story written on a card and sized to fit inside one iteration
A use case with actors, preconditions, and main, alternate, and exception flows
A roadmap theme that shows the product's planned direction over the coming quarters
A requirements traceability matrix row that links each requirement to its test

questions.question: In the three C's of a user story, which element is the acceptance criteria used to confirm the story is finished?
questions.explanation: In the three C's, Confirmation is the acceptance criteria that verify the story is complete. The Card is only the brief reminder and the Conversation is the discussion of details; Commitment is not one of the three C's.  Takeaway: The three C's are Card (reminder), Conversation (details), and Confirmation (acceptance criteria).
choices: Card, the short written reminder that stands in for the whole story
Conversation, the ongoing discussion that fleshes out the story's details
Commitment, the team's pledge to complete the story during this iteration
Confirmation, the acceptance criteria that verify the story is done

questions.question: During a tense status review, a project manager feels a surge of anger at a stakeholder's remark but pauses, stays composed, and responds constructively. Which aspect of emotional intelligence is this, and what does it involve?
questions.explanation: Self-management is the ability to regulate one's own emotions and respond deliberately, which is what pausing and staying composed demonstrates. Regulating emotion is not the same as suppressing or hiding it entirely, and sensing others' emotions or avoiding hard conversations describe different domains and behaviors.  Takeaway: Self-management means regulating emotions, not suppressing or hiding them.
choices: Social awareness, which means accurately sensing the emotions of others present
Relationship management, which means avoiding hard conversations to keep the peace
Self-management, which means regulating one's emotions rather than suppressing them
Self-management, which means hiding all emotion so that none of it is ever visible

questions.question: An event that was never identified and has no entry in the risk register suddenly disrupts the project. What is the appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: An unidentified, unplanned event that has occurred with no prepared response is handled with a workaround, an unplanned response created in the moment. There is no recorded contingency to execute because the risk was never identified, and doing nothing while the disruption continues is not acceptable.  Takeaway: Workarounds address unplanned risks; planned responses handle identified ones.
choices: Execute the contingency response already recorded for this event
Develop a workaround, since the event was unplanned with no response
Take no action, because only identified risks may be responded to
Wait for the next risk register update before responding to it

questions.question: On a control chart, seven consecutive measurements fall on the same side of the mean, even though all are within the control limits. What does the 'rule of seven' say the team should do?
questions.explanation: The rule of seven flags seven or more consecutive points on one side of the mean as a non-random pattern that should be investigated, even when every point is within the control limits. Points inside the limits are not automatically fine if they form such a run, and widening limits hides the signal rather than addressing it.  Takeaway: Seven consecutive points on one side of the mean signal a non-random pattern to investigate, even within control limits.
choices: Investigate, because a run of seven on one side signals a non-random pattern worth examining
Ignore it, because points inside the control limits never require any action
Immediately stop the process, because any point inside the limits is a defect
Widen the control limits so the run no longer looks unusual

questions.question: A Kanban team wants to know how many work items it actually finishes per week and to watch that rate over time. Which metric most directly captures this?
questions.explanation: Throughput is the count of items completed per unit of time, which directly answers how many the team finishes each week. Velocity is an iteration-based points measure and capacity is available effort, so neither captures the finished-item rate that flow teams track.  Takeaway: Throughput is items completed per unit of time in flow-based work.
choices: Velocity, the story points a Scrum team completes each sprint
Capacity, the amount of effort the team has available in a period
Throughput, the number of items completed per unit of time
The sprint goal, the single objective committed for a sprint

questions.question: An auditor reviews whether the team is following the documented testing procedure correctly, without inspecting any finished product. This activity is an example of what?
questions.explanation: Quality assurance is process-focused: it audits whether the correct processes and standards are being followed, which is exactly what reviewing adherence to a documented procedure does. Quality control instead inspects finished outputs against requirements, so a measurement of output would be control, not assurance. Validate Scope concerns customer acceptance, and gold plating means adding unrequested features, neither of which describes a process audit.  Takeaway: Quality assurance audits the process; quality control inspects the output.
choices: Quality control, because finished output is being measured against tolerances
Quality assurance, because it audits the process being used
Validate Scope, because deliverables are being formally accepted
Gold plating, because extra effort beyond requirements is being added

questions.question: An enterprise portfolio review board must decide which proposed initiatives to fund next quarter. On what basis should the board primarily select components for the portfolio?
questions.explanation: Portfolio components are selected and prioritized by how well they advance the organization's strategy, because a portfolio exists to achieve strategic objectives. Requiring the components to be related and share one benefit describes a program instead, and choosing purely by lowest cost or submission order ignores strategic alignment.  Takeaway: Portfolio components are chosen for strategic alignment, not for being related.
choices: On how well each component aligns with and advances the organization's strategic objectives.
On whether the components are closely related to one another and share a single common benefit.
On which components carry the lowest individual cost, regardless of their strategic fit.
On which components were submitted the earliest, in strict first-come, first-served order.

questions.question: During a Daily Scrum, a stakeholder asks the developers to deliver a full status presentation and formally sign off the completed work. How should this be handled?
questions.explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event by and for the developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and re-plan the day; it is not a status meeting or an acceptance gate. Stretching it, using it for sign-off, or turning it into a management report all misuse the event.  Takeaway: The Daily Scrum is the developers' 15-minute re-planning event, not a status or sign-off meeting.
choices: The Daily Scrum is a short event for the developers to plan their day toward the Sprint Goal; a status presentation and sign-off are not its purpose and belong elsewhere.
The developers should extend the Daily Scrum for as long as the full status presentation takes.
The Daily Scrum is the correct place for stakeholders to formally accept completed work.
The Scrum Master should convert the Daily Scrum into a status report delivered to management.

questions.question: An identified risk that the team had already prepared a response for in the risk register now occurs. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: When a response was already planned for an identified risk, the project manager follows that plan and executes the prepared response. Inventing a new workaround is reserved for unplanned events with no prepared response, and doing nothing or escalating first while a planned response exists delays a decision already made.  Takeaway: When a planned response exists for an identified risk, execute it.
choices: Execute the planned risk response already prepared for this risk
Invent a brand-new workaround and ignore the prepared response
Take no action until the risk is re-analyzed from scratch
Escalate to the sponsor before applying any prepared response

questions.question: After a brand-new team finishes only its first sprint, a manager demands that the team lock in a single fixed velocity to drive all future forecasts. What is the most accurate response?
questions.explanation: Velocity is an optional forecasting aid, not a required Scrum artifact, and it becomes a useful trend only after several sprints provide enough history to average. It is distinct from capacity, and the sprint commitment is the sprint goal rather than a velocity number.  Takeaway: Velocity is optional and trustworthy only after several sprints of history.
choices: Velocity is a mandatory Scrum artifact that must be permanently fixed right after the very first sprint
Velocity should always be set exactly equal to the team's available capacity
Velocity is the team's commitment for each sprint, replacing the sprint goal
Velocity is an optional forecasting aid that grows reliable only after several sprints

questions.question: On a predictive project, a change request has just been approved by the change control board. What should happen next?
questions.explanation: Once a change request is approved, the process is to update the affected baselines and subsidiary plan documents and then implement the approved change, so that performance continues to be measured against a current, controlled baseline. Implementing before updating the baselines breaks that control, re-litigating an approved decision reverses the change process, and baselines are controlled rather than permanently frozen.  Takeaway: After approval, update the affected baselines and plans, then implement the change.
choices: Update the affected baselines and plan documents, then implement the approved change
Implement the change first and update the baselines only if problems appear later
Re-evaluate whether the change was truly worth approving before taking any action
Freeze all baselines permanently so that no further changes are ever possible

questions.question: A project planner is reviewing statements captured during planning. Choose TWO statements that are assumptions. (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: An assumption is something accepted as true without proof, which fits expecting the interest rate to hold and expecting the supplier to stay in business. A team-size cap and a building-code height limit are fixed limiting factors, making them constraints, and an outage that has already delayed a test is an issue.  Takeaway: Assumptions are taken as true without proof; fixed limits are constraints and events that already occurred are issues.
choices: The contract limits the project team to a maximum of eight people at any time.
We assume the current interest rate will hold steady until procurement closes.
We expect the incumbent supplier to remain in business throughout delivery.
The building code caps the structure at three stories, and that cannot change.
The server outage this morning has already delayed today's integration test.

questions.question: A branding team produces one rough version of a mascot design, then repeatedly reworks that same design from feedback until it is polished. This way of working is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Iterative work improves the same deliverable through repeated refinement, which matches reworking one mascot until it is polished. Incremental work would instead add distinct new usable pieces rather than reworking a single item.  Takeaway: Iterative refines one deliverable repeatedly; incremental adds new pieces.
choices: Incremental, because each cycle delivers a separate new deliverable
Iterative, because the same deliverable is refined over repeated cycles
Predictive, because the design is frozen right after the first version
Flow-based, because there are no repeating cycles involved at all

questions.question: A network has these activities (duration in days; predecessors in parentheses): A = 5 (none), B = 3 (A), C = 8 (A), D = 6 (B), E = 4 (C), F = 3 (D and E). Which is the critical path and its length?
questions.explanation: Two paths run through the network. A-B-D-F = 5 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 17 days, and A-C-E-F = 5 + 8 + 4 + 3 = 20 days. The critical path is the longest one, A-C-E-F at 20 days, which sets the shortest possible project duration. Naming the correct 20-day length but the A-B-D-F chain points to the wrong sequence of activities, and 17 days for A-C-E-F is an addition slip on the longer path.  Takeaway: The critical path is the longest-duration path; sum each path and pick the maximum.
choices: A-B-D-F, 17 days
A-B-D-F, 20 days
A-C-E-F, 20 days
A-C-E-F, 17 days

questions.question: A project manager wants to record, for each key stakeholder, the difference between how engaged they are today and how engaged they need to be for the project to succeed. Which artifact is designed for this comparison?
questions.explanation: Comparing each stakeholder's current engagement against the desired level is the purpose of a stakeholder engagement assessment matrix. The stakeholder register lists who the stakeholders are and their attributes but does not chart current-versus-desired engagement, and the risk register and charter serve unrelated purposes.  Takeaway: Current-versus-desired engagement is charted in an engagement assessment matrix, not the register.
choices: The project's master stakeholder register
The project's identified risk register
The approved project charter document
A stakeholder engagement assessment matrix

questions.question: An analyst needs to understand, in depth, the undocumented judgment a single veteran loan officer applies when approving complex loans. Which elicitation technique fits best?
questions.explanation: An interview draws out depth and detail from one individual, which suits probing a single expert's undocumented judgment. A survey gathers breadth across many respondents rather than depth, brainstorming generates new ideas instead of capturing an existing process, and a marketing brochure does not reveal the officer's reasoning.  Takeaway: Use interviews for depth from an individual; use surveys for breadth across many.
choices: A broad survey emailed to the entire lending department for quick input.
A one-on-one interview with the veteran loan officer.
A brainstorming session to invent brand-new loan-approval ideas.
A review of the vendor's marketing brochure for the lending system.

questions.question: A team adopting Kanban to manage a continuous flow of work asks which practices are core to this flow-based approach. Which TWO are core Kanban practices? (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Kanban's general practices include visualizing the workflow and limiting work in progress so flow improves and bottlenecks become visible. Fixed iterations and a sprint goal belong to iteration-based Scrum, and Kanban does not require a velocity forecast.  Takeaway: Core Kanban practices include visualizing the workflow and limiting work in progress.
choices: Committing every item to a fixed two-week iteration
Visualizing the workflow so the state of work is transparent
Setting a sprint goal that the whole team commits to
Limiting work in progress to improve flow
Forecasting a velocity number that Kanban requires each cycle

questions.question: An enterprise has a dozen agile teams that must align their plans on a shared cadence and plan together across a multi-iteration horizon. Which of the following is a scaling framework designed for this alignment?
questions.explanation: SAFe is a framework for scaling agile across many teams so they align and plan together on a shared cadence, using a Planning Interval. Kanban and Extreme Programming operate mainly at the single-team level, and a retrospective is an event rather than a scaling framework.  Takeaway: SAFe scales many teams to plan together on a shared cadence.
choices: SAFe, a scaling framework in which many teams plan together on a shared cadence
Kanban, a single-team flow method organized around work-in-progress limits
Extreme Programming, a single-team approach centered on engineering practices
The retrospective, a team event focused on improving how the team works

questions.question: Before committing to build a real-time recommendation feature, an agile team is unsure whether a candidate machine-learning library can meet the required response time. They allocate a short, time-boxed effort purely to research and test that uncertainty. In agile terms, what is this effort called?
questions.explanation: A spike is a short, time-boxed investigation that reduces technical or functional uncertainty before the team estimates or commits to building. A sprint goal is the sprint's single objective; a retrospective improves how the team works; refactoring restructures existing code without changing its behavior. Only a spike is exploratory research to answer an unknown.  Takeaway: A spike is a time-boxed investigation that reduces uncertainty before the team commits to building.
choices: A refactor
A sprint goal
A spike
A retrospective

questions.question: Which responsibility most accurately describes the project sponsor's role?
questions.explanation: The sponsor provides funding and authorizes the project by approving the charter. Performing the technical work and producing detailed estimates are the team's responsibilities, so those do not describe the sponsor's role.  Takeaway: The sponsor funds the project and authorizes it through the charter.
choices: Providing funding and authorizing the project through the charter
Performing the hands-on technical work that builds the deliverables
Producing the detailed activity estimates for every work package
Writing and running the automated tests for each release

questions.question: Midway through a sprint, the product owner tries to insert a new item directly into the sprint backlog and tells the developers they must build it now. Why does this conflict with Scrum?
questions.explanation: The developers own the sprint backlog and decide what work it holds, so the product owner cannot unilaterally force new work into it mid-sprint. The product owner sets priority and value on the product backlog, but changes to sprint work are negotiated with the developers rather than dictated.  Takeaway: Developers own the sprint backlog and decide what it contains.
choices: Because only the Scrum Master is permitted to change any backlog at all
Because the product owner must first get the sponsor to sign a change request
Because the developers own the sprint backlog and decide what it contains
Because the sprint backlog can never change for any reason once the sprint starts

questions.question: A film-shoot plan states, "We assume the coastal weather will stay clear during the outdoor shoot," and also, "Filming on the pier is permitted only between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m." How are these two statements best classified?
questions.explanation: An assumption is something taken to be true without proof, which fits believing the weather will stay clear, while a constraint is a limiting factor, which fits the restricted filming hours. Reversing the two, or forcing both into one category, misapplies the definitions.  Takeaway: Taken as true without proof is an assumption; a limiting factor is a constraint.
choices: Both are assumptions, because each one is merely a statement that happens to be written into the shoot plan.
Both are constraints, because either one of the two statements could clearly restrict how the whole shoot is actually carried out.
The weather statement is really a firm constraint on the shoot itself, while the permitted-hours rule is actually just an assumption.
The weather statement is an assumption taken as true without proof, while the permitted-hours rule is a limiting constraint.

questions.question: A project overhauls the customer returns process. Leadership asks who is accountable for how well the returns process performs overall versus who runs it day to day. Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: The process owner is accountable for how well a process performs, while the process manager runs it day to day. The reversed pairing swaps those two roles, and assigning process accountability to the business analyst, sponsor, product owner, or project manager misplaces it.  Takeaway: Process owner is accountable for the process; process manager runs it daily.
choices: The business analyst is accountable for returns performance, while the sponsor runs the returns process each day.
The process manager is accountable for returns performance, while the process owner runs the returns process each day.
The process owner is accountable for returns performance, while the process manager runs the returns process each day.
The product owner is accountable for returns performance, while the project manager runs the returns process each day.

questions.question: A team plots each candidate item on a grid of expected value against estimated effort and starts with items in the high-value, low-effort corner. Which prioritization approach is this?
questions.explanation: Plotting value against effort and choosing high-value, low-effort items first is value-versus-effort prioritization. MoSCoW sorts by obligation category and Kano classifies by satisfaction type, neither of which is a direct value-to-effort tradeoff.  Takeaway: Value-versus-effort prioritization favors high-value, low-effort items first.
choices: Value-versus-effort prioritization, favoring high value for low effort first
MoSCoW categorization of the items into Must, Should, Could, and Won't-have-this-time
Kano classification of the items into basic, performance, and delighter features
Strict first-in-first-out ordering by the calendar date each item was first written

questions.question: A team performs a SWOT analysis of its organization. Choose TWO factors that are internal to the organization. (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: In SWOT, strengths and weaknesses are internal factors the organization controls, so the skilled in-house team and the outdated internal test lab are internal. A new competitor, a regulatory change, and shifting customer trends are external forces, making them opportunities or threats rather than internal factors.  Takeaway: In SWOT, strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external.
choices: A highly skilled in-house engineering team, treated as a strength
A new competitor entering the market, treated as a threat
An outdated internal test lab that slows releases, treated as a weakness
A favorable change in government regulation, treated as an opportunity
A sudden shift in customer buying trends, treated as an opportunity

questions.question: Without being asked, a landscaping crew adds imported ornamental fountains and premium lighting the client never requested, saying "it makes the garden pop." No change process was followed. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation: Gold-plating occurs when the team adds features or polish the customer did not ask for, which describes the unrequested fountains and lighting. Scope creep comes from uncontrolled changes to requested scope, and this addition originates with the team rather than from an approved change or normal elaboration.  Takeaway: When the team adds unrequested extras, that is gold-plating.
choices: Gold-plating, because the crew added extras the customer never requested.
Scope creep that was driven by the client's own repeated requests.
An approved change properly recorded against the scope baseline.
Normal progressive elaboration of the project's requirements over time.

questions.question: A project manager refers to the project's approved scope baseline. Which combination of components makes up the scope baseline?
questions.explanation: The scope baseline is the approved scope statement together with the WBS and its WBS dictionary. The charter and registers, the schedule and cost baselines, and the business case and subsidiary plans are separate artifacts that are not part of the scope baseline.  Takeaway: The scope baseline is the scope statement plus the WBS and the WBS dictionary.
choices: The project charter, the risk register, and the stakeholder register.
The scope statement, the WBS, and the WBS dictionary.
The schedule baseline, the cost baseline, and the quality plan.
The business case, the benefits plan, and the communications plan.

questions.question: A sponsor signs a document that formally accepts a set of completed deliverables. In which process does this formal acceptance occur?
questions.explanation: Validate Scope is the Monitoring and Controlling process in which the customer or sponsor formally accepts completed deliverables, which is exactly what signing an acceptance document represents. Inspecting deliverables for conformance checks correctness but does not obtain sign-off, closing finalizes the project after acceptance has already happened, and directing project work produces deliverables rather than accepting them.  Takeaway: Formal acceptance of deliverables happens in Validate Scope, a Monitoring and Controlling process.
choices: Validate Scope, a Monitoring and Controlling process
Control Quality, where deliverables are inspected for conformance to requirements
Close Project or Phase, performed during Closing
Direct and Manage Project Work, performed during Executing

questions.question: A bakery chain carries out several efforts. Which one is best classified as a project rather than operations?
questions.explanation: A project is a temporary endeavor that creates a unique result, and opening a first-ever store in a new country is a one-time, unique effort. Baking the daily menu, restocking each morning, and processing payments are ongoing, repetitive operations that sustain the business.  Takeaway: A one-time, unique effort is a project; recurring daily work is operations.
choices: Baking and selling the same daily bread menu across all of its existing stores.
Building and opening its first-ever store in a neighboring country next year.
Restocking the ingredient shelves each morning before the shop opens to customers.
Processing customer payments at the front counter throughout every business day.

questions.question: A risk that had been logged in the register with a probability and an impact has now actually occurred and is disrupting the work. How should it now be regarded?
questions.explanation: A risk is a future uncertain event, so once it actually occurs it has become an issue, a condition that has happened and now requires action. Having been logged in advance does not make it an assumption, and it is not merely a limiting factor or a closure-time note while it is actively disrupting the work.  Takeaway: A risk that occurs becomes an issue requiring action now.
choices: As an issue, because the risk event has occurred and now needs resolving
As an assumption, since the team had already accounted for it well in advance
As a constraint, because it now limits how the team can proceed
As a lesson learned, to be documented only at project closure

questions.question: An agile team regularly reviews upcoming product backlog items to add detail, split items that are too large, and re-estimate them before they are pulled into a Sprint. What is this ongoing activity called?
questions.explanation: Backlog refinement is the ongoing activity of adding detail, splitting, ordering, and re-estimating upcoming backlog items so they are ready for a future Sprint. It is routine adaptive work, not change control against a baseline, and it is distinct from the Retrospective (process) and the Sprint Review (inspecting the increment).  Takeaway: Backlog refinement = ongoing prep (detail, split, estimate) of upcoming items.
choices: A formal change-control review of the approved scope baseline.
Backlog refinement - the ongoing preparation of upcoming backlog items.
The Sprint Retrospective, where the team improves its process.
The Sprint Review, where stakeholders inspect the increment.

questions.question: A team wants a simple chart that shows how much work still remains in the current iteration as each day passes. Which chart is designed for this view?
questions.explanation: A burndown chart shows remaining work trending downward across the iteration, answering how much is left. A burnup chart instead shows completed work rising toward a scope line, and a cumulative flow diagram shows how items move through states.  Takeaway: Burndown shows remaining work falling; burnup shows completed work rising.
choices: A burnup chart, which plots completed work against a scope line
A burndown chart, which plots remaining work falling over time
A cumulative flow diagram, which shows items across workflow states
A probability-impact matrix, which rates the identified risks

questions.question: A telecom project lays fiber-optic cable to a remote town. The cable is installed, the town then gains fast and reliable internet, and over the following year local businesses grow and residents reach online services. Which mapping to output, outcome, and benefit is correct?
questions.explanation: The output is the deliverable produced (the installed cable), the outcome is the change it enables (fast, reliable internet), and the benefit is the realized value (business growth and better access to services). The other mappings swap the deliverable, the change, and the value out of their correct order.  Takeaway: Output (deliverable) leads to outcome (change) leads to benefit (value).
choices: The cable is the benefit, the fast internet is the output, and the business growth is the outcome.
The cable is the outcome, the business growth is the output, and the fast internet is the benefit.
The cable is the output, the fast internet is the outcome, and the business growth is the benefit.
The fast internet is the output, the cable is the outcome, and the business growth is the benefit.

questions.question: A candidate building a study schedule reads a forum post claiming the four CAPM domains are all weighted equally at 25 percent each. Which statement correctly describes where the Business Analysis domain actually stands?
questions.explanation: Business Analysis carries about 27 percent of the exam, which makes it the second-largest domain behind the roughly 36 percent Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts domain. The four domains are not weighted equally at 25 percent each, and Business Analysis is neither the largest domain nor a negligible one.  Takeaway: Business Analysis is about 27 percent - the second-largest CAPM domain, not an equal 25 percent share.
choices: All four domains are weighted equally at 25 percent, so Business Analysis is exactly one quarter of the exam.
Business Analysis is the single largest domain, outweighing even Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts.
Business Analysis is about 27 percent, the second-largest domain, behind Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts.
Business Analysis is a negligible slice that appears in only a handful of scattered items across the exam.

questions.question: Representatives from marketing, legal, and IT hold conflicting views on the scope of a new consent-management feature, and the analyst needs them to reach a shared, agreed scope in one focused session. Which technique fits best?
questions.explanation: A facilitated workshop brings the groups together to build agreement and resolve conflict in one focused session, which is what a cross-group scope dispute needs. Separate surveys collect isolated opinions without reconciling them, document analysis studies existing materials, and observing one specialist reveals behavior rather than resolving disagreement.  Takeaway: Use workshops to build agreement and resolve conflict among stakeholders.
choices: A separate anonymous survey sent individually to each of the three groups.
Silent document analysis of each group's old procedure and policy manuals.
One-on-one observation of a single marketing specialist doing their work.
A facilitated requirements workshop with all three groups in the room together.

questions.question: A director expects the sprint review to be a formal gate where leadership signs off before any further work is allowed. How should this expectation be corrected?
questions.explanation: The sprint review is a collaborative working session where the team and stakeholders inspect the increment and adapt the product backlog, not a formal sign-off gate. It is neither a private planning meeting nor a one-way status report.  Takeaway: The sprint review inspects and adapts; it is not an approval gate.
choices: The review is a private developer-only meeting to plan out the next sprint
The review is a one-way status report the Scrum Master delivers to leadership
The review is the event where the developers select the items for the next sprint
The review is a working session to inspect the increment and adapt the backlog

questions.question: A draft WBS lists only the physical product deliverables and deliberately leaves out the project-management work packages. Which WBS principle does this omission violate?
questions.explanation: The 100 percent rule states that the WBS captures all of the work in scope and no more, and the total authorized scope includes project-management work, not just the product deliverables, so omitting the management work packages leaves the WBS short of the full scope. Rolling wave and progressive elaboration concern how detail is added over time, and the 8/80 heuristic addresses work-package size, none of which is about capturing all of the scope.  Takeaway: The 100 percent rule requires the WBS to capture the total authorized scope, including project-management work.
choices: The rolling wave principle, which delays the detailed planning of work scheduled for later phases
The progressive elaboration principle, which refines the scope and estimates as more detail emerges
The 8/80 heuristic, which limits how many hours of effort a single work package may reasonably contain
The 100 percent rule, requiring the WBS to capture the total authorized scope, including management work

questions.question: An adaptive team's plans are shaped by a collective labor agreement it must honor and by rate limits imposed by a third-party payment service. These influences are best categorized as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Enterprise environmental factors are conditions inside or outside the organization that the team does not directly control, such as a labor agreement and an external provider's rate limits. Organizational process assets differ because they are internal materials the project owns and can tailor.  Takeaway: Conditions outside the team's control, like agreements and external limits, are EEFs.
choices: Enterprise environmental factors, because they are conditions the team does not control
Organizational process assets, because the team created and now owns them
Acceptance criteria, because they define when one particular item is complete
Definition of done, because they establish the shared quality bar applied to every single item

questions.question: A project manager must inform 1,200 customers of a scheduled two-hour maintenance window next weekend. No discussion is needed - only broad awareness by the deadline. Which method is most efficient?
questions.explanation: Push communication such as a bulk email or broadcast dashboard notice efficiently sends one-way awareness to a large audience by a deadline. Individual calls do not scale to 1,200 people for a simple notice, pull methods risk customers never checking, and a workshop is meant to build agreement rather than announce a set window.  Takeaway: Use push communication - email, report, dashboard - to broadcast awareness to many.
choices: Interactive one-on-one phone calls placed individually to each of the roughly 1,200 affected customers.
Pull communication that relies entirely on customers happening to check a status page on their own.
A single facilitated negotiation workshop convened with all 1,200 customers gathered at the same time.
Push communication, such as a bulk notification email or a broadcast dashboard notice.

questions.question: A risk involves possible corrosion in a pipeline segment that only the materials engineer fully understands. When assigning the risk owner, who is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A risk owner should be whoever is best positioned to monitor the risk and carry out its response, and the materials engineer has that specialized expertise for a corrosion risk. Ownership does not default to the project manager or the sponsor, nor does it fall automatically to whoever first identified the risk.  Takeaway: The risk owner is whoever can best monitor and respond, not automatically the PM.
choices: The project manager, since the PM is the default owner of all risks
The sponsor, because technically complex risks must be owned at the top
The materials engineer, who can best monitor and respond to it
The team member who first logged the risk during the workshop

questions.question: A release manager wants a single chart that shows total completed work climbing toward a line representing the overall scope, so scope changes also become visible. Which chart fits this need?
questions.explanation: A burnup chart plots completed work rising toward a scope line, so it shows progress and reveals scope changes when that line moves. A burndown shows remaining work falling and does not display a separate scope line in the same way.  Takeaway: A burnup chart shows completed work rising toward a movable scope line.
choices: A burndown chart, because it simply shows the remaining work steadily declining across the days
A velocity chart, because it compares points across past iterations
A burnup chart, because it shows completed work rising toward a scope line
A Gantt chart, because it lays out task dependencies on a timeline

questions.question: For a password-reset story, a product owner writes the acceptance criterion: 'The reset process should be quick and easy to use.' A developer objects that it cannot be used to confirm the story is done. What is the main problem with this criterion?
questions.explanation: 'Quick and easy' is subjective, so no one can objectively test whether the story meets it - good acceptance criteria are specific and measurable. Writing from the user's viewpoint is fine; criteria may state outcomes without dictating screen layout; and this criterion does address a single story. Its fatal flaw is that it cannot be verified.  Takeaway: Acceptance criteria must be specific and measurable so completion can be objectively verified.
choices: It is written from the end user's point of view rather than from the developer's implementation perspective.
It is subjective and not measurable, so it cannot be objectively tested.
It states an outcome instead of specifying the exact screen layout.
It covers the whole product rather than this single story.

questions.question: A product owner is ordering the backlog. One item has only moderate customer value on its own, but it removes a technical dependency blocking three high-value items and carries significant risk if delayed. How should it be ordered?
questions.explanation: Backlog order reflects overall priority, which balances value with risk, urgency, dependencies, and effort rather than value alone. An item that unblocks several high-value items and carries real risk therefore rises even when its own value is moderate.  Takeaway: Backlog order weighs value together with risk, dependencies, and urgency.
choices: Near the very bottom of the order, because its own standalone customer value is only moderate
Removed from the backlog, because it is not the single highest-value item
High in the order, because priority weighs value together with risk and dependencies
Left unordered, because only raw customer value may drive the backlog order

questions.question: Which of the following is an activity performed during the Closing process group of a predictive project?
questions.explanation: Closing consists of the activities that finalize all work, archive records and lessons learned, release resources, and formally close the project or phase. Decomposing deliverables and approving baselines are Planning activities, and obtaining the customer's formal acceptance of deliverables is Validate Scope, a Monitoring and Controlling activity that occurs before closure rather than during it.  Takeaway: Closing archives records and lessons learned and formally releases resources after acceptance has occurred.
choices: Decomposing deliverables into work packages
Obtaining the customer's formal acceptance of completed deliverables
Developing and approving the schedule and cost baselines
Archiving records and lessons learned and formally releasing resources

questions.question: A team argues that controlling the versions of the product's specifications and drawings is the same thing as approving changes to the project's scope. How do configuration management and change control differ?
questions.explanation: Configuration management controls the product's characteristics - its specifications, drawings, and versions - so everyone works from the right, current definition. Change control governs how proposed changes to the baselines are requested, evaluated, approved, and integrated. They are related but distinct, and both are used in predictive work.  Takeaway: Configuration management controls the product's versions/specs; change control governs approving changes to the baselines.
choices: They are identical activities described by two different names
Configuration management controls the product's specifications and versions, while change control governs approving and integrating changes to the baselines
Configuration management approves budget changes, while change control only stores document versions
Both apply only to agile projects and never to predictive ones

questions.question: Which artifact is most appropriate for communicating current schedule and cost performance, including variances against the baselines, to stakeholders on a predictive project?
questions.explanation: A performance or status report compares actual schedule and cost results against the approved baselines and communicates the resulting variances to stakeholders, which is the core of documenting predictive controls. A ranked backlog, a burndown chart, and a velocity chart are all artifacts associated with adaptive delivery and do not report performance against predictive baselines.  Takeaway: Predictive performance is communicated through status reports comparing actuals against baselines.
choices: A product backlog of user stories ranked by business value and priority
A sprint burndown chart tracking the remaining work in the current iteration
A team velocity chart summarizing delivered throughput from recent iterations
A performance (status) report comparing actuals against the baselines

questions.question: An IT operations team handles a steady stream of incoming requests. It sets no fixed iterations, caps how many requests can be worked at once, and starts a new one only when a slot frees up. Which approach does this describe?
questions.explanation: Kanban manages a continuous flow by limiting work in progress and pulling new work only as capacity frees up, without fixed iterations. Scrum uses fixed sprints, Extreme Programming focuses on engineering practices, and SAFe scales multiple teams, so none matches pull-based flow with WIP limits.  Takeaway: Kanban is flow-based: limit work in progress and pull as capacity frees.
choices: Kanban, a flow-based method using work-in-progress limits and a pull system
Scrum, because absolutely all of the work is strictly organized into fixed-length timeboxed sprints
Extreme Programming, because it concentrates on engineering practices
SAFe, because it coordinates many teams across a planning interval

questions.question: An analyst must tell a frustrated stakeholder that a requested feature is being deferred, and then work through the stakeholder's concerns to reach agreement. Which communication method fits best?
questions.explanation: Interactive communication such as a direct conversation or facilitated meeting allows the real-time give and take needed to deliver sensitive news and work through concerns to agreement. Push and pull methods send or store information but cannot support that back and forth, and a one-way memo dictates rather than resolves.  Takeaway: Use interactive communication for sensitive, nuanced, or negotiation situations.
choices: Push communication, such as a mass email announcing the deferral to everyone at once.
Interactive communication, such as a direct conversation or a facilitated meeting.
Pull communication, such as posting the deferral decision on a wiki for later reading.
A one-way memo that states the deferral as final and invites no discussion at all.

questions.question: A story that reads 'As an administrator, I want to manage user accounts' is too large to finish in one iteration. Which approach best splits it into smaller stories that each still deliver usable value?
questions.explanation: Splitting by workflow step - create, edit, deactivate - yields smaller stories that each deliver usable value and can be prioritized independently. Splitting by technical layer produces pieces that are not independently usable; assigning the whole story to different developers or deferring it does not reduce its size. Good splits preserve end-to-end value in every slice.  Takeaway: Split large stories by workflow slice so each smaller story still delivers independent, usable value.
choices: Split by technical layer: one story for the user-interface screens and a separate story for the database schema, built strictly in sequence.
Leave the story intact and schedule it for a later iteration with more capacity.
Split by workflow step: creating, editing, and deactivating accounts, so each smaller story is usable on its own.
Assign the large story to a different developer each iteration until it is complete.

questions.question: Arrange the steps of closing a project or phase in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Closure first confirms the work is genuinely complete, then obtains formal acceptance from the authorized party, transitions the deliverables, releases resources and closes contracts, and finally archives records and captures lessons learned. Releasing resources or archiving before acceptance would close the project prematurely.  Takeaway: Closure runs confirm-complete, get formal acceptance, transition, release resources, then archive and capture lessons.
sequence: Confirm the work and deliverables are complete and meet acceptance criteria
Obtain formal acceptance of the deliverables from the customer or sponsor
Transition the completed deliverables to operations or the customer
Release project resources and close out contracts
Archive project records and document lessons learned

questions.question: A project manager is assembling the project management plan and wants to include only genuine planning components. Which item is a core planning component of the project management plan?
questions.explanation: Core planning components addressed in the project management plan include how scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, and risk will be managed, so planning the identification, analysis, and response to risks belongs there. A competitor's confidential figures, a customer's private data, and a product marketing jingle are not planning components of the project management plan.  Takeaway: Managing scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, and risk are the core planning components.
choices: How the project's risks will be identified, analyzed, and responded to.
The competitor's confidential internal profit margins for the last quarter.
The customer's personal home address and private banking account details.
The final marketing jingle that the finished product will use on the radio.

questions.question: A CAPM candidate asks how leadership and management relate on a project. Which statement is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Leadership and management are complementary: management works through systems, processes, and positional authority, while leadership works through a shared vision and earned influence. They are not identical, one does not replace the other, and neither is limited to a single development approach.  Takeaway: Management and leadership are complementary, not interchangeable or mutually exclusive.
choices: They complement each other: management uses systems and authority, leadership uses vision
They are identical terms, so the two words may be used interchangeably at will
Leadership entirely replaces management on any project that is run well today
Management applies only to predictive work, while leadership applies only to adaptive work

questions.question: A team agrees that no item is complete until its code is peer-reviewed, all unit tests pass, and its documentation is updated, and it applies this same rule to every item it finishes. What is this shared rule best called?
questions.explanation: A single shared standard that every completed item must satisfy, such as peer review and passing tests, is the Definition of Done. Acceptance criteria differ from item to item, while this rule applies uniformly across all work, and a backlog orders work rather than defining completion.  Takeaway: A rule applied uniformly to every item is the Definition of Done; per-item conditions are acceptance criteria.
choices: Acceptance criteria, because these conditions are written uniquely for each individual story
A product backlog, because it lists the ordered work the team will pull from next each time
The Definition of Done, because it is the shared standard every finished item must meet
A transition requirement, because it is needed only to move across to the new future state

questions.question: An activity has Early Start (ES) = 10, Early Finish (EF) = 16, Late Start (LS) = 14, and Late Finish (LF) = 20 (day-numbering where EF = ES + duration - 1). What is its total float?
questions.explanation: Total float = LS - ES = 14 - 10 = 4 days, which also equals LF - EF = 20 - 16 = 4 days. A value of 0 would place the activity on the critical path, which the gap between the early and late dates rules out. Seven days is the activity duration (EF - ES + 1 = 16 - 10 + 1), and 10 days comes from subtracting ES from LF, neither of which is the float formula.  Takeaway: Total float = LS - ES = LF - EF; zero total float marks a critical activity.
choices: 0 days
4 days
7 days
10 days

questions.question: A vendor's delivery lead insists that because the work is under a firm fixed-price contract, the team is required to use a fully predictive approach and cannot iterate at all. How should a CAPM-minded practitioner respond?
questions.explanation: Contract type shapes governance and documentation but does not by itself dictate the development approach; suitability turns on how stable and well understood the requirements are and how much change is expected, and adaptive or hybrid delivery can be used under a fixed price with appropriate controls. Claiming fixed price eliminates uncertainty overstates one factor, and claiming it forces a fully adaptive approach simply reverses the same error.  Takeaway: Contract type alone does not set the approach; requirement stability and expected change do.
choices: Agree, because a firm fixed-price contract eliminates all scope uncertainty and makes predictive mandatory
Agree, because iterating is contractually impossible whenever the price is fixed in advance
The development approach depends on requirement stability and expected change, not on the contract type by itself
Disagree, because fixed-price contracts actually require a fully adaptive approach to control cost

questions.question: Between iterations, the product owner reorders the backlog because customer feedback shifted what matters most. A predictive-minded auditor asks which change control board approved it. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Reprioritizing and reordering the product backlog is expected, routine work owned by the product owner and does not require formal change control. Formal change requests and control boards are typical of predictive, plan-based governance; adaptive and hybrid projects can still apply formal governance where warranted, but ordinary backlog reprioritization does not go through a change control board.  Takeaway: Backlog reordering is routine product owner work, not formal change control.
choices: A change control board must approve every reordering before the next iteration
Reordering first requires a formal change request and a documented impact analysis
Only the Scrum Master may reorder the backlog, and only after obtaining sign-off
Reordering the backlog is routine product owner work, not formal change control

questions.question: By the end of the sprint the developers achieved the sprint goal and delivered the most valuable items, but three minor items were carried over. A stakeholder calls the sprint a failure. How should this be judged?
questions.explanation: The sprint goal is the commitment for the sprint, so achieving it means the sprint met its purpose even when minor items carry over to the next sprint. A sprint is not defined as finishing every item, and sprints are timeboxed rather than extended.  Takeaway: The sprint goal, not finishing every item, is the sprint's commitment.
choices: The sprint failed because not every backlog item was finished
The sprint met its commitment because the sprint goal was achieved
The sprint must be extended until the remaining items are complete
The sprint goal is irrelevant whenever any single item is left unfinished

questions.question: On a software project, which group is generally responsible for performing the work that actually creates the deliverables?
questions.explanation: The project team members carry out the hands-on activities that produce the deliverables. The portfolio review board, the steering committee, and the sponsor provide governance, oversight, or funding rather than performing the technical work.  Takeaway: The team performs the work that produces the deliverables.
choices: The organization's portfolio review board
The executive project steering committee
The project sponsor acting alone
The project team members themselves

questions.question: Arrange the steps of control Quality vs Validate Scope in the correct order.
questions.explanation: The team first completes the deliverable, then Control Quality inspects it internally against quality requirements, correcting defects until it is verified. Only the verified deliverable moves to Validate Scope, where the customer or sponsor formally accepts it. Control Quality confirms correctness before Validate Scope obtains acceptance; reversing them submits unverified work for sign-off.  Takeaway: Control Quality verifies correctness internally before Validate Scope obtains the customer's formal acceptance.
sequence: The team finishes producing the deliverable
Control Quality inspects the deliverable against the quality requirements
Defects are corrected until the deliverable is verified as correct
The verified deliverable is presented to the customer or sponsor in Validate Scope
The customer or sponsor formally accepts the deliverable

questions.question: A niche calibration instrument must be leased from a sole supplier, and the supplier has not yet confirmed whether a unit will be available when your test phase begins. How is this best classified?
questions.explanation: Uncertainty about whether the instrument will be available in time is a risk, since it is an uncertain condition that could affect the project. A constraint would apply only if the outcome were already known and fixed, and treating the arrival as certain would instead be an assumption rather than a recognized uncertainty.
