Takeaway: Uncertain resource availability is a risk; a known, fixed limit is a constraint.
choices: A constraint, because any supplier dependency firmly limits the plan
A risk, because the availability is uncertain and could affect the project
An assumption, because the team is simply counting on the unit arriving
A milestone, because instrument delivery marks a point in the schedule

questions.question: A project manager is adding entries to the schedule for a warehouse fit-out. Which of the following entries should be represented as a milestone?
questions.explanation: A milestone is a significant point in time that carries zero duration, and fully executing the flooring agreement is such a point rather than work that consumes time. Pouring the slab, installing racking, and wiring the lighting are activities that each consume work periods, so they are not milestones.  Takeaway: A milestone marks a significant point in time and carries zero duration.
choices: Pour and cure the concrete loading dock slab
Install the storage racking across all four aisles
Flooring subcontractor agreement fully executed
Wire the overhead lighting circuits throughout the building

questions.question: In which organizational structure does the project manager hold moderate-to-high authority and control most of the budget, while team members still report to functional managers for their technical discipline?
questions.explanation: A strong matrix gives the project manager moderate-to-high authority and control of most of the budget while staff still report to functional managers for their discipline, blending both lines of authority. A weak matrix leaves most authority with the functional manager, a functional structure gives the project manager little formal authority, and a projectized structure removes the functional reporting line entirely.  Takeaway: A strong matrix gives the project manager high authority while functional reporting still exists.
choices: Functional organization
Weak matrix organization
Projectized organization
Strong matrix organization

questions.question: Five minutes before a museum's members-only preview opens, the main ticket-scanning system stops working and guests cannot be admitted right now. How is this best classified?
questions.explanation: An issue is a condition or event that has already happened and requires action now, which fits the scanning system that is currently down. A risk is a future, uncertain event, so it does not describe something that has already occurred.  Takeaway: Already happened is an issue; future and uncertain is a risk.
choices: An issue, because it is a condition that has already occurred and needs resolving now.
A risk, because the failure could eventually reduce the preview's overall attendance.
An assumption, because the team had taken for granted that the scanners would keep working.
A constraint, because the outage now limits what the event team is able to do.

questions.question: A construction firm groups its logically related activities into stages, each ending with one or more completed deliverables such as a finished foundation or a closed-in structure. Each such stage is best called...
questions.explanation: A project phase is a collection of logically related activities that ends with the completion of one or more deliverables, which describes each construction stage. A work package is the lowest level of the WBS, a portfolio groups components for strategy, and a change request proposes a baseline change.  Takeaway: A project phase is a set of related activities ending in one or more deliverables.
choices: A project phase.
A work package.
A project portfolio.
A submitted change request.

questions.question: On a project, team members are assigned full time and report directly to the project manager, who controls the budget and reassigns them when the project ends. Which organizational structure is this?
questions.explanation: In a projectized organization, teams are dedicated to the project and report directly to the project manager, who controls the budget, which matches the full-time reporting and reassignment described. A functional organization would have staff reporting to functional managers with little project-manager authority, and matrix structures share authority between project and functional managers rather than concentrating it fully with the project manager.  Takeaway: Dedicated teams reporting to a project manager who controls the budget describe a projectized structure.
choices: Projectized organization
Functional organization
Weak matrix organization
Balanced matrix organization

questions.question: A project uses both team resources and physical resources. Choose TWO items that are team resources. (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Team resources are the people who perform project work, which describes the scheduling coordinator and the quality assurance tester. The excavator, the cabling stock, and the leased warehouse space are equipment, materials, and facilities, making them physical resources rather than team resources.  Takeaway: Team resources are people; physical resources are equipment, materials, and facilities.
choices: The excavator leased for the earthworks
The scheduling coordinator assigned to track the plan
The bulk cabling stock consumed during installation
The quality assurance tester reviewing each build
The leased warehouse space used for staging materials

questions.question: While evaluating suppliers, a project manager discovers that one of the bidding firms is owned by her brother-in-law. Which action best reflects the value of fairness in the Code of Ethics?
questions.explanation: Fairness requires impartial, consistent evaluation and disclosing conflicts of interest, so disclosing the relationship and scoring every bid against the same criteria is correct. Favoring the relative, automatically rejecting the bid, or stalling the decision all fail to treat every bidder impartially.  Takeaway: Fairness means disclosing conflicts and evaluating impartially against consistent criteria.
choices: Disclose the family relationship and have all bids scored against the same criteria.
Give the relative's bid a small edge to keep the peace within the extended family.
Reject the relative's bid outright without review to appear beyond any reproach.
Postpone the award decision indefinitely so the awkward choice never has to be faced.

questions.question: At the discovery kickoff for a new loyalty app, the team wants to generate as many candidate feature ideas as possible before evaluating any of them. Which technique fits this goal?
questions.explanation: Brainstorming is built to generate a large volume of ideas quickly before any are evaluated, which matches producing many candidate features without early judgment. An interview draws depth from one person, and observation studies existing behavior rather than inventing new possibilities.  Takeaway: Use brainstorming to generate many ideas quickly before evaluating them.
choices: A structured one-on-one interview with a single power user of the current app.
Observation of customers as they use the current version of the app in daily life.
A brainstorming session to generate a wide range of ideas before any are judged.
A formal sign-off review of the already baselined requirements for the app.

questions.question: An activity has a duration of 5 work days and starts on a Thursday. The team works Monday through Friday only, and there are no holidays. On what day does the activity finish, and why?
questions.explanation: Duration measures work periods, not calendar days, so five work days from Thursday run Thursday and Friday, skip the nonworking weekend, then Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, finishing on Wednesday. Treating work days as calendar days or counting the weekend as working time both misapply the meaning of duration.  Takeaway: Duration is measured in work periods, so nonworking days extend the calendar span.
choices: It finishes the following Monday, since five work days equal five calendar days
It finishes the following Wednesday, since duration counts work periods only
It finishes on Saturday, since duration includes every calendar day counted
It cannot be determined, since duration has no relationship to the calendar

questions.question: An online store releases a working product-catalog page in one cycle, a usable shopping cart in the next, and a working payment page after that, each usable when released. This pattern is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery builds the product as a sequence of usable additions, matching a catalog, then a cart, then payment shipped as separate working slices. Iterative delivery would refine one deliverable repeatedly rather than add new features.  Takeaway: Incremental delivery adds usable slices one after another.
choices: Iterative, because a single feature is refined again and again
Big-bang, because everything is released only at the very end
Incremental, because each cycle adds a new usable slice
Predictive, because the scope is fixed and never changes

questions.question: Late in a project, a data-privacy officer who was never engaged blocks the release because a mandatory consent-handling requirement was never captured. Which principle does this best illustrate?
questions.explanation: A missed stakeholder means a missed requirement, and stakeholder identification is ongoing, so the data-privacy officer should have been found and engaged earlier. Locking requirements at kickoff would not have surfaced a person no one identified, and an officer who can block release is clearly a stakeholder.  Takeaway: A missed stakeholder is a missed requirement - keep identifying stakeholders throughout.
choices: Requirements should have been locked at kickoff so that no additional needs could ever surface later.
A missed stakeholder is a missed requirement, so stakeholder identification must continue throughout the project.
A data-privacy officer is not really a project stakeholder and can simply be consulted after release.
The project manager should have personally approved the consent requirement without any further review.

questions.question: At a Sprint's end the developers have finished several backlog items, but none are integrated together or meet the Definition of Done. Do they have a valid increment?
questions.explanation: An increment is a usable, integrated step toward the Product Goal that meets the Definition of Done; unintegrated or not-done work is not a valid increment. It is not merely 'whatever was finished' or the sprint backlog list, and it does not require Sprint Review sign-off to exist - the Sprint Review inspects it, it is not an acceptance gate.  Takeaway: A valid increment is usable, integrated, and meets the Definition of Done.
choices: Yes - any items the team finishes during the Sprint automatically form the increment.
No - an increment must be a usable, integrated piece of product that meets the Definition of Done.
Yes - the increment is simply the list of items the team pulled into the Sprint.
No - an increment exists only after the Sprint Review formally signs off the work.

questions.question: The site's only tower crane is contractually committed to another contractor and is unavailable to your project until March 3, a date that cannot be changed. In planning, this is best treated as...
questions.explanation: A known, fixed limitation on the plan is a constraint, and the crane's confirmed unavailability until March 3 is exactly that. It would be a risk only if the availability were uncertain, nothing has yet gone wrong to make it an issue, and it is a stated fact rather than something taken on faith.  Takeaway: A known, fixed limitation on the plan is a constraint; uncertain availability is a risk.
choices: a constraint, because the crane's unavailability is already known and fixed
a risk, because the crane might yet be released to your project earlier than promised
an assumption, to be validated only once execution has begun
an issue, because it must be escalated to the sponsor right away

questions.question: On one project, a client keeps getting extra reports slipped into scope with no change control, while, separately, an engineer adds an unrequested premium dashboard "to wow the users." What best names these two situations, in that order?
questions.explanation: Scope creep is uncontrolled scope growth without change control regardless of source, so the client-driven additions accepted without change control are scope creep. Gold-plating is the team adding extras the customer never asked for, which is exactly the engineer's unrequested dashboard, so the two situations fall into different categories.  Takeaway: Uncontrolled additions are scope creep; team-added unrequested extras are gold-plating.
choices: Both are gold-plating, because in each case extra features end up added to the product.
Both are scope creep, because in each case the scope grows past the approved baseline.
The client-driven additions are gold-plating, while the engineer's extra dashboard is scope creep.
The client-driven additions are scope creep, while the engineer's extra dashboard is gold-plating.

questions.question: A startup is building a brand-new consumer app whose feature set is expected to evolve continuously as early users give feedback. Requirements are uncertain and change is frequent. Which approach best fits, and why?
questions.explanation: Adaptive approaches earn their value when requirements are uncertain or volatile and change is expected, which is precisely the situation described, so short iterations that incorporate feedback fit best. A fixed budget does not force predictive; suitability turns on requirement stability. Delivering in a few large planned releases describes a predictive cadence, so pairing it with adaptive is internally contradictory.  Takeaway: Uncertain, frequently changing requirements point to an adaptive approach, not predictive.
choices: Predictive, because every software effort should be fully planned before any coding begins
Predictive, because the startup has a fixed launch budget that rules out any change
Adaptive, because the requirements are uncertain and change is expected to be frequent
Adaptive, because consumer products must be handed over in a few large, planned releases

questions.question: In business analysis, which role is accountable for how well a business process performs over the long term, rather than running it day to day?
questions.explanation: The process owner is accountable for a business process's performance and outcomes over time and authorizes changes to it; the process manager operates it day to day. The sponsor funds the project and the Scrum Master coaches the team - neither owns process performance.  Takeaway: Process owner = accountable for the process; process manager = runs it daily.
choices: The process owner, who is accountable for the process's overall performance.
The process manager, who runs the process day to day.
The project sponsor, who funds the project.
The Scrum Master, who coaches the delivery team.

questions.question: A department head claims that adopting agile means the team will have no deadlines, no priorities, and can build whatever it likes. How should this view of the agile mindset be corrected?
questions.explanation: The agile mindset keeps a regular cadence and an ordered backlog so the most valuable work is done first, while staying open to change as the team learns. Claiming agile has no priorities, or that it forbids revising the plan, both misstate the mindset.  Takeaway: Agile keeps cadence and prioritized work while embracing change; it is not the absence of discipline.
choices: The head is entirely correct; agile teams simply work with no deadlines and no priorities at all
Agile teams still work to a cadence and an ordered backlog while responding to change
Agile removes all planning so the team can maximize its raw output
Agile requires a fixed, detailed plan that can never be revised once set

questions.question: Arrange the steps of Tuckman team development in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Tuckman's model describes how teams mature: they Form (orient and stay cautious), Storm (surface conflict over roles and approach), Norm (agree on ways of working), Perform (deliver at high effectiveness), and finally Adjourn (disband when the work ends). Most teams must work through the Storming stage rather than skip it to reach Norming.  Takeaway: Teams typically develop through Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, and Adjourning.
sequence: Forming: members meet and are polite but unsure of roles
Storming: members push against boundaries and conflict surfaces
Norming: the team settles into shared norms and cooperation
Performing: the team works effectively toward its goals
Adjourning: the team completes the work and disbands

questions.question: A game studio builds a rough version of one character model, then repeatedly reworks that same model based on art reviews until it looks right. This way of working is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Iterative work improves the same deliverable through repeated cycles of refinement, which matches reworking one character model until it is right. Incremental work instead adds new, separate usable pieces rather than refining a single artifact.  Takeaway: Iterative refines the same deliverable; incremental adds new usable pieces.
choices: Incremental, because each cycle ships a brand-new, separate feature
Predictive, because the model is frozen right after the first draft
Iterative, because the team refines the same deliverable over successive cycles
Flow-based, because there are no repeating cycles involved at all

questions.question: A team finishing a bike-share station rollout debates what "closing" actually means. Which statement best describes closing in project management terms?
questions.explanation: Closing consists of the activities carried out to formally complete or close the project or a phase, confirming that deliverables are accepted and results are transitioned, so it is a process and set of activities rather than a fixed phase or a single instant. Framing it as always including procurement closeout is wrong because that step applies only when procurements exist.  Takeaway: Closing is a process of formal completion activities, not a mandatory phase or a single moment.
choices: An optional wrap-up step that teams perform only when the customer specifically requests it.
A distinct project phase that always occurs and always includes closing out signed procurements.
The single moment when the last deliverable is built, after which no further work remains at all.
A set of activities performed to formally finish the project or phase and hand off its results.

questions.question: In a 'Transfer Funds' use case, the analyst records that the customer must already be authenticated and hold at least two eligible accounts before the interaction can start. Which part of the use case is being described?
questions.explanation: A precondition is a state that must hold before a use case can begin, such as being authenticated and having eligible accounts. The main success flow is the normal path, an exception flow handles failures, and an actor is a participant rather than a starting condition.  Takeaway: A state that must be true before a use case starts is a precondition.
choices: The main success flow, the normal step-by-step path to the goal
An exception flow, describing what happens when a step fails
A precondition, a state that must be true before the use case begins
An actor, the person or system that initiates the interaction

questions.question: While working on-site, a team member is offered a competitor's confidential pricing document by an acquaintance who says it will help your bid. Under the Code of Ethics, what should the team member do?
questions.explanation: Responsibility and honesty require acting ethically and lawfully and not using information obtained improperly, so declining the confidential document is correct. Accepting it, reading it in secret, or distributing it to the team all rely on information the team member has no right to use.  Takeaway: Do not accept or use confidential information obtained improperly.
choices: Accept and use the document, since winning the bid benefits the project.
Accept it but only read it privately without telling anyone about it.
Decline the confidential document, because using it would violate honest and responsible conduct.
Share it with the whole team so the decision is made collectively.

questions.question: While planning a documentary film's post-production schedule, the project manager needs realistic time estimates for editing, color grading, and sound mixing. Who is generally best positioned to provide these estimates?
questions.explanation: Those who will actually perform the work are usually best able to estimate it because they understand the effort and complexity involved, so the editing, grading, and mixing specialists should estimate their own tasks. The sponsor and customer set funding and delivery expectations but are not the source of task-level estimates.  Takeaway: The people doing the work are best positioned to estimate it.
choices: The sponsor, because the sponsor approves the budget and therefore effectively sets the timeline.
The team members who will perform the work, because they best understand what each task requires.
The customer, because the customer ultimately decides the date on which the documentary must ship.
The project manager alone, because estimating is solely a project management responsibility.

questions.question: A startup wants to test whether customers will pay for a new subscription box before investing in a full platform. What is the primary purpose of releasing a minimum viable product first?
questions.explanation: An MVP is the smallest usable version that lets the team test a key assumption and gain validated learning from real users, which reduces the risk of building the wrong thing. It is neither the complete feature set nor a hidden throwaway, and it is not a scope-locking baseline.  Takeaway: An MVP exists to gain validated learning from the smallest usable release, not to ship everything.
choices: To deliver every single planned feature all at once so that costly rework is never needed at any later point
To release the smallest usable version that produces validated learning about a key assumption
To build a throwaway demo that is deliberately never placed in front of real customers
To lock the full product scope into a baseline before any development begins

questions.question: Before eliciting any requirements on a new hospital scheduling initiative, a business analyst decides which elicitation techniques to use, what requirements deliverables to produce, how much detail is needed, and whether the work will follow a predictive or adaptive path. What is the analyst doing?
questions.explanation: Planning the business analysis approach means deciding up front how the analysis work will be conducted: techniques, deliverables, level of detail, and whether the path is predictive or adaptive. Stakeholder analysis identifies who to engage, acceptance criteria define when an item is done, and backlog prioritization orders work; none sets the overall approach.  Takeaway: Planning the business analysis approach decides how the requirements work itself will be carried out before elicitation begins.
choices: Performing a stakeholder analysis
Planning the business analysis approach
Defining acceptance criteria
Prioritizing items in the product backlog

questions.question: A vaccine-storage upgrade must be finished before a fixed, non-negotiable grant expiration date. The team separately notes that the health ministry might tighten cold-chain rules partway through the work. How are the fixed date and the possible rule change best classified, in that order?
questions.explanation: A known, immovable date is a limiting factor and therefore a constraint, while a possible future tightening of the rules is an uncertain future event and therefore a risk. Labeling both the same, or reversing which is which, misapplies the definitions of constraint and risk.  Takeaway: A fixed, known limit is a constraint; a possible future event is a risk.
choices: Both are risks, because each depends on external decisions the team cannot control.
Both are constraints, because each involves an external authority affecting the project.
The fixed date is an uncertain risk, while the possible future rule change firmly limits the work as a constraint.
The fixed date is a constraint that limits the project, while the possible rule change is an uncertain future risk.

questions.question: A business analyst is asked to also set the schedule baseline, approve the budget, and sign the final scope commitment, on the grounds that the analyst knows the requirements best. Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Owning the schedule and scope commitment is project-manager work and approving the budget is the sponsor's, while the analyst's contribution is the requirement activities that inform those decisions. Knowing the requirements does not transfer delivery or funding authority to the analyst, and withholding requirement information would undermine the support the analyst is there to give.  Takeaway: The analyst informs schedule, budget, and scope decisions but does not own them.
choices: The analyst should take on all three responsibilities without hesitation, since knowing the requirements better than anyone else clearly makes the analyst the single right owner of the schedule, the budget, and the final scope commitment.
These belong to the project manager and sponsor; the analyst supports them by eliciting, analyzing, and managing requirements, not by owning schedule, budget, or the commitment.
The analyst should take the schedule and budget but let the product owner sign the scope commitment.
The analyst should refuse to share any requirements information so the roles stay clearly separated.

questions.question: Halfway through a live webinar for 5,000 registrants, the streaming platform crashes and no attendee can view the session right now. How is this best classified?
questions.explanation: An issue is a condition or event that has already happened and requires action now, which fits the streaming platform that is currently down. A risk is a future, uncertain event, so it does not describe something that has already occurred.  Takeaway: Already happened is an issue; future and uncertain is a risk.
choices: A constraint, because the outage now limits what the project team is able to do.
A risk, because the crash could eventually reduce the event's overall attendance.
An assumption, because the team had taken for granted that the stream would stay online.
An issue, because it is a condition that has already occurred and needs resolving now.

questions.question: A developer says a story is finished because the feature works on their machine, but the team's agreed standard also requires code review, passing automated tests, and updated documentation before anything counts as complete. That agreed standard is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: A shared standard for what 'complete' means, applied to every item, is the Definition of Done. Acceptance criteria are specific to one item, and a product backlog is the ordered list of work rather than a completion standard.  Takeaway: The Definition of Done is a broad, shared completion standard applied across all items.
choices: The story's acceptance criteria, which are unique to this single item
A product backlog, the ordered list the team pulls its work from
The Definition of Done, a shared completion standard applied across items
A transition requirement needed only to reach the new state

questions.question: A firm completes a granite war memorial engineered to endure for centuries. A new hire argues it could not have been a project, because a project must be temporary and the memorial will stand for generations. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Temporary describes the endeavor that creates the result, not the durability of the deliverable, so building a long-lasting memorial is still a project. A long service life does not turn the one-time build into operations, and a single structure is not a program.  Takeaway: Temporary refers to the effort, not to how long the result lasts.
choices: The new hire is correct; a deliverable meant to last for generations cannot be the result of a project.
It was really a program, because a monument built to endure must be managed as related components.
Temporary refers to the effort of creating the memorial, not to how long the finished memorial lasts, so it was a project.
It was operations, because the finished memorial will be visited continuously by the public for many years.

questions.question: During refinement, a story cannot begin until a separate authentication story is completed first, forcing a strict build order. Which INVEST characteristic does this most clearly challenge?
questions.explanation: The 'independent' characteristic asks that stories have minimal dependence so they can be sequenced freely; a hard requirement to build another story first challenges that independence. 'Valuable' concerns delivering benefit and 'small' concerns fitting an iteration, neither of which is the issue described.  Takeaway: A hard build-order dependency on another story challenges the 'Independent' of INVEST.
choices: Valuable, because the story delivers no benefit to any user
Independent, because the story depends on another being built first
Estimable, because the effort simply cannot be sized at all
Small, because the story is far too large for one iteration

questions.question: A museum is planning a traveling dinosaur exhibit and wants to document, for each key stakeholder, how engaged they are today compared with how engaged the project needs them to be. Which tool captures this current-versus-desired comparison?
questions.explanation: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix is built to compare each stakeholder's current engagement with the level the project desires, exposing the gaps to close. The stakeholder register catalogs who stakeholders are and what interests them but does not track the current-versus-desired gap, and the communications plan governs information flow rather than engagement.  Takeaway: Current-versus-desired engagement is tracked in the engagement assessment matrix, not the stakeholder register.
choices: The risk register, because a poorly engaged stakeholder is a threat that must be rated for probability.
The stakeholder register, because it lists every stakeholder's contact details, roles, and interests.
The communications management plan, because it schedules the messages each stakeholder receives.
The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix, because it compares current with desired engagement levels.

questions.question: A scaling startup wants to separate who decides the long-term direction of the product from who is accountable in Scrum for ordering the backlog. Which assignment is correct?
questions.explanation: Product strategy and direction belong to the product manager, while ordering the backlog is a Scrum accountability held by the product owner. The two roles are distinct rather than interchangeable, and neither one funds the product, which is the sponsor's responsibility.  Takeaway: Product manager owns product strategy; product owner is the Scrum accountability that orders the backlog.
choices: The product manager provides the project funding, while the product owner delivers the completed product.
The product owner personally sets the entire long-term product strategy and overall market direction, while the product manager is limited to maintaining the day-to-day order of the sprint backlog.
Either title may take either responsibility, because the two roles are defined identically.
The product manager sets the product's long-term strategy and direction, while the product owner is the Scrum accountability that orders the backlog.

questions.question: While reviewing a schedule for a rooftop beehive installation, an intern points to two entries: "Assemble hive frames" (3 days of work) and "First honey harvest approved" (no work, single date). Which statement correctly classifies these two entries?
questions.explanation: An activity is a distinct piece of scheduled work that consumes time, which fits the 3-day frame assembly, while a milestone is a zero-duration marker of a significant point, which fits the approval event that carries no work. Labeling both entries the same way ignores that only one of them consumes work periods.  Takeaway: Work that consumes time is an activity; a zero-duration significant point is a milestone.
choices: Both are milestones, because each represents progress the team wants to celebrate.
Both are activities, because each appears as its own line on the project schedule.
"Assemble hive frames" is a zero-duration milestone and "First honey harvest approved" is an activity.
"Assemble hive frames" is an activity with duration, and "First honey harvest approved" is a milestone.

questions.question: A holding company's investment board funds, pauses, or cancels a shifting mix of one construction program, several unrelated standalone ventures, and some ongoing rental operations, selecting each component only by how well it advances the company's strategy. The components need not relate to one another. What is this mix?
questions.explanation: A portfolio is a collection of projects, programs, subsidiary portfolios, and operations managed together to achieve strategic objectives, and its components need not be related, which matches this strategy-driven mix. A program requires related components working toward a shared benefit, so it does not fit an intentionally unrelated set.  Takeaway: A strategy-driven mix of possibly unrelated components is a portfolio.
choices: A project phase, because the funding is released to the work in successive stages.
A program, because several related components are managed under one board for a shared benefit.
One large project, because a single board directs and funds all of the work involved.
A portfolio, because it groups projects, programs, and operations chosen to advance strategy.

questions.question: A startup wants to launch a project to build a customer loyalty app. Which responsibility most clearly belongs to the project sponsor?
questions.explanation: The sponsor provides resources and funding and authorizes the project, typically by championing and approving the project charter, which gives the effort its mandate. Detailed estimating is the team's contribution and integrating and delivering the daily work is the project manager's role, neither of which is the sponsor's core responsibility.  Takeaway: The sponsor funds and authorizes the project, chiefly by approving the charter.
choices: Producing the detailed activity estimates for each individual development task on the schedule.
Integrating the work of the team and managing the day-to-day delivery of the finished app.
Providing the funding and authorizing the project by championing and approving the charter.
Writing the application code and testing each feature before it is released to customers.

questions.question: A cost manager is assembling the approved, time-phased budget that performance will be measured against. Which TWO components make up the cost baseline?
questions.explanation: The cost baseline is the approved, time-phased budget: aggregated work package cost estimates plus contingency reserves for identified risks. Management reserves sit outside the baseline for unknown-unknowns, actual costs are execution results, and reporting formats belong to the cost management plan; none of these form the baseline itself.  Takeaway: The cost baseline equals work package estimates plus contingency reserves; management reserve stays outside it.
choices: The aggregated cost estimates of the project's work packages
Contingency reserves set aside for identified risks
Management reserves held outside the baseline for unforeseen work
Actual costs (AC) as they are recorded during execution
The reporting formats and units of measure defined in the cost management plan

questions.question: Two team leads disagree sharply over which testing tool to adopt. Rather than split the difference or defer the choice, the project manager brings them together to surface the underlying needs behind each position and works out a solution both leads fully endorse. Which conflict-resolution approach is this?
questions.explanation: Collaborating, or problem-solving, digs into the interests behind each position to craft a solution both parties genuinely support, and it usually yields the most durable outcome. Compromising would split the difference, leaving each side partly unsatisfied. Smoothing emphasizes points of agreement over the real issue, and forcing imposes one side's view.  Takeaway: Collaborating resolves conflict by addressing the underlying interests to reach a solution both sides own, unlike a compromise that merely splits the difference.
choices: Compromising (bargain to a middle ground)
Collaborating (problem-solving)
Smoothing (accommodating the other side)
Forcing (imposing one side's decision)

questions.question: A team asks how to judge whether a completed backlog item was truly successful. Which measure best reflects success for that item?
questions.explanation: An item is successful when it delivers its intended outcome and satisfies both its acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done. Hours spent, merely starting the item, or its relative size do not establish that the item achieved its purpose.  Takeaway: Task success is delivering the intended outcome, verified by acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done.
choices: The number of hours the team spent building it during the sprint
Whether it was simply moved into the in-progress column on the board
Whether it delivers its intended outcome and meets its acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done
Whether it was the largest item the team happened to complete that sprint

questions.question: Throughout a release, a Product Owner and Developers regularly add detail, split large items, re-estimate, and reorder upcoming backlog items so they are ready for future iterations. What is this ongoing activity called?
questions.explanation: Backlog refinement is the ongoing activity of adding detail, splitting, re-estimating, and reordering upcoming items so they are ready for future iterations. Sprint planning sets up a single sprint, the daily scrum re-plans the day, and the retrospective improves the team's process.  Takeaway: Backlog refinement continuously keeps upcoming items detailed, estimated, and ordered.
choices: Sprint planning, held once at the very start of the whole release
Backlog refinement, an ongoing activity to keep upcoming items ready
The daily scrum, a 15-minute event held by the developers
The retrospective, focused on improving the team's own process

questions.question: During risk planning for a suspension footbridge, a threat is identified that a specialty cable supplier could miss its delivery window. The procurement lead understands that supplier relationship better than anyone on the team. Who should most appropriately be assigned as the risk owner?
questions.explanation: A risk owner is the individual best positioned to monitor the risk and carry out its response, and the procurement lead's insight into the supplier makes that person the natural owner, so ownership is not automatically the project manager's. Assigning every risk to the project manager or the sponsor by default ignores who can actually watch and act on the specific threat.  Takeaway: The risk owner is whoever can best monitor and respond, not automatically the project manager.
choices: The project sponsor, because the sponsor holds ultimate accountability for every project outcome.
The project manager, because the project manager owns every risk on the project by default.
The procurement lead, because the person best positioned to monitor and respond should own the risk.
The whole project team collectively, so that responsibility for the threat is shared across everyone.

questions.question: An analyst moving from a predictive program to an adaptive one asks how requirements will be handled differently. Which description is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Predictive work baselines requirements in a specification early and controls changes formally, while adaptive work keeps requirements emerging and refines the backlog progressively. Business analysis serves the same purpose in both approaches, and the two mechanisms are not reversed.  Takeaway: Predictive baselines a spec up front; adaptive refines the backlog progressively; the BA purpose is the same.
choices: Both approaches baseline every single requirement up front and then change them only through a formal change control board
Adaptive baselines a full specification first, while predictive refines a backlog continuously
Predictive baselines requirements in a spec up front, while adaptive refines them progressively in a backlog
Neither approach documents requirements, because business analysis applies only to predictive work

questions.question: A team ships a usable reporting feature, gathers user feedback, and then reworks that same feature while also adding a new export feature in later cycles. How is this combined way of working best described?
questions.explanation: Adding new usable features while also refining existing ones combines incremental delivery with iterative refinement, a common pattern in adaptive work. Describing it as purely iterative ignores the added export feature, and calling it predictive ignores the ongoing change from feedback.  Takeaway: Many adaptive projects blend incremental delivery with iterative refinement.
choices: It is purely iterative delivery, since no genuinely new features are ever added to the product
It combines incremental delivery of new slices with iterative refinement of existing ones
It is purely predictive, since the scope was fixed at the very start
It is neither iterative nor incremental, because user feedback is used

questions.question: A build plan states, "We assume the imported components will clear customs within five days," and also, "All welding must be performed by certified marine welders." How are these two statements best classified?
questions.explanation: An assumption is something taken to be true without proof, matching the belief that the components will clear customs in five days, while a constraint is a limiting factor, matching the certified-welder requirement. Reversing the two, or forcing both into one category, misapplies the definitions.  Takeaway: Taken as true without proof is an assumption; a limiting factor is a constraint.
choices: Both are constraints, because either statement could restrict how the work is carried out.
Both are assumptions, because each is merely a statement that was written down in the plan.
The customs-clearance statement is an assumption taken as true without proof, while the certified-welder rule is a limiting constraint.
The customs-clearance statement is actually a firm constraint, while the certified-welder rule is really just an assumption.

questions.question: A commercial bakery bakes and delivers the same sourdough loaves to 200 grocery stores every morning on a fixed route. Separately, it assembles a small team to design and open its first standalone cafe by a set opening date. How are these two efforts best classified?
questions.explanation: Operations are ongoing, repetitive work that sustains the business, so the recurring morning deliveries are operations, while a temporary endeavor that creates a unique result is a project, which fits opening the first cafe. Treating recurring deliveries as a project misreads temporary, and calling both operations ignores the one-time, unique nature of the cafe launch.  Takeaway: Ongoing repetitive work is operations; a temporary effort with a unique result is a project.
choices: Both are projects, because each is carefully planned and delivers value the bakery's customers will appreciate.
The daily loaf deliveries are operations because they are ongoing and repetitive, while opening the first cafe is a temporary, unique project.
The daily loaf deliveries are a project because they follow a strict route, while later running the finished cafe is the true operations work.
Both are operations, because the bakery performs each of them as part of running its normal everyday business.

questions.question: During release planning, executives insist the business analyst personally rank the initiative's benefits and commit the company to which outcomes it will pursue. What is the analyst's most appropriate stance?
questions.explanation: The analyst elicits and analyzes information to inform the choice, but deciding which benefits and value the organization pursues belongs to the business decision-makers. The project manager delivers the project rather than owning benefit selection, and withholding analysis removes the very support the analyst exists to provide.  Takeaway: The analyst informs value and benefit decisions; the business owns them.
choices: Accept full ownership of the benefit ranking and the commitment, since analyzing the requirements in careful detail makes the analyst the natural and rightful owner of the organization's business value.
Delegate the ranking to the project manager, who holds final authority over which benefits the organization pursues.
Decline to provide any analysis at all, so the executives are forced to decide with no input.
Provide analysis of value, risk, and feasibility to inform the ranking, while the business decision-makers own which benefits to pursue.

questions.question: Match each procurement document to its purpose.
questions.explanation: An RFI only gathers market and capability information; no award follows directly. An RFQ seeks a price for standard items, while an RFP invites full solutions to a complex need. The SOW is not a solicitation at all; it describes the work so sellers can respond. Swapping RFQ (price) and RFP (solution) is the frequent mistake.  Takeaway: RFI gathers information, RFQ asks for price, RFP asks for a solution, and the SOW defines the work itself.
pairs: Request for Information (RFI)
Gathers general market and seller-capability data before a purchase decision
Request for Quotation (RFQ)
Asks sellers for a price on well-defined, standard items
Request for Proposal (RFP)
Invites detailed solution proposals for a complex or ill-defined need
Statement of Work (SOW)
Describes the work to be procured in enough detail for sellers to respond

questions.question: A retailer's analyst documents how the current manual returns process works today, then maps how leadership wants returns to work after a new system is in place, and identifies the specific capabilities missing between the two. Which technique is being used?
questions.explanation: Gap analysis compares the current state with the desired future state to reveal the capabilities that must be added to close the difference. Variance analysis compares planned versus actual performance, not current versus future state. Root cause analysis finds why a problem occurs, and interface analysis examines system connections.  Takeaway: Gap analysis measures the distance between the current state and the desired future state to define what must change.
choices: Variance analysis
Root cause analysis
Gap analysis
Interface analysis

questions.question: A hospital redesigning its patient-discharge process needs to name who is accountable for how well discharge performs overall versus who runs discharge each shift. Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Accountability for a process's overall performance rests with the process owner, while day-to-day operation is the process manager's job. The first pairing reverses those responsibilities, and the others hand process accountability to roles that do not hold it.  Takeaway: The process owner is accountable for the process; the process manager runs it day to day.
choices: The process manager is the one held accountable for how well the discharge process performs overall, while the process owner merely runs the process during each individual shift.
The process owner is accountable for how well discharge performs overall, while the process manager runs it each shift.
The sponsor is accountable for the discharge process, while the business analyst runs it each shift.
The product owner is accountable for the discharge process, while the project manager runs it each shift.

questions.question: A government agency must build a bridge to a fixed, code-mandated design whose requirements are well understood and very unlikely to change. Which development approach fits best?
questions.explanation: A predictive, plan-based approach suits work whose requirements are clear and stable early, letting scope, schedule, and cost be defined up front. Adaptive and iterative approaches are chosen when requirements are expected to change, which is the opposite of this stable, fixed design.  Takeaway: Stable, well-defined requirements favor a predictive approach.
choices: Adaptive, because well-understood requirements still call for frequent iterations.
Predictive, because the scope can be defined up front and change is expected to be minimal.
Iterative, because a fixed design must be reworked over repeated cycles.
Extreme programming, because a public authority is the customer.

questions.question: Match each schedule dependency type to its description.
questions.explanation: Mandatory (hard logic) is physically required by the work; discretionary (soft logic) is merely preferred and can be resequenced. External ties the project to something outside it, such as a permit, while internal ties two project activities the team controls. Mandatory is easily confused with internal, but one is about necessity and the other about location.  Takeaway: Mandatory versus discretionary asks 'is it required?'; external versus internal asks 'is it inside the team's control?'
pairs: Mandatory dependency
Inherent in the work itself, such as building walls only after the foundation is poured
Discretionary dependency
Based on best practice or team preference, not physically required
External dependency
Between a project activity and a non-project factor, such as a regulator's permit
Internal dependency
Between two project activities and within the team's own control

questions.question: A hospital's new patient check-in kiosk project is wrapping up. The kiosks are built, tested, and accepted by the customer. What is a key closing activity the project manager must ensure happens next?
questions.explanation: A core part of closing is transitioning the final product, service, or result, along with the documentation needed to sustain it, to the group that will operate it, so handing the accepted kiosks to operations is the right next activity. A project is temporary, so the project manager does not run the product forever, and reopening scope at closure invites uncontrolled change.  Takeaway: Closing includes transitioning accepted deliverables and their documentation to the operating group.
choices: Reopen the scope baseline so late enhancement ideas from staff can still be added before finishing.
Keep the full project team staffed indefinitely so they can run the kiosks day to day going forward.
Convert the temporary project into an ongoing operation managed permanently by the project manager.
Transition the accepted kiosks and their supporting documentation to the operations team that will run them.

questions.question: At the end of a sprint the increment falls short of being valuable and usable. A director wants to blame a single developer. Where does Scrum place accountability for a valuable increment?
questions.explanation: Scrum makes the whole Scrum Team accountable for creating a valuable, usable increment each sprint, so accountability is shared rather than pinned on one person. The Scrum Master and Product Owner have their own accountabilities, but neither is singled out as the sole owner of the increment.  Takeaway: The whole Scrum Team, not one individual, is accountable for a valuable increment.
choices: With the Scrum Master alone, who must personally guarantee the increment each sprint
With the whole Scrum Team, which is accountable for creating a valuable, usable increment
With the Product Owner alone, who must build the increment during the sprint
With the individual developer whose name is on the last code commit

questions.question: A backlog contains 'Loyalty Program,' a large initiative that will be split into many smaller items across several releases, and 'Redeem points at checkout,' one specific capability within it. How should these be labeled?
questions.explanation: An epic is a large body of work that is decomposed into smaller items, while a feature is a specific capability the product offers, so the broad initiative is the epic and the specific capability is the feature. An epic is not the same as a feature, and not every splittable item is an epic.  Takeaway: An epic is large and gets decomposed; a feature is a single capability within it; the two are not the same.
choices: 'Loyalty Program' is a feature and 'Redeem points at checkout' is the epic that contains it
'Loyalty Program' is an epic and 'Redeem points at checkout' is a feature within it
Both are epics, because any item that can be split further is by definition an epic
Both are features, because every capability the product offers is called a feature

questions.question: A backlog item passes all of its own written conditions, but the team's standard security scan has not been run on it. A stakeholder says the item is done because it met its conditions. What is the most accurate response?
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are specific to one item, while the Definition of Done is a broader standard every increment must meet, so an item that skips a required security scan is not done even after passing its own conditions. Acceptance criteria do not override the Definition of Done, and the Definition of Done is not exclusive to any one framework.  Takeaway: An item is done only when it meets both its acceptance criteria and the broader Definition of Done.
choices: It is not done yet, because an item must meet both its acceptance criteria and the broader Definition of Done
It is done, because acceptance criteria always override the team's Definition of Done
It is done, because the Definition of Done applies only in Kanban and not here
It is not done, because the item's acceptance criteria and the team's Definition of Done are exactly the same checklist

questions.question: A quality analyst finds that a small number of defect causes account for most of the defects. Applying the Pareto principle, where should improvement effort go first?
questions.explanation: The Pareto principle (roughly 80/20) holds that most effects come from a few causes, so effort should target the 'vital few' causes producing most defects for the biggest improvement. Spreading effort evenly, starting with trivial causes, or reacting to recency ignores where the impact actually concentrates.  Takeaway: Pareto: tackle the vital few causes that create most of the defects first.
choices: At the few 'vital' causes that generate most of the defects, for the greatest impact
Evenly across every cause, so each receives exactly the same attention
At the many minor causes first, because there are more of them to fix
At whichever cause was reported most recently, regardless of its impact

questions.question: In a predictive project, detailed requirements were captured in a large specification produced up front. On an adaptive project, how is that detailed scope primarily developed instead?
questions.explanation: Adaptive scope is expressed as backlog items whose detail is elaborated progressively, just in time as items near development, rather than fully specified up front. Producing a complete specification first or freezing scope contradicts the adaptive intent to respond to learning.  Takeaway: Adaptive scope is elaborated just in time as backlog items, not fully specified up front.
choices: By producing an even larger, complete specification before any work starts
By freezing all scope after the first planning session and never revising it
As backlog items that are elaborated just in time as they near development
By letting each developer build whatever seems useful without any backlog

questions.question: Arrange the risk management processes in order.
questions.explanation: Risk work starts with Plan Risk Management (how risk will be handled), then Identify Risks, then prioritize them in qualitative analysis. Quantitative analysis - used for the most significant risks and not performed on every project - can follow. Responses are planned, then implemented, and risks are monitored throughout. Quantitative follows qualitative, and implementation precedes ongoing monitoring.  Takeaway: Plan, identify, qualify, (optionally) quantify, plan responses, implement them, then monitor throughout.
sequence: Plan Risk Management
Identify Risks
Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis
Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis
Plan Risk Responses
Implement Risk Responses
Monitor Risks

questions.question: A team is about to begin a new sprint. What is the main purpose of Sprint Planning?
questions.explanation: Sprint Planning is where the team agrees a sprint goal, selects the backlog items it will work on, and plans how the work will be done. Improving teamwork happens in the retrospective, the daily progress check is the daily scrum, and formal sign-off is not the purpose of planning.  Takeaway: Sprint Planning sets the sprint goal, selects items, and plans the work.
choices: To let stakeholders formally sign off on the finished product before release
To improve how the team worked together during the previous sprint
To hold a 15-minute daily check on progress toward the sprint goal
To agree a sprint goal, select backlog items, and plan how to do the work

questions.question: A city approves a project to install public electric-vehicle chargers. What is the primary purpose of the project charter for this effort?
questions.explanation: The project charter formally authorizes the existence of the project and grants the project manager the authority to apply organizational resources to the work, providing the mandate to proceed. Detailed activity plans, final acceptance records, and engagement comparisons are produced by other documents, not the charter.  Takeaway: The charter formally authorizes the project and empowers the PM to apply resources.
choices: To list every activity, estimate, and cost needed to install all of the chargers in full detail.
To formally authorize the project and give the project manager authority to apply organizational resources.
To record the signed acceptance of the finished chargers by the city at the very end of the project.
To compare each stakeholder's current engagement with the level of engagement the project desires.

questions.question: A backlog item has only modest business value on its own, but a new regulation makes it legally required by a hard deadline, and missing it would expose the company to heavy fines. How should the Product Owner treat it when ordering the backlog?
questions.explanation: Backlog order reflects overall priority, which weighs value together with risk, urgency, dependencies, and effort, so a legally required item with a hard deadline and heavy fines rises even when its own value is modest. Ordering by raw value alone or removing the item ignores the risk and urgency that drive its priority.  Takeaway: Backlog order weighs value with risk and urgency; a high-risk, time-critical item rises even at modest value.
choices: Place it near the bottom, since ordering should follow raw business value alone
Place it high, because ordering weighs value together with risk and urgency, not value alone
Remove it from the backlog, since it is not the single highest-value item there
Delay it until a change control board formally approves the new regulation first

questions.question: The communications management plan for an e-sports arena build states that stakeholders receive a status report by email every Friday. Midway through the project, a stakeholder phones asking why he has not gotten an update. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: When a communications management plan already defines how and when information is shared, the project manager follows that plan, so the response is to ensure the agreed Friday reports are going out on schedule. Inventing a separate channel or discarding the plan for everyone abandons an agreed approach the team should be executing.  Takeaway: When a communications plan defines the approach, follow it rather than improvise new channels.
choices: Create a brand-new reporting method just for that stakeholder, separate from the existing plan.
Escalate the complaint to the sponsor as a communications risk that requires a formal decision.
Follow the communications plan and confirm the agreed Friday email reports are being sent as scheduled.
Stop the weekly reports entirely and switch every stakeholder to on-demand phone updates instead.

questions.question: A story arrives pre-written with exact screen layouts, field labels, and button colors, leaving the team no room to discuss how best to meet the need. Which INVEST characteristic is most clearly missing?
questions.explanation: The 'negotiable' characteristic treats a story as a placeholder for a later conversation rather than a rigid contract; specifying every design detail up front removes that room to negotiate. 'Testable' concerns being able to confirm the story is met, and 'independent' concerns ordering dependencies.  Takeaway: Locking every detail up front, leaving no room to discuss, fails the 'Negotiable' of INVEST.
choices: Negotiable, because the details are locked with no room for discussion
Testable, because there is no way to confirm the story is satisfied
Independent, because the story relies on another story being built first
Valuable, because the story provides no benefit to any user

questions.question: An approved scope change needs a durable, auditable record of exactly what was agreed and by whom. Which communication approach best fits?
questions.explanation: Decisions that must be traceable and defensible call for formal written communication, which preserves an auditable record of what was agreed. A hallway chat leaves no record, a push notification is for broad awareness not a formal record, and an informal chat message is not an authoritative record.  Takeaway: Need a durable, auditable record -> use formal written communication.
choices: Formal written communication that creates a durable, auditable record.
A quick hallway conversation with the stakeholder.
A brief push notification on a dashboard.
An informal message in a team group chat.

questions.question: An activity has Early Start (ES) = 12, Early Finish (EF) = 18, Late Start (LS) = 16, and Late Finish (LF) = 22 (day-numbering where EF = ES + duration - 1). What is its total float?
questions.explanation: Total float = LS - ES = 16 - 12 = 4 days, which also equals LF - EF = 22 - 18 = 4 days. A value of 0 would place the activity on the critical path, which the gap between its early and late dates rules out. Seven days is the activity duration (EF - ES + 1), and 10 days comes from subtracting ES from LF, neither of which is the float formula.  Takeaway: Total float = LS - ES = LF - EF; zero total float marks a critical activity.
choices: 4 days
0 days
7 days
10 days

questions.question: A greenhouse-automation team identified earlier that a key sensor supplier might be delayed, and they planned a response: switch to a pre-qualified backup supplier if a shipment slips. The shipment now slips. What should the team do?
questions.explanation: When a risk that was analyzed already has a planned response, the team follows that response as the risk occurs, so moving to the pre-qualified backup supplier is the correct action. Improvising a workaround is reserved for unplanned risks, and re-logging an already-identified risk or reflexively escalating ignores the response the team deliberately prepared.  Takeaway: When a planned response exists for a risk that occurs, execute the plan rather than improvise.
choices: Treat the delay as a brand-new problem and improvise a fresh solution on the spot without the plan.
Execute the planned response by switching to the pre-qualified backup supplier exactly as agreed.
Escalate immediately to the sponsor for a decision, since any delay changes the project's direction.
Log the delay in the risk register as a newly discovered risk and continue to watch it for now.

questions.question: A craft distillery brainstorms for a new export project using SWOT. It groups "award-winning master distiller" with "aging warehouse near capacity," and groups "rising overseas demand" with "new import tariffs." Which reading correctly reflects SWOT?
questions.explanation: SWOT separates internal factors (strengths and weaknesses) from external factors (opportunities and threats), so the master distiller (a strength) and the near-full warehouse (a weakness) are internal, while overseas demand (an opportunity) and import tariffs (a threat) arise outside the organization. Mixing internal and external items across the groupings misapplies the framework.  Takeaway: SWOT groups strengths and weaknesses as internal, opportunities and threats as external.
choices: All four items are strengths, because a SWOT analysis focuses only on the positive project factors.
The distiller and the tariffs are internal factors, while the warehouse and the demand are external factors.
The demand and the tariffs are internal factors, while the distiller and the warehouse are external factors.
The distiller and the warehouse are internal factors, while the demand and the tariffs are external factors.

questions.question: A newly assigned project manager for a solar carport installation is asked whether she can sign her own project charter to get started faster. What is the most accurate view of her authority?
questions.explanation: The project manager often helps develop the charter and then integrates and delivers the work, but the authority to authorize the project rests with the sponsor, so a project manager does not self-authorize by signing her own charter. Barring her from contributing to the charter is also wrong, since she commonly helps develop it.  Takeaway: A PM may help write the charter but cannot self-authorize; the sponsor authorizes the project.
choices: She may help develop the charter, but the sponsor authorizes it; she does not authorize her own project.
She should sign the charter herself, since the project manager holds final authority over the project.
She cannot touch the charter at all, because only the project team is permitted to draft that document.
She must wait for the customer to write and sign the charter before any project work can begin.

questions.question: A project manager must notify 400 store employees that the timekeeping system changes over this weekend. No discussion is needed - only broad, timely awareness. Which method is most efficient?
questions.explanation: Push communication such as a bulk email or broadcast sends one-way awareness to a large audience quickly and by the deadline. Individual meetings do not scale to 400 people, pull methods risk employees never checking, and a workshop is for building agreement rather than announcing a decided change.  Takeaway: Use push communication to broadcast timely awareness to a large audience.
choices: Individual interactive meetings held with each of the 400 employees.
Pull communication that waits for each employee to look up the change on a portal.
Push communication, such as a bulk announcement email or an intranet broadcast.
A negotiation workshop that brings all 400 employees together to agree on the change.

questions.question: For a single 'upload profile photo' story, the product owner writes: 'accepts JPG and PNG up to 5 MB; rejects other formats with an error; displays the new photo immediately.' What is this an example of?
questions.explanation: Specific, testable conditions written for one backlog item are acceptance criteria. The Definition of Done is a broader standard applied across all items, and a roadmap theme shows direction over time rather than item-level pass or fail conditions.  Takeaway: Acceptance criteria are specific, testable, per-item conditions for accepting one story.
choices: Acceptance criteria, the specific testable conditions for accepting this one story
A Definition of Done, the shared standard applied to every backlog item
A non-functional requirement covering the entire product's quality attributes
A product roadmap theme showing the direction of the work over time

questions.question: What does a work breakdown structure (WBS) represent on a predictive project?
questions.explanation: The WBS is a deliverable-oriented hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work the team must carry out to meet objectives, and that scope includes project-management work, not just the product. A time-ordered list of activities with dependencies is the schedule, and a chart of reporting relationships is an organizational breakdown. Excluding project-management work would leave the WBS short of the full authorized scope.  Takeaway: The WBS decomposes 100 percent of the authorized scope, including project-management work, not just product deliverables.
choices: A time-ordered list of activities with their durations and dependencies
A chart of the reporting relationships among team members
Only the tangible product deliverables, deliberately excluding project-management work
A hierarchical decomposition of the total authorized scope, including project-management work

questions.question: A flash flood damages a road that a bridge-inspection crew needed to reach the site, an event no one had identified or planned for. With work halted, what is the most appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: A workaround is an unplanned response developed to deal with a risk that was not previously identified or for which no response existed, which fits an unforeseen flood that has already struck. Following a nonexistent contingency plan is impossible for an unidentified risk, and waiting passively lets the impact grow unchecked.  Takeaway: An unidentified risk that occurs calls for a workaround; a planned risk calls for its planned response.
choices: Follow the contingency plan already written for this exact flooding scenario in the risk register.
Do nothing until the next scheduled risk review, since only previously logged risks warrant a response.
Record the flood as an accepted risk and simply wait for the water to recede on its own timeline.
Develop a workaround, because an unplanned event that has occurred requires an unplanned response.

questions.question: A company is migrating its accounting system to comply with a new tax-reporting regulation whose rules are fully published in advance. Requirements are fixed, the technical solution is well understood, and little change is expected during the work. Which development approach best fits?
questions.explanation: A predictive, plan-based approach fits work whose scope is defined up front and stable, whose solution is well understood, and where change is unlikely, so it can be planned in detail and executed against baselines. Adaptive approaches earn their value under uncertainty and volatility, which is the opposite of the stability described, so treating all software or all regulated work as adaptive is wrong. Wanting frequent demos is a signal for an adaptive cadence, not a reason to choose predictive.  Takeaway: Predictive fits stable, well-defined scope with low expected change; uncertainty and frequent demos point to adaptive.
choices: Predictive, because the requirements are fully specified up front and little change is expected
Adaptive, because every software effort benefits from frequent short iterations
Adaptive, because complying with a published regulation requires continuous re-planning
Predictive, because the sponsor wants a working demo at the end of each week

questions.question: Customers are abandoning an online checkout at a high rate, and executives want to add new payment buttons immediately. Before recommending any solution, the analyst investigates why abandonment is really happening and traces it to surprise shipping costs shown late in the flow. Which technique is the analyst applying?
questions.explanation: Root cause analysis digs beneath the visible symptom to find the underlying cause of a business problem before solutions are chosen: here, surprise shipping costs rather than missing payment options. Gap analysis contrasts current and future states, solution evaluation judges a delivered solution, and prioritization only orders work without diagnosing the cause.  Takeaway: Root cause analysis identifies why a problem truly occurs so effort targets the cause rather than the symptom.
choices: Root cause analysis
Gap analysis
Solution evaluation
Requirements prioritization

questions.question: A Kanban team wants measures that reflect how quickly and how much work flows through its system. Which TWO measures are appropriate for this purpose? (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Cycle time captures how long an item takes from start to done, and throughput captures how many items are completed per unit of time, so both reflect flow. Counting meetings attended or documentation pages measures activity rather than flow, and Kanban does not require reporting a story-point total.  Takeaway: Kanban measures flow with cycle time and throughput, not activity counts.
choices: Cycle time, the time an item takes from work starting until it is done
The number of daily stand-up meetings the team attended this week
Throughput, the number of items completed per unit of time
The count of story points the team is required to report to leadership
The number of pages in the team's written process documentation

questions.question: A project has two parts: a hardware installation with fixed, well-known steps, and a mobile interface whose features are still uncertain and likely to change. Which way of working is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Tailoring lets the team apply a predictive approach to the stable, well-known hardware steps and an adaptive approach to the uncertain, changing interface, matching each method to its part. Forcing one method onto both parts, or dropping needed scope, ignores the different levels of uncertainty.  Takeaway: Tailor the approach to each part's uncertainty; predictive and adaptive can be combined in one project.
choices: Use a fully predictive plan for both parts to keep one consistent method
Use a fully adaptive approach for both parts to avoid any up-front planning
Cancel the uncertain mobile interface entirely so that the whole project can be run as fully predictive
Tailor the approach: predictive for the fixed hardware and adaptive for the uncertain interface

questions.question: A design team builds a rough version of one feature, gets feedback, and reworks that same feature repeatedly until it is right, before moving on. Which approach best describes this?
questions.explanation: Iterative work refines the same thing over successive passes as understanding improves. Incremental work instead adds a new usable slice each cycle; predictive fixes scope up front; big-bang releases everything at the end. Refining one feature repeatedly is iterative (most agile blends iterative and incremental).  Takeaway: Iterative = refine the same thing repeatedly; incremental = add new slices.
choices: Iterative delivery, because the same feature is refined repeatedly through feedback.
Incremental delivery, because each cycle adds a different usable slice.
Predictive delivery, because the design is fixed up front and never revised.
Big-bang delivery, because everything is built and released at once.

questions.question: Three months into a project, a new regional office opens that the solution must also serve, and the analyst adds its manager to the stakeholder register. How should this be viewed?
questions.explanation: Identifying stakeholders is a continuous activity, so registering a newly relevant office manager is exactly right. The register is not locked at charter signing, an office the solution must serve is a stakeholder, and adding one does not require re-signing the charter.  Takeaway: Stakeholder identification is ongoing; add new stakeholders whenever they emerge.
choices: As an error, because the stakeholder register is locked once the charter is signed.
As unnecessary, because regional offices are never considered project stakeholders.
As sound practice, because stakeholder identification is ongoing and new stakeholders can emerge at any time.
As acceptable only after the project sponsor formally reopens, revises, and personally re-signs the entire project charter first.

questions.question: On a predictive project, a schedule baseline is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: A schedule baseline is the approved version of the schedule against which performance is measured, and it can be changed only through formal change control. It is controlled rather than frozen, so calling it unchangeable is inaccurate. Actual progress dates are compared against the baseline but are not the baseline, and a draft made before approval has not yet become a baseline.  Takeaway: A baseline is an approved, controlled plan changed only through formal change control, not a frozen document.
choices: The most recent set of actual progress dates recorded to date
The approved version of the schedule, changed only through formal change control
A schedule permanently frozen so that it can never be altered under any circumstances
An informal draft schedule prepared before stakeholder review

questions.question: A team member reports to both a functional manager and the project manager, with authority shared roughly equally between them. What is the most common challenge of this balanced-matrix arrangement?
questions.explanation: A balanced matrix splits authority between the functional and project managers, so team members answer to two bosses and face competing demands on their time - its classic drawback. The other options describe projectized or functional structures, not a balanced matrix.  Takeaway: Balanced matrix = shared authority and the two-boss / competing-priorities problem.
choices: Team members effectively have two bosses, creating competing priorities for their time.
The project manager has total authority, so resource conflicts never occur.
There is no functional manager involved, so technical guidance is missing.
The team reports only to the project manager, eliminating any dual reporting.
